title: Week 2: Decision Theory and Graphical Models
text:
From inference to decision
Overview. Week 1 showed how to estimate a joint distribution p(x,c) from data. This lecture asks the next question: once we have that distribution, or an estimate of it, how do we actually act on it? We build up statistical decision theory from misclassification rate to a general loss-based discriminant rule, then do the same for regression. The second half returns to a problem from Week 1: a joint over N binary variables needs 2^N-1 parameters in general. Directed graphical models are a way to write down which conditional independencies we are willing to assume, and get a much smaller parameter count in return. The Bayes Ball algorithm reads those independencies directly off the graph. The tutorial’s Naive Bayes classifier ties the two halves together: it is a graphical model whose independence assumption is exactly what makes its maximum likelihood estimate as simple as Week 1’s Bernoulli MLE.
There were no logistics slides to skip this week.
Suppose we want to decide whether a chest X-ray shows cancer. Call the pixel intensities x and the class c, with \mathcal{C}_1 for cancer present and \mathcal{C}_2 for cancer absent. Estimating the joint p(x,c) from training data, as in Week 1, is called inference. But estimating the joint is not the same task as acting on it: at the end, we must commit to one decision (treat, or do not treat) for each new X-ray.
Given a new image, one route to the class is Bayes’ theorem (Worked example: a diagnostic test, Week 1):
p(\mathcal{C}_k \mid x) = \frac{p(x \mid \mathcal{C}_k)\, p(\mathcal{C}_k)}{p(x)}.
If our goal is to minimize the expected number of mistakes, this suggests picking whichever class has the largest posterior p(\mathcal{C}_k \mid x). The next section makes this precise, then asks whether “count of mistakes” is even the right thing to minimize.
crumbs: 4  Week 2: Decision Theory and Graphical Models

title: Week 2: Decision Theory and Graphical Models
text:
TipRecap: From inference to decision





What the symbols stand for:

x: the input (the pixel intensities of one X-ray).
\mathcal{C}_k: class k. Here \mathcal{C}_1 is cancer present and \mathcal{C}_2 is cancer absent.
p(\mathcal{C}_k): the prior, how common class k is before we look at the image.
p(x \mid \mathcal{C}_k): the class-conditional, how likely this image is if the class is k.
p(\mathcal{C}_k \mid x): the posterior, how likely class k is after seeing the image.

Taking Bayes’ theorem apart:

The numerator p(x \mid \mathcal{C}_k)\,p(\mathcal{C}_k) is the joint p(x, \mathcal{C}_k): “this class, and this image”.
The denominator p(x) = \sum_k p(x \mid \mathcal{C}_k)\,p(\mathcal{C}_k) is the same for every class. It only rescales the numerators so the posteriors sum to 1, so it never changes which class is largest.

A teaching example. Suppose for one image p(x \mid \mathcal{C}_1) = 0.3 with prior p(\mathcal{C}_1) = 0.1, and p(x \mid \mathcal{C}_2) = 0.05 with prior p(\mathcal{C}_2) = 0.9. The numerators are 0.03 and 0.045, so p(x) = 0.075 and the posteriors are 0.4 (cancer) and 0.6 (no cancer). The image fits cancer six times better, but the low prior still leaves “no cancer” as the larger posterior. Whether we should act on that larger posterior is what the following sections examine.

title: Week 2: Decision Theory and Graphical Models
text:
Misclassification rate

Definition. A decision region \mathcal{R}_k is a subset of the input space such that every x \in \mathcal{R}_k is assigned to class \mathcal{C}_k. The decision regions partition the input space.

For a single continuous input and two classes, a decision rule reduces to one cut point. Call it \hat x, the decision boundary: everything left of \hat x falls in \mathcal{R}_1 and is assigned to \mathcal{C}_1, everything at or right of \hat x falls in \mathcal{R}_2 and is assigned to \mathcal{C}_2. Sliding \hat x left or right trades one kind of error for the other: moving it right shrinks \mathcal{R}_2 and enlarges \mathcal{R}_1, so fewer points are wrongly called \mathcal{C}_2 but more are wrongly called \mathcal{C}_1, and vice versa. The question this section answers is which placement of \hat x minimizes the total probability of a mistake.
For two classes, the probability of a mistake is the probability that x lands in the wrong region:
p(\text{mistake}) = I_1 + I_2,
I_1 = \int_{\mathcal{R}_1} p(x, \mathcal{C}_2)\,dx,
I_2 = \int_{\mathcal{R}_2} p(x, \mathcal{C}_1)\,dx.
I_1 is the probability of assigning \mathcal{C}_1 when the true class is \mathcal{C}_2; I_2 is the other direction.
Since the regions are disjoint, we can minimize this quantity region by region: for a given x, assign it to \mathcal{C}_1 whenever p(x,\mathcal{C}_1) > p(x,\mathcal{C}_2), and to \mathcal{C}_2 otherwise. Using the product rule p(x,\mathcal{C}_k) = p(\mathcal{C}_k \mid x)\,p(x), this is the same as assigning x to whichever class has the larger posterior p(\mathcal{C}_k \mid x). That confirms the rule suggested in the previous section, and shows it is optimal for this particular objective: the best placement for \hat x is exactly the point where p(x,\mathcal{C}_1) = p(x,\mathcal{C}_2), the crossing of the two densities. Moving \hat x away from that crossing in either direction only grows the mistake probability, because it starts including a stretch of x on the wrong side of the posterior comparison.


  Decision regions from two overlapping densities
  
  
  
  boundary
  
  R1: assign to C1
  
  R2: assign to C2
  
  x


Figure 1. Two overlapping class densities p(x,\mathcal{C}_1) (blue) and p(x,\mathcal{C}_2) (magenta). Moving the boundary changes how much of each tail falls on the wrong side; the misclassification-minimizing boundary sits where the two densities cross.






TipRecap: Misclassification rate





What the symbols stand for:

\mathcal{R}_1, \mathcal{R}_2: the decision regions, the inputs we label \mathcal{C}_1 and \mathcal{C}_2.
\hat x: the decision boundary between them, for a one-dimensional input.
p(x, \mathcal{C}_k): the joint density of seeing input x with true class k.
I_1, I_2: the two kinds of error probability.

Taking the equations apart:

I_1 = \int_{\mathcal{R}_1} p(x, \mathcal{C}_2)\,dx: integrate over the region where we say \mathcal{C}_1, but use the density of the other class. That adds up the probability of every input we call \mathcal{C}_1 that is really \mathcal{C}_2.
I_2 is the mirror image: inputs we call \mathcal{C}_2 that are really \mathcal{C}_1.
p(\text{mistake}) = I_1 + I_2 because the two kinds of error cannot happen at once.
Each x lands in exactly one region, so the best choice can be made one x at a time: put x in the region of the class with the larger joint p(x, \mathcal{C}_k).

A teaching example. Replace the continuous x with three bins, so integrals become sums. The joint is p(x, \mathcal{C}_1) = 0.30, 0.20, 0.05 and p(x, \mathcal{C}_2) = 0.05, 0.10, 0.30 for bins 1, 2, 3 (all six numbers sum to 1).

Boundary after bin 2, so \mathcal{R}_1 = \{1, 2\}: I_1 = 0.05 + 0.10 = 0.15 and I_2 = 0.05, so p(\text{mistake}) = 0.20.
Boundary after bin 1, so \mathcal{R}_1 = \{1\}: I_1 = 0.05 and I_2 = 0.20 + 0.05 = 0.25, so p(\text{mistake}) = 0.30.

Bin 2 has 0.20 > 0.10, so it belongs with \mathcal{C}_1. Moving the boundary past the crossing point costs 0.10 of extra mistakes, exactly the gap in bin 2.

title: Week 2: Decision Theory and Graphical Models
text:
Expected loss
Minimizing the raw count of mistakes treats every kind of mistake as equally bad, which is rarely realistic. In the cancer-screening example, missing an actual cancer (predicting healthy when the patient is sick) is far worse than a false alarm (predicting cancer when the patient is healthy). The misclassification rate of Misclassification rate cannot tell these two kinds of error apart: it counts them both as one mistake. A loss function fixes this by attaching a separate cost to each combination of true class and decision.

Definition. A loss function assigns a cost L_{kj} to deciding class \mathcal{C}_j when the true class is \mathcal{C}_k (the (k,j) entry of a loss matrix). The expected loss of a choice of decision regions is \mathbb{E}[L] = \sum_k \sum_j \int_{\mathcal{R}_j} L_{kj}\, p(x, \mathcal{C}_k)\, dx.

Read the definition of \mathbb{E}[L] one piece at a time. The double sum \sum_k \sum_j runs over every (true class, decision) pair, so it visits every cell of the loss matrix once. For a fixed pair (k,j), the inner integral \int_{\mathcal{R}_j} p(x,\mathcal{C}_k)\,dx is the probability that x both falls in the region we decide is \mathcal{C}_j and truly belongs to \mathcal{C}_k: exactly the rate at which that particular (k,j) outcome happens. Multiplying by L_{kj} converts that rate into a cost, and summing over every (k,j) pair adds up the cost contributed by every possible outcome, correct calls included (their loss is normally 0, so they drop out). \mathbb{E}[L] is a weighted version of p(\text{mistake}) from Misclassification rate: instead of every error counting for 1, each error counts for whatever L_{kj} says it costs.
For the cancer example, the lecture’s loss matrix charges 1000 for missing an actual cancer (true cancer, decided normal) and only 1 for a false alarm (true normal, decided cancer), with 0 loss for a correct call:







Decision




cancer
normal




Truth
cancer
0
1000


normal
1
0





Plugging this matrix into the definition of \mathbb{E}[L] leaves only two non-zero terms, since L_{\text{cancer},\text{cancer}} = L_{\text{normal},\text{normal}} = 0:
\mathbb{E}[L] = 1000 \int_{\mathcal{R}_{\text{normal}}} p(x,\mathcal{C}_{\text{cancer}})\,dx {}+ \int_{\mathcal{R}_{\text{cancer}}} p(x,\mathcal{C}_{\text{normal}})\,dx.
The first term is the rate of missed cancers, weighted 1000 times over; the second is the rate of false alarms, weighted only once. A decision rule with a higher misclassification rate can still have lower expected loss than one with a lower misclassification rate, if it makes its mistakes on the cheap side (false alarms) rather than the expensive side (misses). This asymmetry pulls the optimal boundary toward calling more borderline cases “cancer”: every point x shifted out of \mathcal{R}_{\text{normal}} and into \mathcal{R}_{\text{cancer}} trades a chance at a 1000-cost miss for at most a 1-cost false alarm, which is a good trade unless that x is overwhelmingly more likely to be a true negative.






TipRecap: Expected loss





What the symbols stand for:

k: the true class. j: the class we decide.
L_{kj}: the cost of deciding j when the truth is k. Row k, column j of the loss matrix. Correct calls (k = j) usually cost 0.
\mathcal{R}_j: the region of inputs where we decide class j.
\mathbb{E}[L]: the average cost per case if we use these regions on many inputs.

Taking the equation apart, from the inside out:

\int_{\mathcal{R}_j} p(x, \mathcal{C}_k)\,dx: the probability that a case is truly k and we decide j.
L_{kj} \times that probability: the average cost contributed by this one (truth, decision) combination.
\sum_k \sum_j: add the contributions of every cell of the loss matrix.

With every error costing 1 and every correct call costing 0, \mathbb{E}[L] becomes p(\text{mistake}) from Misclassification rate.
A teaching example. Use a milder matrix than the lecture’s: a missed cancer costs 10, a false alarm costs 1. Three bins of x have p(x, \text{cancer}) = 0.02, 0.03, 0.05 and p(x, \text{normal}) = 0.60, 0.20, 0.10.

Rule A calls cancer only in bin 3. Misses: 0.02 + 0.03 = 0.05. False alarms: 0.10. \mathbb{E}[L] = 10(0.05) + 1(0.10) = 0.60, with a mistake rate of 0.15.
Rule B calls cancer in bins 2 and 3. Misses: 0.02. False alarms: 0.20 + 0.10 = 0.30. \mathbb{E}[L] = 10(0.02) + 1(0.30) = 0.50, with a mistake rate of 0.32.

Rule B makes more than twice as many mistakes, yet it costs less, because it moves its mistakes to the cheap side.

title: Week 2: Decision Theory and Graphical Models
section: The discriminant rule and the reject option
text:
The discriminant rule and the reject option
Swapping the order of summation in \mathbb{E}[L] and defining g_j(x) = \sum_k L_{kj}\, p(x,\mathcal{C}_k) turns the expected loss into \mathbb{E}[L] = \sum_j \int_{\mathcal{R}_j} g_j(x)\, dx, which is minimized region by region exactly as in Misclassification rate:

\mathcal{R}_j = \{x : g_j(x) < g_i(x) \text{ for all } i \neq j\}.

Using the product rule again, g_j(x) = p(x) \sum_k L_{kj}\, p(\mathcal{C}_k \mid x), and the factor p(x) does not affect which j minimizes it. So the rule can be stated entirely in terms of posteriors:






Note



Discriminant rule. Assign x to the class j that minimizes \sum_k L_{kj}\, p(\mathcal{C}_k \mid x).


Setting every off-diagonal L_{kj} = 1 and every diagonal L_{kk} = 0 recovers the misclassification-rate rule from Misclassification rate as a special case: the loss matrix is a strict generalization, not a different framework.
Some inputs sit in a region of genuine uncertainty, where the posteriors of the leading classes are close. Rather than force a decision, we can decline to decide whenever the largest posterior falls below a threshold \theta. This is the reject option: the reject region is exactly where every p(\mathcal{C}_k \mid x) < \theta.






Note



Practice question. Return to the cancer-screening loss matrix from Expected loss. For a particular X-ray, the estimated posteriors are p(\mathcal{C}_{\text{cancer}} \mid x) = 0.2 and p(\mathcal{C}_{\text{normal}} \mid x) = 0.8. Which decision does the discriminant rule make? Compare this to what the plain misclassification-rate rule from Misclassification rate would decide.
Solution. The discriminant rule compares the two costs \sum_k L_{kj}\,p(\mathcal{C}_k\mid x), one for each candidate decision j: \text{cost(decide cancer)} = L_{\text{cancer,cancer}}(0.2) + L_{\text{normal,cancer}}(0.8) = 0(0.2) + 1(0.8) = 0.8, \text{cost(decide normal)} = L_{\text{cancer,normal}}(0.2) + L_{\text{normal,normal}}(0.8) = 1000(0.2) + 0(0.8) = 200. The rule picks whichever cost is smaller, so it decides cancer, even though p(\mathcal{C}_{\text{cancer}}\mid x) = 0.2 is well under one half. The misclassification-rate rule, which only compares posteriors directly, would have decided normal since 0.8 > 0.2. The two rules disagree precisely because the loss matrix charges 1000 times more for a missed cancer than for a false alarm, so a small chance of cancer is still worth acting on.
Now suppose a second X-ray gives posteriors p(\mathcal{C}_{\text{cancer}}\mid x) = 0.48 and p(\mathcal{C}_{\text{normal}}\mid x) = 0.52, with a reject threshold \theta = 0.6. Neither posterior clears \theta, so the reject option applies: rather than force a call, we decline to decide and send the case for a second test.








TipRecap: The discriminant rule and the reject option





What the symbols stand for:

g_j(x) = \sum_k L_{kj}\,p(x, \mathcal{C}_k): the expected-loss contribution at input x if we decide j there.
\sum_k L_{kj}\,p(\mathcal{C}_k \mid x): the same quantity divided by p(x). It is the expected cost of deciding j for this particular input.
\theta: the reject threshold, the smallest top posterior we are willing to act on. (This \theta is a threshold, not the model parameter \theta from Week 1.)

Taking the rule apart:

For each candidate decision j, walk down column j of the loss matrix. Multiply each cost L_{kj} by how likely that true class is, then add.
Pick the column with the smallest total. That is the decision with the lowest expected cost for this input.
The reject option sits on top: if \max_k p(\mathcal{C}_k \mid x) < \theta, make no decision at all.

A teaching example. Use a matrix where a missed cancer costs 10 and a false alarm costs 1. Write p = p(\text{cancer} \mid x).

Cost of deciding cancer: 1 \cdot (1-p), paid only if the patient is normal.
Cost of deciding normal: 10 \cdot p, paid only if the patient has cancer.

Deciding cancer is cheaper when 1 - p < 10p, which is p > 1/11 \approx 0.091. So a posterior of p = 0.15 gives costs 0.85 (cancer) against 1.5 (normal), and the rule calls cancer. The loss matrix has moved the cut-off from 0.5 to about 0.09. With a reject threshold \theta = 0.7, an image with posteriors 0.65 and 0.35 would be rejected, because neither reaches 0.7.

title: Week 2: Decision Theory and Graphical Models
text:
Loss functions for regression
The same reasoning applies when the target t is continuous rather than a discrete class. Now the joint is p(x,t), and instead of decision regions we look for a regression function y(x) that approximates t. Using the squared loss L(y(x), t) = (y(x)-t)^2, the goal is to minimize
\mathbb{E}[L] = \int\!\!\int (y(x) - t)^2\, p(x,t)\, dx\, dt.
The rest of this section works through that minimization one algebraic step at a time.
Step 1: add and subtract \mathbb{E}[t\mid x]. Adding zero never changes a quantity, and \mathbb{E}[t\mid x] - \mathbb{E}[t\mid x] = 0, so we can insert it inside the square without changing \mathbb{E}[L]:
\mathbb{E}[L] = \int\!\!\int \big(y(x) - \mathbb{E}[t\mid x] + \mathbb{E}[t\mid x] - t\big)^2\, p(x,t)\, dx\, dt.
This looks like it made things worse, but it regroups the single quantity y(x)-t into two pieces, u = y(x) - \mathbb{E}[t\mid x] (how far our predictor is from the conditional mean) and v = \mathbb{E}[t\mid x] - t (how far the conditional mean is from the actual target), so that y(x) - t = u + v.
Step 2: expand the square. Using (u+v)^2 = u^2 + 2uv + v^2 and distributing the double integral over the three resulting terms:
\mathbb{E}[L] = A + B + C,
where
\text{term A} = \int\!\!\int u^2 p(x,t)\,dx\,dt,
\text{term B} = \int\!\!\int v^2 p(x,t)\,dx\,dt,
\text{term C} = 2\int\!\!\int u v\, p(x,t)\,dx\,dt.
Terms A and B are each a squared quantity times a density, so both are non-negative no matter what y(x) is. Term C is the only one whose sign is not yet obvious, which is what the next step settles. Substituting back u = y(x)-\mathbb{E}[t\mid x] and v = \mathbb{E}[t\mid x]-t recovers the expanded integrals if you want them written without u and v.
Step 3: show term C is zero. Factor the joint using the product rule, p(x,t) = p(t\mid x)\,p(x), exactly the manoeuvre from Week 1’s Bayes’ rule:
\text{term C} = 2\int\!\!\int \big(y(x) - \mathbb{E}[t\mid x]\big)\big(\mathbb{E}[t\mid x] - t\big)\, p(t\mid x)\, p(x)\, dx\, dt.
The factor y(x) - \mathbb{E}[t\mid x] does not involve t at all, so for each fixed x it can be pulled out of the inner integral over t:
\text{term C} = 2\int \big(y(x) - \mathbb{E}[t\mid x]\big) \left\{ \int \big(\mathbb{E}[t\mid x] - t\big)\, p(t\mid x)\, dt \right\} p(x)\, dx.
The braced inner integral is \mathbb{E}[t\mid x] (a constant, for fixed x) minus \int t\,p(t\mid x)\,dt, which is \mathbb{E}[t\mid x] itself by the definition of conditional expectation. The two copies cancel:
\int \big(\mathbb{E}[t\mid x] - t\big)\, p(t\mid x)\, dt = \mathbb{E}[t\mid x] - \mathbb{E}[t\mid x] = 0.
That zero holds for every x, so the outer integral over x in term C is an integral of zero, which is zero: \text{term C} = 0.
Step 4: read off the decomposition. With term C gone, only the two non-negative pieces remain:
\mathbb{E}[L] = \int\!\!\int \big(y(x) - \mathbb{E}[t\mid x]\big)^2 p(x,t)\, dx\, dt \;+\; \int\!\!\int \big(\mathbb{E}[t\mid x] - t\big)^2 p(x,t)\, dx\, dt.
The second term does not depend on y(x) at all: it is the average conditional variance of t given x, the noise intrinsic to the data that no choice of y can remove. The first term is non-negative and can always be driven to exactly zero, which happens precisely when

y(x) = \mathbb{E}[t \mid x].

The best regression function, under squared loss, is the conditional expectation of the target given the input. This parallels The discriminant rule and the reject option: in classification the loss-minimizing rule routed everything through the posterior p(\mathcal{C}_k\mid x); here it routes everything through the conditional mean \mathbb{E}[t\mid x].






Note



Practice question. Fix an input x. Given that x, the target t takes the values 2, 4, and 9, each with probability \tfrac{1}{3}. Compare the expected squared loss of the predictor y(x) = 4 against the predictor y(x) = \mathbb{E}[t\mid x], and confirm the theorem above by checking which is smaller.
Solution. First compute the conditional mean: \mathbb{E}[t\mid x] = \tfrac{1}{3}(2+4+9) = 5. For y(x)=4, \mathbb{E}[L] = \tfrac{1}{3}\big[(4-2)^2+(4-4)^2+(4-9)^2\big] = \tfrac{1}{3}(4+0+25) = \tfrac{29}{3} \approx 9.67. For y(x)=\mathbb{E}[t\mid x]=5, \mathbb{E}[L] = \tfrac{1}{3}\big[(5-2)^2+(5-4)^2+(5-9)^2\big] = \tfrac{1}{3}(9+1+16) = \tfrac{26}{3} \approx 8.67. The conditional mean gives the smaller expected loss, as the theorem guarantees it must for any competing choice of y(x), not only y(x)=4.








TipRecap: Loss functions for regression





What the symbols stand for:

t: the continuous target we want to predict.
y(x): our prediction for input x, the regression function.
(y(x) - t)^2: the squared loss for one case.
p(x, t): the joint density of inputs and targets.
\mathbb{E}[t \mid x] = \int t\,p(t \mid x)\,dt: the conditional mean, the average target among cases with input x.
u = y(x) - \mathbb{E}[t \mid x]: how far our prediction is from that average. v = \mathbb{E}[t \mid x] - t: how far a real target is from the average.

Taking the final decomposition apart:
\mathbb{E}[L] = \int\!\!\int u^2\, p(x,t)\,dx\,dt + \int\!\!\int v^2\, p(x,t)\,dx\,dt

The first term is zero when y(x) = \mathbb{E}[t \mid x] and positive otherwise.
The second term is the spread of t around its conditional mean. No predictor can reduce it.
The cross term 2\int\!\!\int uv\,p\,dx\,dt vanished because v averages to zero for every fixed x.

A teaching example. Fix one input x. Its target is 1, 3, or 8 with probabilities 0.5, 0.3, 0.2. The conditional mean is 0.5 + 0.9 + 1.6 = 3. The noise term is 0.5(1-3)^2 + 0.3(3-3)^2 + 0.2(8-3)^2 = 2 + 0 + 5 = 7. Now predict y = 2 instead. Its expected loss is 0.5(2-1)^2 + 0.3(2-3)^2 + 0.2(2-8)^2 = 0.5 + 0.3 + 7.2 = 8. That is the noise 7 plus our own error (2-3)^2 = 1, exactly as the decomposition says.

title: Week 2: Decision Theory and Graphical Models
section: Free parameters and the cost of the full joint
text:
Free parameters and the cost of the full joint
Section 2 of Week 1 introduced the joint distribution p(H,Y) for two variables (Joint, marginal, and conditional distributions): a table listing the probability of every combination of outcomes of H and Y. That same idea, listing one probability per combination of outcomes, is what scales badly once there are many variables instead of two. For N binary variables x_1,\dots,x_N, specifying p(x_1,\dots,x_N) in full means a table with one row per combination of outcomes, and there are 2^N such combinations.
Not every entry in that table can be chosen freely, though. A free parameter is a number we are actually at liberty to set, independent of the others already fixed. Since all 2^N table entries are probabilities that must sum to 1, only 2^N-1 of them are free: once any 2^N-1 entries are chosen, the last one is forced, because the whole table still has to add up to 1. So the joint over N binary variables costs 2^N-1 free parameters, not 2^N.
Calling this a “cost” is not just a figure of speech. Every free parameter is a number that has to come from somewhere in practice: it is estimated from data (as in Week 1’s maximum likelihood estimation, Maximum likelihood estimation), stored somewhere, and used every time the model computes a probability. A table of 2^N-1 free parameters needs enough data to pin down each of those numbers reliably, enough memory to hold the table, and enough computation to look values up in it or sum over it. When N is even modestly large this is not a minor inconvenience: at N=20 binary variables, 2^{20}-1 is already over a million free parameters, far more than any realistic dataset could estimate.
This is why we generally want fewer free parameters, not more, for the same reason Week 1 restricted attention to parametric families in the first place (Parametric models and the likelihood): fewer parameters are cheaper to estimate and cheaper to compute with. But fewer is not automatically better without limit. Every free parameter removed from the full table corresponds to an assumption that some variables do not depend on some others. If that assumption is false, that is, if the variables really do depend on each other in the way the removed parameter would have captured, the resulting model misrepresents the true distribution no matter how much data we feed it. So the goal is not to drive the parameter count as low as possible, but to spend free parameters only on the dependencies we actually believe exist, and drop the rest. The next section takes the first step toward doing that.






TipRecap: Free parameters and the cost of the full joint





What the symbols stand for:

N: the number of binary variables x_1, \dots, x_N.
2^N: the number of rows in the full joint table, one per combination of 0s and 1s.
2^N - 1: the number of free parameters, the rows we may set independently.

Taking the count apart:

Each variable has 2 values, and the choices multiply, so N variables give 2 \times 2 \times \cdots \times 2 = 2^N combinations.
The rows must sum to 1. That one constraint fixes the last row once the others are chosen, which removes one free parameter.

A teaching example. Take N = 3. The table has 2^3 = 8 rows. Suppose we fill in seven of them as 0.10, 0.05, 0.20, 0.10, 0.15, 0.10, 0.05. These add to 0.75, so the eighth row has no freedom left: it must be 0.25. That is 8 - 1 = 7 free parameters. With N = 10 the same count gives 2^{10} - 1 = 1023, and each extra variable roughly doubles it.

title: Week 2: Decision Theory and Graphical Models
text:
Why factor the joint
This section’s title asks a specific question: why bother rewriting a joint distribution as a product of conditional factors, rather than just working with the full table from Free parameters and the cost of the full joint directly? The answer is that the rewriting below, called the chain rule, is always exact and costs the same 2^N-1 parameters as the full table when applied with no assumptions, but unlike the full table it is built as a product of smaller factors, which is exactly the structure that will let us drop some of those factors later, once we are willing to assume a dependency is not really there (Directed graphical models).
This exact cost holds for any distribution, since the chain rule lets us rewrite the joint, for any ordering of the variables, as
p(x_1,\dots,x_N) = \prod_{j=1}^N p(x_j \mid x_1,\dots,x_{j-1}),
with p(x_1\mid x_0) := p(x_1). Nothing has been assumed yet: this factorization is always available and always exact, and it still costs 2^N-1 parameters in total, because p(x_j\mid x_1,\dots,x_{j-1}) is itself a table with 2^{j-1} rows, one row per possible setting of the j-1 conditioning variables x_1,\dots,x_{j-1}.
For a concrete instance, take N=4 binary variables and look at the third factor, p(x_3\mid x_1,x_2). Its conditioning variables x_1,x_2 can each be 0 or 1, giving 2^2=4 possible settings: (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1). The factor needs one row of its table for each of those four settings, e.g. a row giving p(x_3=1\mid x_1{=}0,x_2{=}1), since that number can differ for every setting of (x_1,x_2). (Within each row only one number is free, since p(x_3=0\mid x_1,x_2) = 1-p(x_3=1\mid x_1,x_2), so the factor as a whole has 4 free parameters, matching 2^{j-1}=2^{3-1}=4 for j=3.) The same pattern applies to every factor: p(x_j\mid x_1,\dots,x_{j-1}) needs 2^{j-1} rows because that is how many settings its j-1 conditioning variables can take, and adding up 2^{j-1} across j=1,\dots,N is exactly what reproduces the 2^N-1 total from two paragraphs above.
The only way to reduce the parameter count below 2^N-1 is to assume that some of these conditionals do not really depend on all of their conditioning variables, i.e. to assume conditional independencies. Directed graphical models are a bookkeeping device for exactly this.






Note



Practice question. For N=4 binary variables x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4, how many parameters does the general chain-rule factorization need? Now suppose we are willing to assume that x_4 depends only on x_3, not on x_1 or x_2, so that p(x_4\mid x_1,x_2,x_3) is replaced by p(x_4\mid x_3) while every other factor stays as general as before. How many parameters does the factorization need now?
Solution. With no assumptions, the chain rule gives p(x_1)p(x_2\mid x_1)p(x_3\mid x_1,x_2)p(x_4\mid x_1,x_2,x_3), whose tables need 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15 parameters, matching 2^4-1=15 exactly, since nothing has been assumed away yet. Replacing the last factor with p(x_4\mid x_3) shrinks its table from 2^3=8 parameters (one per configuration of three parents) to 2^1=2 (one per configuration of a single parent), for a new total of 1+2+4+2=9 parameters. Dropping the dependence on just two conditioning variables in the last factor already saves 6 parameters out of 15, and the saving grows quickly with N since the dropped table shrinks exponentially in the number of variables removed.








TipRecap: Why factor the joint





What the symbols stand for:

\prod_{j=1}^N: multiply the factors for j = 1, 2, \dots, N.
p(x_j \mid x_1, \dots, x_{j-1}): the distribution of variable j given every variable before it in the chosen order.
p(x_1 \mid x_0) := p(x_1): a convention so the first factor, which has nothing before it, is just a marginal.

Taking the chain rule apart:
p(x_1, x_2, x_3) = p(x_1)\;p(x_2 \mid x_1)\;p(x_3 \mid x_1, x_2)

Each factor is a conditional of the kind defined in Week 1, so the product is just “joint = marginal times conditional” applied repeatedly.
Factor j has j - 1 binary conditioning variables, so it needs 2^{j-1} rows, each with one free number.
The row counts 1 + 2 + 4 + \cdots + 2^{N-1} add to 2^N - 1, the same as the full table.

A teaching example. Take N = 3 with p(x_1{=}1) = 0.5, p(x_2{=}1 \mid x_1{=}1) = 0.4, and p(x_3{=}1 \mid x_1{=}1, x_2{=}1) = 0.25. Then one joint entry is p(1,1,1) = 0.5 \times 0.4 \times 0.25 = 0.05. Filling the whole table this way uses 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 numbers, the same 2^3 - 1 as listing the table directly. The savings only appear when we shorten a conditioning list, as in the practice question above.

title: Week 2: Decision Theory and Graphical Models
text:
Directed graphical models

Definition. A directed acyclic graphical model (DAG, or Bayes net) represents each random variable as a node and each assumed direct dependence as a directed edge. A DAG with no cycles implies the factorization p(x_1,\dots,x_N) = \prod_{i=1}^N p\big(x_i \mid \text{parents}(x_i)\big), where \text{parents}(x_i) is the set of nodes with an edge pointing into x_i.

This is the same chain-rule factorization as Why factor the joint, restricted so that each x_i’s conditioning set is only its parents rather than every variable before it in some ordering. A conditional probability table (CPT) stores p(x_i \mid \text{parents}(x_i)): for binary variables, a node with K_i parents needs 2^{K_i} free parameters (one probability per parent configuration, since the two outcomes sum to 1). The total across the graph is roughly N \cdot 2^{\max_i K_i}, which is far smaller than 2^N - 1 whenever the graph is sparse. Restricting every node to a small number of parents is what buys the savings; a fully-connected DAG recovers the general chain rule and its full 2^N-1 parameter cost, with no savings at all.






TipQuestion: Does an arrow in a DAG mean implication, causation, or dependence?





An arrow A\to B means different things in different places, and none of them is by itself a statement about independence. The lecture’s examples (low pressure, rain, traffic, a ballgame, a project deadline, busy forums, a full lab) separate three meanings.
1. Logical implication between events. If A and B are events, A\Rightarrow B means A\subseteq B: whenever A happens, B happens. If rain always caused heavy traffic, the event “rain” would be contained in the event “traffic”, and P(\text{traffic}\mid\text{rain}) = \frac{P(\text{rain}\cap\text{traffic})}{P(\text{rain})} = \frac{P(\text{rain})}{P(\text{rain})} = 1. Independence would need P(\text{traffic}\mid\text{rain}) = P(\text{traffic}), which then forces P(\text{traffic})=1 (or P(\text{rain})=0). So implication is close to the opposite of independence: A tells us everything about B.
2. A causal edge. Reading rain \to traffic causally says traffic is generated from rain plus other inputs: changing the weather would change the traffic. That is a claim about intervening, setting rain by force, which is not the same as observing rain. This chapter’s DAGs only use the factorization, so this causal reading is extra.
3. Dependence is not causation. The lecture’s common-cause example has a project deadline (the shared cause) \to busy forums and deadline \to full lab. Observing busy forums makes a full lab more likely, so the two are dependent. Yet forcing the forums to be busy would do nothing to the lab, because only the deadline affects it. Averaging over the deadline Y with its own distribution, rather than the one implied by the forums, gives the effect of setting the forums X=x on the lab Z: \sum_y P(Z\mid X=x,Y=y)\,P(Y=y) = \sum_y P(Z\mid Y=y)\,P(Y=y) = P(Z). The first equality uses X\perp Z\mid Y from Conditional independence: three canonical structures. The observational P(Z\mid X=x) instead weights each y by P(Y=y\mid X=x), which is why it differs. A shared cause that creates this gap is called a confounder. When the observed variable also has a real effect of its own, confounding can even reverse the apparent direction of that effect, which is Simpson’s paradox.
What an edge does and does not say about the data.

An edge alone constrains nothing. Any joint over two variables factors both ways, p(\text{rain})\,p(\text{traffic}\mid\text{rain}) = p(\text{traffic})\,p(\text{rain}\mid\text{traffic}), so rain \to traffic and traffic \to rain fit the same data equally well.
Missing edges are what constrain. In the chain low pressure \to rain \to traffic, the absent edge from low pressure to traffic is what asserts low pressure \perp traffic \mid rain. Every independence a DAG encodes comes from a missing edge (Conditional independence: three canonical structures).
Causation usually, but not always, produces dependence. If an effect works through two routes that exactly cancel, the variables can be independent despite a causal link. Assuming this never happens is called faithfulness, and only under it does independence rule out a causal effect.
Dependence needs an explanation. If two variables are dependent, then one causes the other or they share a common cause, as busy forums and a full lab share the deadline. Within a data set there is one more source: conditioning on a common effect, as in explaining away, where rain and a ballgame become dependent once we observe the traffic.






  
    
      
    
  
  A DAG and its factorization
  
  x1
  
  x2
  
  x3
  
  x4
  
  x5
  
  x6
  
  
  
  
  
  


Figure 2. A DAG on six nodes. Reading parents off the picture gives the factorization p(x_1,\dots,x_6) = p(x_1)\,p(x_2\mid x_1)\,p(x_3\mid x_1)\,p(x_4\mid x_2)\,p(x_5\mid x_3)\,p(x_6\mid x_2,x_5): each factor’s conditioning set is exactly its incoming arrows, not every earlier node.






Note



Practice question. For the DAG in Figure 2, treat every node as binary. How many parameters does each node’s CPT need, and what is the total across the whole graph? How does that total compare to the 2^6-1 a fully-connected DAG on six nodes would need?
Solution. Read the parent count straight off the arrows into each node: x_1 has no parents (K=0, so 2^0=1 parameter); x_2 and x_3 each have one parent, x_1 (K=1, 2^1=2 parameters each); x_4 has one parent, x_2 (2 parameters); x_5 has one parent, x_3 (2 parameters); x_6 has two parents, x_2 and x_5 (K=2, 2^2=4 parameters). Summing these, 1+2+2+2+2+4=13 parameters for the whole graph, against 2^6-1=63 for the fully-connected case. Compared with the chain rule in the order x_1,\dots,x_6 (costs 1,2,4,8,16,32), every node from x_3 on has fewer parents (costs 1,2,2,2,2,4). The largest single saving is x_6’s CPT, 32 down to 4: it depends on x_2 and x_5 but not on x_1, x_3, or x_4, which is exactly the kind of assumption Why factor the joint said was the only way to cut the parameter count.








TipRecap: Directed graphical models





What the symbols stand for:

A node: one random variable. An arrow x_a \to x_b: x_a is a parent of x_b.
\text{parents}(x_i): the set of nodes with an arrow into x_i. It may be empty.
CPT: the conditional probability table storing p(x_i \mid \text{parents}(x_i)).
K_i: the number of parents of node i. A binary node then needs 2^{K_i} free numbers.

Taking the factorization apart:

\prod_i p(x_i \mid \text{parents}(x_i)) is the chain rule with each conditioning list cut down to the parents.
Every arrow that is missing is a conditioning variable dropped from some factor, and every dropped variable halves that factor’s table.
Total cost: \sum_i 2^{K_i}, compared with 2^N - 1 for the full joint.

A teaching example. Take three binary nodes with x_1 \to x_2 and x_1 \to x_3 and no arrow between x_2 and x_3. The factorization is p(x_1)\,p(x_2 \mid x_1)\,p(x_3 \mid x_1), costing 1 + 2 + 2 = 5 numbers instead of 7. With p(x_1{=}1) = 0.3, p(x_2{=}1 \mid x_1{=}1) = 0.9, and p(x_3{=}1 \mid x_1{=}1) = 0.5, one entry of the joint is p(1,1,1) = 0.3 \times 0.9 \times 0.5 = 0.135. The factor for x_3 never asks about x_2, which is the assumption the missing arrow encodes.

title: Week 2: Decision Theory and Graphical Models
text:
Conditional independence: three canonical structures

Definition. For disjoint sets of variables A, B, C, we write x_A \perp x_B \mid x_C (“x_A and x_B are conditionally independent given x_C”) if any of the following equivalent conditions hold: p(x_A, x_B \mid x_C) = p(x_A\mid x_C)\,p(x_B\mid x_C), \quad p(x_A\mid x_B, x_C) = p(x_A\mid x_C), \quad p(x_B\mid x_A, x_C) = p(x_B\mid x_C).

A DAG’s edges encode a specific pattern of these independencies. Three three-node structures cover the cases, each checked directly from the factorization it implies.
Causal chain (X \to Y \to Z). The joint factors as p(x)p(y\mid x)p(z\mid y), so p(z\mid x,y) = \frac{p(x)p(y\mid x)p(z\mid y)}{p(x)p(y\mid x)} = p(z\mid y). Once Y is known, X tells us nothing more about Z: X \perp Z \mid Y.
Common cause (X \leftarrow Y \rightarrow Z). The joint factors as p(y)p(x\mid y)p(z\mid y), so p(x,z\mid y) = \frac{p(y)p(x\mid y)p(z\mid y)}{p(y)} = p(x\mid y)\,p(z\mid y). Again X \perp Z \mid Y: two effects of a shared cause become independent once that cause is observed.
Explaining away (X \to Y \leftarrow Z). The joint factors as p(x)p(z)p(y\mid x,z), and now p(z\mid x,y) = \frac{p(x)p(z)p(y\mid x,z)}{p(x)p(y\mid x)} = \frac{p(z)p(y\mid x,z)}{p(y\mid x)} \neq p(z\mid y) in general. X and Z are marginally independent (with Y unobserved), but conditioning on their common effect Y can make them dependent: learning that it rained (X) makes a ballgame (Z) a less likely explanation for heavy traffic (Y), even though rain and ballgames have nothing to do with each other on their own.






TipQuestion: How big is the explaining-away effect in numbers?





Take invented numbers for rain X, a ballgame Z, and heavy traffic Y: p(X=1)=0.1, p(Z=1)=0.2, and p(Y=1\mid x,z) equal to 0.05, 0.8, 0.7, 0.9 for (x,z)=(0,0),(1,0),(0,1),(1,1). The joint with heavy traffic observed is p(x)\,p(z)\,p(Y=1\mid x,z):



(x,z)
p(x)\,p(z)\,p(Y=1\mid x,z)




(0,0)
0.9\times0.8\times0.05=0.036


(1,0)
0.1\times0.8\times0.8=0.064


(0,1)
0.9\times0.2\times0.7=0.126


(1,1)
0.1\times0.2\times0.9=0.018



The column sums to p(Y=1)=0.244.

Traffic alone raises the probability of rain from 0.1 to p(X=1\mid Y=1)=(0.064+0.018)/0.244\approx0.336.
Traffic and a ballgame: p(X=1\mid Y=1,Z=1)=0.018/(0.126+0.018)=0.125. The ballgame already accounts for the traffic, so rain becomes less likely.
Traffic and no ballgame: p(X=1\mid Y=1,Z=0)=0.064/(0.036+0.064)=0.64. Something has to explain the traffic, so rain becomes more likely.

Learning Z moves our belief about X, so X and Z are dependent given Y. Without Y observed, summing it out uses \sum_y p(y\mid x,z)=1 and leaves p(x)\,p(z), so they are independent, as the factorization above says.









Note



Practice question. Three variables from the lecture’s own examples exercise each structure in turn. For each, say which structure it is and whether the two outer variables are independent, both before and after conditioning on the middle one.

Low pressure (X) \to rain (Y) \to traffic (Z).
A project deadline (Y) makes the forums busy (X) and, separately, fills up the lab (Z): X \leftarrow Y \to Z.
Rain (X) and a ballgame (Z) both feed into traffic (Y): X \to Y \leftarrow Z.

Solution.

Causal chain. Marginally, X and Z are dependent (low pressure raises the chance of rain, which raises the chance of traffic). Conditioned on Y (we already know whether it is raining), X tells us nothing more about Z: X \perp Z \mid Y, exactly the causal-chain result above.
Common cause. Marginally, X and Z are dependent: busy forums are a signal that the deadline is near, which makes a full lab more likely too, so the two are correlated through the shared cause even though neither directly affects the other. Conditioned on Y (we already know whether the deadline is near), that shared explanation is used up, and X \perp Z \mid Y.
Explaining away. Marginally, X and Z are independent: whether it rains has nothing to do with whether there is a ballgame. But conditioned on Y (we observe heavy traffic), they become dependent: learning it rained makes the ballgame a less likely explanation for the traffic, and vice versa. This is the one structure where conditioning on the middle node creates a dependency rather than removing one, which is why it is the case worth double-checking whenever a homework or the Bayes Ball algorithm below asks about a head-to-head node.









TipRecap: Conditional independence: three canonical structures





What the symbols stand for:

x_A, x_B, x_C: three disjoint groups of variables.
x_A \perp x_B \mid x_C: once x_C is known, learning x_B tells us nothing more about x_A.
X, Y, Z: the three nodes of each small structure, with Y in the middle.

Taking the definition apart:

p(x_A, x_B \mid x_C) = p(x_A \mid x_C)\,p(x_B \mid x_C): given x_C, the joint of A and B splits into a product, just like ordinary independence.
p(x_A \mid x_B, x_C) = p(x_A \mid x_C): adding x_B to what we condition on leaves the distribution of x_A unchanged. This is the form used in each check above.
Chain and common cause: observing Y blocks the dependence. Explaining away: observing Y creates it.

A teaching example for the chain X \to Y \to Z. Let p(X{=}1) = 0.5, p(Y{=}1 \mid X{=}1) = 0.8, p(Y{=}1 \mid X{=}0) = 0.2, p(Z{=}1 \mid Y{=}1) = 0.9, p(Z{=}1 \mid Y{=}0) = 0.1.

Without Y: p(Z{=}1 \mid X{=}1) = 0.8(0.9) + 0.2(0.1) = 0.74, but p(Z{=}1 \mid X{=}0) = 0.2(0.9) + 0.8(0.1) = 0.26. Knowing X changes our belief about Z, so they are dependent.
With Y{=}1 known: p(Z{=}1 \mid X, Y{=}1) = 0.9 whatever X is, because the factor p(z \mid y) never looks at x. So X \perp Z \mid Y.

For a numeric explaining-away case, see the dropdown on its size earlier in this section.

title: Week 2: Decision Theory and Graphical Models
text:
The Bayes Ball algorithm
Checking x_A \perp x_B \mid x_C by hand from the joint, as in Conditional independence: three canonical structures, does not scale: for more than three variables, writing out the full factorization and cancelling terms gets unwieldy fast. D-separation is a purely graph-theoretic condition, built only from paths and arrows, that guarantees conditional independence in every distribution the DAG represents. Unlike the joint-distribution algebra of Conditional independence: three canonical structures, it can be checked by eye on the picture, which is what makes it useful.
D-separation is built from the same three junction types as Conditional independence: three canonical structures, now named for their shape on a path rather than their causal story: a chain node (\to Y \to), a fork node (\leftarrow Y \to, what Conditional independence: three canonical structures called common cause), and a collider node (\to Y \leftarrow, what Conditional independence: three canonical structures called explaining away). Fix a conditioning set C.

Definition. A path between two nodes is blocked by C if it contains at least one node Y where either:

Y is a chain or fork node on that path, and Y \in C (the path is cut at an observed non-collider), or
Y is a collider node on that path, and neither Y nor any descendant of Y is in C (the path is cut at an unobserved collider).

A path that is not blocked is active. Two disjoint sets of nodes A and B are d-separated by C if every path between a node in A and a node in B is blocked by C.

D-separation is a statement about the graph alone, no probabilities involved, which is exactly why it is worth having:

Result. If A and B are d-separated by C, then x_A \perp x_B \mid x_C in every distribution that factorizes according to the DAG. If they are not d-separated, the independence fails in almost every such distribution (it can hold only by an exact cancellation of the numbers in the tables).

This is the fact that licenses reading independence off a picture. The Bayes Ball algorithm is a mechanical way to check d-separation without enumerating every path by hand:






Note



Bayes Ball procedure. To test whether A and B are d-separated by C: shade every node in C (observed). Place a ball at each node in A and let it bounce along edges, obeying the rules below at every node it reaches. If any ball can reach a node in B, some path is active and the graph does not guarantee x_A \perp x_B \mid x_C. If no ball can reach B, every path is blocked and x_A \perp x_B \mid x_C.


The bouncing rules are exactly the blocking condition above, restated as what a ball is and is not allowed to cross:

Chain (\to Y \to): the ball passes through Y if Y is unshaded, and is blocked if Y is shaded.
Fork (\leftarrow Y \to): the ball passes through Y if Y is unshaded, and is blocked if Y is shaded.
Collider (\to Y \leftarrow): the ball is blocked at Y if Y is unshaded, and passes through if Y or any of its descendants is shaded.

That last rule is the one that reverses the usual pattern, and it is exactly the explaining-away asymmetry from Conditional independence: three canonical structures: observing a collider, or anything downstream of it, opens a dependency between its causes that was not there before.
Worked example (from the tutorial). The tutorial’s practice graph has a and f both pointing into e, e pointing into c, and f pointing into b:


  
    
      
    
  
  
    (a) c shaded
    
    
    
    
    
    a
    
    f
    
    e
    
    c
    
    b
  
  
    (b) f shaded
    
    
    
    
    
    a
    
    f
    
    e
    
    c
    
    b
  


Figure 3. The tutorial’s practice graph (a\to e, f\to e, e\to c, f\to b), shaded (grey) nodes are the conditioning set. Panel (a) conditions on c; panel (b) conditions on f.
The only path from a to b is a \to e \leftarrow f \to b, with two junctions to check: e is a collider on this path (both a\to e and f\to e point into it), and f is a fork node on this path (both edges, f\to e and f\to b, point out of f), which blocks under the same rule as a chain: shaded blocks, unshaded passes.
In panel (a), C=\{c\}. At the collider e: is e or a descendant of e in C? Yes, e’s child c is shaded, so the collider is open. At the fork f: is f shaded? No, so the fork is also open. Both junctions on the only path are open, so the path is active: a \not\perp b \mid c. This is worth sitting with, since it runs against plain intuition: shading c, which is not on the direct route between a and f at all, is exactly what creates the dependency, because c is a descendant of the collider e. This is the explaining-away asymmetry from Conditional independence: three canonical structures, one hop removed.
In panel (b), C=\{f\}. At the collider e: neither e nor its descendant c is shaded, so the collider stays blocked, which is already enough to block the whole path regardless of what happens at f. (The fork at f is separately blocked too, since f itself is shaded, but the collider alone already settles it.) So a \perp b \mid f.
Larger example. In the six-node DAG of Figure 2, is x_1 \perp x_6 \mid \{x_2,x_3\}? There are two paths from x_1 to x_6: x_1\to x_2\to x_6 and x_1\to x_3\to x_5\to x_6. On the first path, x_2 is a chain node, and it is shaded, so that path is blocked. On the second, x_3 is a chain node and is also shaded, blocking that path too. Every path is blocked, so yes, x_1 \perp x_6 \mid \{x_2,x_3\}.
Is x_2 \perp x_3 \mid \{x_1,x_6\}? Path 1 is x_2 \leftarrow x_1 \to x_3: x_1 is a fork on this path and is shaded, so this path is blocked. Path 2 is x_2 \to x_6 \leftarrow x_5 \leftarrow x_3: x_6 is a collider on this path (both x_2\to x_6 and x_5\to x_6 point into it), and x_6 is shaded, so the collider is open; continuing along the path, x_5 is a chain node (between x_3\to x_5 and x_5\to x_6) and is unshaded, so it is open too. Both junctions on path 2 are open, so path 2 is active. One active path is enough: x_2 \not\perp x_3 \mid \{x_1,x_6\}, and the reason is the same collider-opened-by-a-shaded-descendant pattern as Figure 3(a).
crumbs: 4  Week 2: Decision Theory and Graphical Models

title: Week 2: Decision Theory and Graphical Models
section: Naive Bayes as a graphical model
text:
Naive Bayes as a graphical model
The tutorial applies Directed graphical models and Conditional independence: three canonical structures to a concrete problem: classifying a text as spam (C=1) or not (C=0) from which words it contains. Represent a text with a bag-of-words vector X = (X_1,\dots,X_d), one binary entry per dictionary word, where X_i=1 means word i appears (order and repetition are discarded). We want the posterior p(C\mid X), and since p(X) does not depend on C, this is proportional to p(C,X).
Applying the chain rule of Why factor the joint with no independence assumptions, in the order C, X_1,\dots,X_d, gives p(C,X) = p(C)\,p(X_1\mid C)\prod_{i=2}^d p(X_i \mid X_1,\dots,X_{i-1}, C). As a DAG this is fully connected: node X_i has i parents, so its CPT alone needs 2^i parameters, and the total is 1 + \sum_{i=1}^d 2^i = 2^{d+1}-1, exactly the general joint-distribution cost from Why factor the joint on d+1 binary variables. Writing the chain rule down bought nothing yet, because no independence was assumed.






Note



Homework-relevant. The next step, the Naive Bayes independence assumption, is where the parameter count collapses, and its MLE derivation is a direct extension of Week 1’s Bernoulli MLE (Maximum likelihood estimation). If a current or upcoming assignment touches maximum likelihood for a probabilistic model, this derivation pattern (Bernoulli log-likelihood, set derivative to zero, read off an empirical frequency) is worth understanding in full rather than only recognizing.


The assumption. Naive Bayes removes every edge between the X_i’s and keeps only the edges from C: p(X_i \mid X_1,\dots,X_{i-1}, C) = p(X_i \mid C), i.e. X_i \perp X_j \mid C for every j \neq i. This is an instance of the common-cause structure from Conditional independence: three canonical structures, with C as the shared cause of every word’s appearance. The factorization becomes p(X,C) = p(C)\prod_{i=1}^d p(X_i \mid C), with 1 + 2d parameters: linear in d instead of exponential. The assumption is not literally true (word co-occurrences do carry information about topic), but it is a Week-1-style parametric simplification: it trades some accuracy in the model for a tractable number of parameters to estimate.
Maximum likelihood. Parameterize p(C{=}1) = \pi and p(X_j{=}1\mid C{=}c) = \theta_{jc}. Given N i.i.d. labelled texts (x^{(i)}, c^{(i)}), the log-likelihood factors, by the same independence assumption, into a sum of Bernoulli log-likelihoods: one for the labels (governed by \pi) and one per word per class (governed by \theta_{jc}): \ell(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^N \log p(c^{(i)}) \;+\; \sum_{j=1}^d \sum_{i=1}^N \log p(x_j^{(i)} \mid c^{(i)}). Each piece is a Bernoulli log-likelihood of exactly the shape solved in Week 1 (Maximum likelihood estimation): p(c^{(i)}) = \pi^{c^{(i)}}(1-\pi)^{1-c^{(i)}} and p(x_j^{(i)}\mid c) = \theta_{jc}^{x_j^{(i)}}(1-\theta_{jc})^{1-x_j^{(i)}}. Setting each derivative to zero reproduces the Week 1 pattern, \hat\theta_{\text{MLE}} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i x^{(i)}, applied separately to each piece: \hat\pi = \frac{\sum_i \mathbb{1}[c^{(i)}=1]}{N} = \frac{\#\text{ spam texts}}{\#\text{ texts}}, \hat\theta_{jc} = \frac{\sum_i \mathbb{1}[x_j^{(i)}=1 \,\&\, c^{(i)}=c]}{\sum_i \mathbb{1}[c^{(i)}=c]}. In words, \hat\theta_{jc} is the fraction of class-c texts in which word j appears. Each MLE is again an observed relative frequency, exactly as in the Bernoulli case: the independence assumption did not change how we estimate parameters, only how many there are to estimate.






TipRecap: Naive Bayes as a graphical model





What the symbols stand for:

C: the class label, 1 for spam and 0 for not spam.
X = (X_1, \dots, X_d): the bag-of-words vector. X_j = 1 if dictionary word j appears in the text.
d: the dictionary size. N: the number of labelled training texts.
\pi = p(C{=}1): the prior probability of spam.
\theta_{jc} = p(X_j{=}1 \mid C{=}c): the probability that word j appears in a text of class c.
\mathbb{1}[\cdot]: the indicator, 1 if the condition holds and 0 otherwise.

Taking the equations apart:

p(X, C) = p(C)\prod_j p(X_j \mid C): pick the class, then let each word appear or not on its own, using only the class. This is the common-cause structure with C as the cause.
The log-likelihood splits into one Bernoulli piece for the labels and one Bernoulli piece per (word, class) pair, so each parameter is fitted separately.
\hat\pi = fraction of texts that are spam. \hat\theta_{jc} = among class-c texts, the fraction containing word j.

A teaching example. Six texts, two dictionary words (“free”, “meeting”). Three are spam: “free” appears in two of them and “meeting” in one. Three are not spam: “free” appears in one and “meeting” in two. The MLEs are \hat\pi = 3/6 = 0.5, \hat\theta_{\text{free},1} = 2/3, \hat\theta_{\text{meeting},1} = 1/3, \hat\theta_{\text{free},0} = 1/3, \hat\theta_{\text{meeting},0} = 2/3, which is 1 + 2d = 5 numbers. A new text contains “free” but not “meeting”.

Spam: 0.5 \times \tfrac{2}{3} \times (1 - \tfrac{1}{3}) = \tfrac{4}{18}.
Not spam: 0.5 \times \tfrac{1}{3} \times (1 - \tfrac{2}{3}) = \tfrac{1}{18}.

Normalizing, p(C{=}1 \mid X) = 4/5 = 0.8. An absent word still counts, through the factor 1 - \theta_{jc}.
crumbs: 4  Week 2: Decision Theory and Graphical Models

title: Week 2: Decision Theory and Graphical Models
text:
DGMs in the wild, briefly
The tutorial surveys a few more graphical models to show the same “assume some independencies, save parameters” idea recurring in different shapes. None of these are derived in depth in this lecture; the point is to recognize the pattern.

Markov chains. A first-order chain p(x_{1:T}) = p(x_1)\prod_{t=2}^T p(x_t\mid x_{t-1}) assumes each state depends only on the immediately previous one; a second-order chain conditions on the two previous states instead.
Hidden Markov models (HMMs). A chain of unobserved (hidden) states Z_t, each taking one of K discrete values, each emitting an observed X_t: p(X_{1:T}, Z_{1:T}) = p(Z_1)\prod_{t=2}^T p(Z_t\mid Z_{t-1}) \prod_{t=1}^T p(X_t\mid Z_t). This is a Markov chain over the hidden layer, with an emission model attached to each step.
Medical diagnosis networks. The Quick Medical Reference network is a bipartite DAG: hidden disease nodes as parents, observed symptom nodes as children, with a noisy-OR conditional probability table (any positive parent disease tends to make a symptom positive). The Alarm network is a hand-built DAG of 37 ICU-monitoring variables; because it is sparse, it needs only 509 parameters (the tutorial quotes 504), against far more than 2^{37}-1 for a full joint table, since most of its variables have three or four states, and its edges are drawn from known causal relationships in medicine rather than fit as a generic template.







TipRecap: DGMs in the wild, briefly





What the symbols stand for:

x_{1:T}: the sequence x_1, x_2, \dots, x_T of states over T time steps.
p(x_t \mid x_{t-1}): the transition probability, how the state at time t depends on the state just before it.
Z_t: the hidden state at time t in an HMM, one of K values. X_t: what we observe at time t.
p(X_t \mid Z_t): the emission probability, how the hidden state produces the observation.

Taking the factorizations apart:

Markov chain: p(x_1) starts the sequence, then each factor p(x_t \mid x_{t-1}) steps it forward one time step. Each node has one parent, the previous step.
HMM: the same chain runs on the hidden Z’s, and each step adds one factor p(X_t \mid Z_t) for the observation. Each X_t has one parent, its own Z_t.

A teaching example. A binary chain with states rain and dry has p(x_1 = \text{rain}) = 0.3, p(\text{rain} \mid \text{rain}) = 0.6, p(\text{rain} \mid \text{dry}) = 0.2. The sequence rain, rain, dry has probability 0.3 \times 0.6 \times (1 - 0.6) = 0.072. If the transition table is shared across time steps, this chain is fully described by 3 numbers for any length T, whereas a full joint over T binary steps needs 2^T - 1.
crumbs: 4  Week 2: Decision Theory and Graphical Models

title: Week 2: Decision Theory and Graphical Models
text:
Summary






Note



Key takeaways from Week 2:

Decision theory separates inference (estimating p(x,c)) from decision (acting on it). Minimizing misclassification rate is the special case of minimizing expected loss where every error costs the same.
The general discriminant rule minimizes \sum_k L_{kj}\,p(\mathcal{C}_k\mid x) over the decision j; the reject option lets us decline to decide when no posterior clears a threshold.
For regression under squared loss, the best predictor is the conditional expectation y(x) = \mathbb{E}[t\mid x].
A general joint over N binary variables costs 2^N-1 parameters. Directed graphical models trade that cost down by assuming each variable depends only on its parents.
Three structures (chain, common cause, common effect) cover how conditioning opens or blocks dependence; the Bayes Ball algorithm reads x_A\perp x_B\mid x_C directly off the graph using these rules.
Naive Bayes is a common-cause DAG over word features given the class label; its independence assumption is what makes its MLE reduce to per-word, per-class Bernoulli MLEs, in the same shape as Week 1’s Bernoulli derivation.



Next week: Markov Random Fields, as listed on the course roadmap (not written yet).

title: Week 2: Decision Theory and Graphical Models
text:
Quick self-check
If you can explain, in your own words, why the discriminant rule and the best regressor \mathbb{E}[t\mid x] are really the same idea applied to two different loss functions, and why the Naive Bayes assumption is a special case of the “common cause” independence structure, you have understood the core of Week 2.

title: Week 2: Decision Theory and Graphical Models
text:
High-level overview
This section retells each part of the week in plain language and without formulas, using the lecture’s own examples. Read it before the chapter for orientation, or after it as a review.
From inference to decision (From inference to decision). Knowing the chances is not the same as acting on them. From a chest X-ray, a model might say there is a small chance of cancer, but a doctor still has to choose: treat or not. The week separates the two steps. Inference estimates the chances, and a decision rule turns them into an action.
Misclassification rate (Misclassification rate). If every mistake counts the same, the best rule is simple: pick whichever class is more probable. For the X-ray, call it cancer when cancer is the more likely explanation, and healthy otherwise. Any other cut-off makes more mistakes overall.
Expected loss (Expected loss). Real mistakes do not cost the same. Missing a real cancer is far worse than a false alarm that leads to an extra test. Expected loss weighs each kind of mistake by its cost, so a rule that makes more mistakes overall can still be the better rule if its mistakes are the cheap kind.
The discriminant rule and the reject option (The discriminant rule and the reject option). With costs in the picture, choose the action with the lowest expected cost. When a missed cancer is very expensive, the rule calls cancer even at a fairly low probability, because acting on a small chance is worth it. The reject option adds a third choice: if no answer is confident enough, hand the case to a human instead of guessing.
Loss functions for regression (Loss functions for regression). The same idea works when the answer is a number rather than a category. If being off by twice as much costs four times as much (squared loss), the best prediction for an input is the average of the outcomes that input can lead to.
Free parameters and the cost of the full joint (Free parameters and the cost of the full joint). Writing down the chance of every combination of many yes/no variables quickly becomes hopeless, because each added variable doubles the size of the table. With 30 variables the table has over a billion entries, and each one would have to be learned from data.
Why factor the joint (Why factor the joint). Breaking a joint distribution into a chain of “this variable given the earlier ones” is always allowed, but on its own it saves nothing. The savings come from deciding that each variable depends on only a few others.
Directed graphical models (Directed graphical models). A DAG draws those decisions as a picture: an arrow into a variable means its probabilities are specified given the variables pointing into it. Low pressure, rain, and traffic form a natural chain. Arrows are often drawn in the causal direction because that is easy to think about, but mathematically they only record how the joint distribution breaks into pieces.
Conditional independence: three canonical structures (Conditional independence: three canonical structures). Three small patterns explain how information flows through a graph.

Chain (low pressure, then rain, then traffic). Once we know it is raining, the pressure tells us nothing more about the traffic.
Common cause (a project deadline fills both the forums and the lab). Once we know about the deadline, busy forums tell us nothing more about the lab.
Common effect (rain or a ballgame can each cause traffic). The two causes are unrelated until we see traffic. Then learning there was a ballgame makes rain less likely, because the ballgame already explains the traffic. This is explaining away.

The Bayes Ball algorithm (The Bayes Ball algorithm). In a large graph, checking independence by algebra is tedious. Bayes Ball builds on the three patterns above to decide whether a “ball” can travel along each path. If no ball can get from one group of variables to another, the two groups are independent given what we observed. An algebra question becomes a picture-reading exercise.
Naive Bayes as a graphical model (Naive Bayes as a graphical model). To filter spam, treat “spam or not” as the common cause of which words appear in a text, and assume the words are independent once the label is known. The assumption is not literally true (some words tend to appear together), but it shrinks the model to one simple probability per word per class, each learned from counts.
DGMs in the wild (DGMs in the wild, briefly). A quick tour of other models built the same way, including Markov chains for sequences and hidden Markov models, which return in Weeks 5 and 6.

title: Week 2 practice: Decision theory and graphical models
text:
Problem 1: Two ways to be wrong
Overview. These problems drill Week 2. Try each stem before opening the worked solution. The loss matrices, distributions, and graphs here are invented for practice; they are not the cancer-screening, regression, or Bayes-Ball examples from the lecture. Notation matches the week chapter. The exception is the final section, Tutorial questions, which restates the Week 2 tutorial’s own examples.
A helpdesk routes each incoming ticket either to an autoresponder (for routine questions) or to a human agent (for anything else). Two people disagree about how to design the router:
Which objective from the lecture, misclassification rate or expected loss, matches each person’s goal? Could the two objectives ever recommend the same decision rule?
crumbs: 5  Week 2 practice: Decision theory and graphical models

title: Week 2 practice: Decision theory and graphical models
text:
Person A wants to minimize the fraction of tickets sent to the wrong handler.
Person B points out that sending a genuinely urgent ticket to the autoresponder is much worse than sending a routine ticket to a human (wasted agent time, but no harm done), and wants the router to reflect that.








TipWorked solution





This uses Week 2, From inference to decision and Misclassification rate.
Person A wants to minimize p(\text{mistake}), the plain count of wrong handler assignments from Misclassification rate: every error counts as one, regardless of which direction it runs. Person B wants a loss function (Week 2, Expected loss): a loss matrix that charges more for “urgent ticket sent to autoresponder” than for “routine ticket sent to a human,” and then minimizes the resulting expected loss.
The two objectives can agree. Misclassification rate is the special case of expected loss where the loss matrix has 0 on the diagonal and 1 everywhere off it, so if Person B’s matrix happened to be symmetric with equal off-diagonal costs, the discriminant rule would reduce to Person A’s rule exactly. They diverge only once the loss matrix is asymmetric, which is what Person B is actually asking for.
Answer. Person A: misclassification rate. Person B: expected loss with an asymmetric loss matrix. The two agree whenever the loss matrix has zero diagonal and equal off-diagonal costs (the 0/1 matrix or any positive multiple of it); a loss matrix is a strict generalization, not a different framework.
crumbs: 5  Week 2 practice: Decision theory and graphical models

title: Week 2 practice: Decision theory and graphical models
section: Problem 2: Inspecting a batch of widgets
text:
Problem 2: Inspecting a batch of widgets
A factory’s inspection station decides whether a widget is defective (\mathcal{C}_1) or good (\mathcal{C}_2). Passing a defective widget into a shipment costs 50 (recalls, refunds); scrapping a good widget costs 5 (wasted material). Correct calls cost 0.
For one widget, the classifier’s estimated posteriors are p(\mathcal{C}_1 \mid x) = 0.15 and p(\mathcal{C}_2 \mid x) = 0.85.

Write the 2\times 2 loss matrix (rows: truth, columns: decision).
Compute the discriminant rule’s two candidate costs and state its decision.
Compare this to what the misclassification-rate rule (from Problem 1’s Person A) would decide.







TipWorked solution





This uses Week 2, Expected loss and The discriminant rule.
1. Loss matrix. L_{\text{defective},\text{scrap}} = 0, L_{\text{defective},\text{ship}} = 50, L_{\text{good},\text{scrap}} = 5, L_{\text{good},\text{ship}} = 0.
2. Discriminant rule. The rule assigns x to the decision j minimizing \sum_k L_{kj}\,p(\mathcal{C}_k\mid x):
\text{cost(ship)} = L_{\text{defective},\text{ship}}(0.15) + L_{\text{good},\text{ship}}(0.85) = 50(0.15) + 0(0.85) = 7.5, \text{cost(scrap)} = L_{\text{defective},\text{scrap}}(0.15) + L_{\text{good},\text{scrap}}(0.85) = 0(0.15) + 5(0.85) = 4.25.
Scrapping is cheaper, so the discriminant rule decides scrap, even though the widget is more likely good (0.85 > 0.15) than defective.
3. Comparison. The plain misclassification-rate rule from Misclassification rate only compares posteriors and would decide ship, since p(\mathcal{C}_2\mid x)=0.85 is the larger posterior. The rules disagree because the loss matrix charges 10 times more for shipping a defective widget than for scrapping a good one, so even a fairly low probability of defect is still worth acting on, exactly the same asymmetry that moved the lecture’s cancer-screening boundary.
Answer. Loss matrix as above; discriminant rule decides scrap (cost 4.25 vs. 7.5); the misclassification-rate rule would have decided ship.
crumbs: 5  Week 2 practice: Decision theory and graphical models

title: Week 2 practice: Decision theory and graphical models
text:
Problem 3: A different conditional distribution
Fix an input x. Given that x, a continuous target t takes the values 1, 3, and 14, each with probability \tfrac13.
Compute \mathbb{E}[t\mid x]. Then compare the expected squared loss of the predictor y(x) = 8 against y(x) = \mathbb{E}[t\mid x], and confirm which one the lecture’s theorem says must be smaller.






TipWorked solution





This uses Week 2, Loss functions for regression.
Conditional mean: \mathbb{E}[t\mid x] = \tfrac13(1+3+14) = 6.
For y(x) = 8: \mathbb{E}[L] = \tfrac13\big[(8-1)^2+(8-3)^2+(8-14)^2\big] = \tfrac13(49+25+36) = \tfrac{110}{3} \approx 36.67.
For y(x) = \mathbb{E}[t\mid x] = 6: \mathbb{E}[L] = \tfrac13\big[(6-1)^2+(6-3)^2+(6-14)^2\big] = \tfrac13(25+9+64) = \tfrac{98}{3} \approx 32.67.
The conditional mean gives the smaller expected loss, matching the theorem: y(x) = \mathbb{E}[t\mid x] minimizes squared loss for any competing choice, not only y(x)=8. The decomposition behind this splits \mathbb{E}[L] into a piece that depends on y(x) (driven to zero exactly at the conditional mean) and a piece that does not (the irreducible noise), so no other constant can do better.
Answer. \mathbb{E}[t\mid x] = 6. Expected loss at y=8 is 110/3 \approx 36.67; at y=6 it is 98/3 \approx 32.67, confirming the conditional mean wins.
crumbs: 5  Week 2 practice: Decision theory and graphical models

title: Week 2 practice: Decision theory and graphical models
section: Problem 4: Counting parameters for five variables
text:
Problem 4: Counting parameters for five variables
Take N=5 binary variables x_1,\dots,x_5. Using the chain rule in the order x_1,\dots,x_5 with no assumptions, how many parameters does the factorization need?
Now suppose we are willing to assume x_5 depends only on x_2 and x_4 (not on x_1 or x_3), while every other factor stays as general as before. How many parameters does the factorization need now, and how many were saved?






TipWorked solution





This uses Week 2, Free parameters and the cost of the full joint and Why factor the joint.
With no assumptions, the chain rule gives p(x_1)p(x_2\mid x_1)p(x_3\mid x_1,x_2)p(x_4\mid x_1,x_2,x_3)p(x_5\mid x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4). Each factor p(x_j\mid x_1,\dots,x_{j-1}) needs 2^{j-1} parameters, so the totals are 1,2,4,8,16 for j=1,\dots,5, summing to 1+2+4+8+16=31, matching 2^5-1=31 exactly.
Replacing the last factor with p(x_5\mid x_2,x_4) shrinks its table from 2^4=16 parameters (one per configuration of four parents) to 2^2=4 (one per configuration of two parents). The new total is 1+2+4+8+4 = 19.
Savings: 31-19=12 parameters, all from dropping x_5’s dependence on x_1 and x_3. This is the same pattern as the lecture’s N=4 example: dropping dependence on conditioning variables shrinks that one factor’s table exponentially, and the saving compounds because that factor was the largest one in the sum.
Answer. No assumptions: 31 parameters. With x_5\mid x_2,x_4: 19 parameters. Savings: 12.
crumbs: 5  Week 2 practice: Decision theory and graphical models

title: Week 2 practice: Decision theory and graphical models
section: Problem 5: CPT sizes for an invented graph
text:
Problem 5: CPT sizes for an invented graph
Consider a DAG on five binary nodes y_1,\dots,y_5 with edges y_1 \to y_2, y_1 \to y_3, y_2 \to y_4, y_3 \to y_4, y_4 \to y_5 (so y_4 has two parents, y_2 and y_3).
For each node, state its parent count K_i and its CPT size 2^{K_i}. Sum these to get the total number of parameters, and compare to the 2^5-1 a fully-connected DAG on five nodes would need.






TipWorked solution





This uses Week 2, Directed graphical models.
Read the parent count off the incoming edges at each node:

y_1: no parents, K=0, CPT size 2^0=1.
y_2: one parent (y_1), K=1, CPT size 2^1=2.
y_3: one parent (y_1), K=1, CPT size 2.
y_4: two parents (y_2,y_3), K=2, CPT size 2^2=4.
y_5: one parent (y_4), K=1, CPT size 2.

Total: 1+2+2+4+2 = 11 parameters, against 2^5-1=31 for the fully-connected case on five nodes. The saving comes from every node having at most two parents instead of depending on every node before it; y_4’s CPT is the largest single piece because it is the only node with two parents.
Answer. K = (0,1,1,2,1), CPT sizes (1,2,2,4,2), total 11 parameters, versus 31 fully connected.
crumbs: 5  Week 2 practice: Decision theory and graphical models

title: Week 2 practice: Decision theory and graphical models
section: Problem 6: Chain, common cause, or collider?
text:
Problem 6: Chain, common cause, or collider?
Three sensors on a machine: a temperature reading (X), an internal wear level (Y), and a vibration reading (Z). Consider this causal story: high internal wear (Y) tends to raise both the temperature reading (X) and the vibration reading (Z), but the temperature and vibration sensors do not affect each other directly: X \leftarrow Y \rightarrow Z.
Which of the lecture’s three canonical structures is this? Are X and Z independent before observing Y? What happens once Y (the wear level) is observed?






TipWorked solution





This uses Week 2, Conditional independence: three canonical structures.
This is the common cause structure, X \leftarrow Y \rightarrow Z, with wear level Y as the shared cause of both readings.
Marginally (before observing Y), X and Z are dependent: a high temperature reading is evidence of high wear, which in turn makes a high vibration reading more likely, so the two readings move together even though neither sensor affects the other. This is the same “two effects of a shared cause are correlated” pattern as the lecture’s deadline example.
Once Y is observed, the joint factors as p(y)p(x\mid y)p(z\mid y), so p(x,z\mid y) = p(x\mid y)p(z\mid y): conditioning on the wear level uses up the shared explanation, and X \perp Z \mid Y. Knowing the wear level directly, the temperature reading tells us nothing more about the vibration reading.
Answer. Common cause. X and Z are marginally dependent, and become conditionally independent given Y: X \perp Z \mid Y.
crumbs: 5  Week 2 practice: Decision theory and graphical models

title: Week 2 practice: Decision theory and graphical models
section: Problem 7: Bayes Ball on a small graph
text:
Problem 7: Bayes Ball on a small graph
Consider a DAG with edges p \to q, r \to q, q \to s, r \to t (so q is a collider with parents p and r, and r also has a second child t).

Is p \perp r \mid \emptyset (no conditioning set)?
Is p \perp r \mid \{s\}?
Is p \perp t \mid \{r\}?

For each, name the only path between the two nodes, identify the junction type(s) on it, and apply the Bayes Ball rules.






TipWorked solution





This uses Week 2, The Bayes Ball algorithm.
1. p \perp r \mid \emptyset. The only path between p and r is p \to q \leftarrow r. Here q is a collider. With C=\emptyset, neither q nor any descendant of q (that is, s) is in C, so the collider is blocked. The one path is blocked, so p \perp r \mid \emptyset.
2. p \perp r \mid \{s\}. Same path, p \to q \leftarrow r, same collider q. Now C=\{s\}, and s is a descendant of the collider q (via q \to s), so the collider is open: shading a descendant of a collider opens it, exactly the explaining-away rule. The path is active, so p \not\perp r \mid \{s\}. Conditioning on s, which is not even on the direct route between p and r, is what creates the dependency, the same pattern as the lecture’s c-shaded example.
3. p \perp t \mid \{r\}. The only path between p and t is p \to q \leftarrow r \to t. There are two junctions: q is a collider (parents p,r), and r is a fork on this path (edges r\to q and r\to t both point out of r). With C=\{r\}: at the fork r, r is shaded, so the fork is blocked. That already blocks the whole path regardless of q (checking anyway: at the collider q, neither q nor its descendant s is in C=\{r\}, so q is also blocked). So p \perp t \mid \{r\}.
Answer. (1) p\perp r\mid\emptyset: yes. (2) p\perp r\mid\{s\}: no. (3) p\perp t\mid\{r\}: yes.
