Figure 6. A precision matrix’s nonzero pattern (shaded cells; diagonal is always nonzero) determines the graph edges directly: here K_{12},K_{23},K_{34},K_{45},K_{15} are nonzero and every other off-diagonal entry is zero, giving the 5-cycle 1\text{-}2\text{-}3\text{-}4\text{-}5\text{-}1.






Note



Practice question. For the precision matrix in Figure 6, is X_1 \perp X_3? Is X_1 \perp X_3 \mid X_2?
Solution. Marginal independence is governed by \Sigma, not K, so the zero pattern of K alone does not answer the first question; in general \Sigma_{13}\neq 0 even though K_{13}=0, since matrix inversion mixes entries. For the conditional question, K_{13}=0 directly gives X_1 \perp X_3 \mid X_{\text{rest}} = X_1 \perp X_3 \mid \{X_2,X_4,X_5\}, conditioning on every other variable, not just X_2. Whether X_1\perp X_3\mid X_2 alone holds is a separate, graph-separation question: in the 5-cycle, removing only node 2 leaves a path 1-5-4-3 still connecting 1 and 3, so \{2\} does not separate them and X_1\not\perp X_3\mid X_2 in general.








Note



Homework-relevant. Fitting a Gaussian graphical model by maximum likelihood is a direct continuous-variable analogue of Week 1’s Bernoulli MLE (Maximum likelihood estimation in Week 1): same “write the log-likelihood, then optimize” pattern, different sufficient statistic.


Suppose we observe i.i.d. data \boldsymbol{x}_{1:n} = \{\boldsymbol{x}_1,\dots,\boldsymbol{x}_n\} from an m-variate Gaussian with (for simplicity, after centering the data) mean zero, and write K=\Sigma^{-1}. The log-density is \log f(\boldsymbol{x}; K) = -\tfrac{m}{2}\log(2\pi) + \tfrac{1}{2}\log\det K - \tfrac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{x}^\top K \boldsymbol{x}. Dropping the constant that does not involve K, the log-likelihood over n points is \ell_n(K;\boldsymbol{x}_{1:n}) = \frac{n}{2}\log\det(K) - \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^n \boldsymbol{x}_i^\top K \boldsymbol{x}_i. The sum simplifies using the trace identity u^\top K u = \mathrm{tr}(Kuu^\top) and linearity of trace: \sum_{i=1}^n \boldsymbol{x}_i^\top K \boldsymbol{x}_i = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathrm{tr}(K\boldsymbol{x}_i\boldsymbol{x}_i^\top) = n\,\mathrm{tr}(K S_n), S_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \boldsymbol{x}_i \boldsymbol{x}_i^\top, where S_n is the sample covariance matrix, playing the same role here that the sample mean played in Week 1’s Bernoulli MLE: it is the sufficient statistic that summarizes all n data points for the purpose of estimating K. Substituting back, \ell_n(K;\boldsymbol{x}_{1:n}) = \frac{n}{2}\big(\log\det(K) - \mathrm{tr}(KS_n)\big). Two facts about this objective, useful for actually solving the maximization: \log\det(K) is a strictly concave function of K, so the objective has at most one maximizer, and exactly one when S_n is invertible, and \mathrm{tr}(KS_n) is linear in K. Their gradients are \nabla \log\det(K) = K^{-1} and \nabla\, \mathrm{tr}(KS_n) = S_n, so setting the gradient of \ell_n to zero gives K^{-1} = S_n, i.e. the maximum likelihood estimate of the covariance matrix is simply the sample covariance matrix, and \hat K_{\text{MLE}} = S_n^{-1}: the same “set the derivative to zero, read off an empirical average” pattern as every MLE derivation so far this course, just with a matrix-valued statistic in place of a scalar one.






TipRecap: Gaussian graphical models





What the symbols stand for:

m: the number of variables. \mu: the mean vector.
\Sigma: the covariance matrix. \Sigma_{ij} measures how X_i and X_j move together when nothing else is fixed.
K = \Sigma^{-1}: the precision matrix. K_{ij} = 0 means X_i and X_j are independent given all the others.
\Sigma_{AB} and similar: blocks of \Sigma for the variable groups A and B.
S_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i \boldsymbol{x}_i\boldsymbol{x}_i^\top: the sample covariance of centred data.
\mathrm{tr}(\cdot): the trace, the sum of a matrix’s diagonal entries.

Taking the equations apart:

In the conditional, the mean \mu_A + \Sigma_{AB}\Sigma_{BB}^{-1}(x_B - \mu_B) starts at the prior mean and shifts by how far x_B landed from its own mean, scaled by how strongly A and B co-vary.
The conditional covariance \Sigma_{AA} - \Sigma_{AB}\Sigma_{BB}^{-1}\Sigma_{BA} is the prior spread minus what observing B explains. It does not involve x_B.
The log-likelihood \frac{n}{2}(\log\det K - \mathrm{tr}(KS_n)) has the data only through S_n, and its maximum is at K^{-1} = S_n.

A teaching example. Take three variables with precision matrix and covariance
K = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}, \Sigma = K^{-1} = \frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}.
K_{13} = 0, so the graph is the chain 1 - 2 - 3 and X_1 \perp X_3 \mid X_2. But \Sigma_{13} = 0.25 \neq 0, so X_1 and X_3 are dependent when X_2 is not observed. The middle formula confirms the conditional statement: \Sigma_{13} - \Sigma_{12}\Sigma_{22}^{-1}\Sigma_{23} = 0.25 - 0.5 \cdot 1 \cdot 0.5 = 0.

title: Week 3: Markov Random Fields and Exact Inference
section: Exact inference as a conditional distribution
text:
Exact inference as a conditional distribution
Everything up to here has been about representation: which distributions a graph describes, and how to parameterize them. Having built up two families of graphical models (DAGs in Week 2, MRFs in this lecture), we now turn to computation, with a question common to both: given the model, how do we compute an actual number?

Definition. In a graphical model over \boldsymbol{x}, split the variables into x_E (the observed evidence), x_F (the unobserved variable(s) we want to infer), and x_R = \boldsymbol{x} - \{x_F,x_E\} (remaining variables, summed out). Inference is computing the conditional distribution p(x_F\mid x_E) = \frac{p(x_F,x_E)}{p(x_E)} = \frac{p(x_F,x_E)}{\sum_{x_F} p(x_F,x_E)}, where the joint over the subject of inference and the evidence is obtained by marginalizing out the remaining variables, p(x_F,x_E) = \sum_{x_R} p(x_F,x_E,x_R).







TipQuestion: When does the 1/Z appear, and why does it cancel?





Where 1/Z comes from. An MRF defines its joint through potentials, not probabilities. The potentials need not sum to 1, so the product is scaled by a constant: p(\boldsymbol{x}) = \frac{1}{Z}\prod_c \psi_c(x_c), \qquad Z = \sum_{\boldsymbol{x}}\prod_c \psi_c(x_c). Z is the sum of the unnormalized product over every configuration of every variable, so that p sums to 1. This is the form that carries 1/Z. Any time we write a joint as potentials, the constant has to be there or the result is not a probability.
Why the definition does not show it. In the definition, p means the joint, and the joint is already normalized. Marginalizing a normalized joint gives a normalized marginal, so p(x_F, x_E) = \sum_{x_R} p(x_F, x_E, x_R) is a probability with no extra constant. The 1/Z is inside p, hidden in the symbol.
Where it cancels. Expand both p terms in the potential form. The numerator and the denominator each pick up the same 1/Z, so it cancels in the ratio: p(x_F\mid x_E) = \frac{\frac{1}{Z}\sum_{x_R}\prod_c \psi_c}{\frac{1}{Z}\sum_{x_F,x_R}\prod_c \psi_c} = \frac{\sum_{x_R}\prod_c \psi_c}{\sum_{x_F,x_R}\prod_c \psi_c}. The denominator is p(x_E) times Z: the sum over x_F and x_R with x_E fixed is the probability of the evidence, unnormalized. This is why the week 4 derivation can drop the 1/Z and let a single normalizing sum do the work.
Where it never appears. A DAG defines its joint as a product of conditional probabilities, such as p(x_1)\,p(x_2 \mid x_1). Each factor already sums to 1 over its own variable, so the product is already normalized and no Z is needed.
A teaching example. Take two binary variables X and Y joined by one MRF edge with \psi(x,y) = 2 when x = y and \psi(x,y) = 1 when x \neq y. Here \psi(0,0) = \psi(1,1) = 2 and \psi(0,1) = \psi(1,0) = 1, so Z = 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 6. Observe Y = 1 and ask for p(X = 0 \mid Y = 1).

With the constant: p(X = 0, Y = 1) = \tfrac{1}{6}\,\psi(0,1) = \tfrac{1}{6} and p(Y = 1) = \tfrac{1}{6}(\psi(0,1) + \psi(1,1)) = \tfrac{1}{6}(1 + 2) = \tfrac{1}{2}, so p(X = 0 \mid Y = 1) = \tfrac{1/6}{1/2} = \tfrac{1}{3}.
Without the constant: \psi(0,1) / (\psi(0,1) + \psi(1,1)) = 1 / 3.

The two routes agree. The \tfrac{1}{6} appears in both numerator and denominator and cancels, so the conditional does not need Z at all.



Both the numerator and the normalizing sum over x_F require summing over x_R (and, for the denominator, over x_F too), so the real computational question is how to perform these sums efficiently, which is exactly what variable elimination addresses.






TipRecap: Exact inference as a conditional distribution





What the symbols stand for:

x_F: the variables we are asking about (the query).
x_E: the variables we have observed (the evidence).
x_R: every other variable, which we neither ask about nor observe.

Taking the two equations apart:

p(x_F, x_E) = \sum_{x_R} p(x_F, x_E, x_R): sum out the variables we do not care about, to get a joint over the query and the evidence.
p(x_F \mid x_E) = p(x_F, x_E) / \sum_{x_F} p(x_F, x_E): divide by the total over the query, which is the probability of the evidence. This is the “joint over marginal” rule from Week 1.

A teaching example on the chain A \to B \to C with p(A{=}1) = 0.2, p(B{=}1 \mid A{=}1) = 0.9, p(B{=}1 \mid A{=}0) = 0.3, p(C{=}1 \mid B{=}1) = 0.8, p(C{=}1 \mid B{=}0) = 0.1. We observe C = 1 and ask about A, so x_F = A, x_E = C, x_R = B.

p(A{=}1, C{=}1) = 0.2\,[0.9(0.8) + 0.1(0.1)] = 0.2 \times 0.73 = 0.146.
p(A{=}0, C{=}1) = 0.8\,[0.3(0.8) + 0.7(0.1)] = 0.8 \times 0.31 = 0.248.
Normalize: p(A{=}1 \mid C{=}1) = 0.146 / (0.146 + 0.248) \approx 0.37, up from the prior 0.2.

title: Week 3: Markov Random Fields and Exact Inference
text:
Variable elimination
The definition above reduces inference to sums over x_R. Done naively, a sum over n variables with k states each enumerates all k^n joint settings. The factorizations of Weeks 2 and 3 are what let us do better.
The order in which we marginalize out variables changes the computational cost dramatically, even though the final answer is the same regardless of order (summation commutes). Variable elimination is a simple, general exact-inference algorithm that applies to any graphical model, DAG or MRF, whose computational complexity depends on the graph structure and the chosen elimination order; it is a form of dynamic programming that avoids enumerating every joint assignment.
Worked example: a simple chain. Consider A\to B\to C\to D, and suppose we want the marginal p(D) with no evidence, so x_F=\{D\}, x_E=\{\}, x_R=\{A,B,C\}. Week 2’s chain rule gives p(A,B,C,D) = p(A)p(B\mid A)p(C\mid B)p(D\mid C).


  
    
      
    
  
  A simple chain
  
  
  
  
  A
  
  B
  
  C
  
  D


Figure 7. A chain of four variables, used to compare naive marginalization against variable elimination.
Assume each variable takes k possible values. Marginalizing naively, p(D) = \sum_{A,B,C} p(A,B,C,D) = \sum_C \sum_B \sum_A p(A)p(B\mid A)p(C\mid B)p(D\mid C), costs O(k^4): every joint assignment of the four variables must be visited. Instead, choose an elimination order and push each sum as far inward as it will go, past every factor that does not mention the variable being summed: p(D) = \sum_C p(D\mid C) \left(\sum_B p(C\mid B) \sum_A p(A)p(B\mid A)\right). Working from the inside out, the innermost sum depends only on B once A is gone: \sum_A p(A)p(B\mid A) = p(B). Substituting back and repeating the same move for B: \sum_B p(C\mid B)\,p(B) = p(C). So the whole expression collapses to p(D) = \sum_C p(D\mid C)\,p(C). Every intermediate sum here touches at most two variables at once (k^2 terms), and there are n such sums, so the total cost is O(nk^2), compared to O(k^n) for constructing and marginalizing the full joint table directly: an exponential-to-polynomial improvement from exactly the same reordering trick that made Week 2’s chain-rule factorization efficient (Why factor the joint in Week 2).






TipQuestion: Where do the costs nk squared and k to the n actually come from?





What the symbols stand for:

n: the number of variables in the chain (here A, B, C, D, so n = 4).
k: the number of values each variable can take (for binary variables, k = 2).

How to count the cost of a sum. We count how many terms get evaluated, written in big O notation (keep only the fastest-growing part, drop constants).

For one sum, list every variable it mentions: the variable being summed out, plus any variable the result still depends on.
If it mentions m variables, it has to evaluate one product for every joint setting of those m variables, which is k^m terms.
Add up the cost of every sum you perform, then keep the dominant term.

The naive way. \sum_{A,B,C} p(A,B,C,D) is one sum that mentions all four variables: we must fill in a table with one entry per joint setting of (A, B, C, D), so m = n and the cost is k^n terms.
Variable elimination. Each step mentions only two variables:

\sum_A p(A)\,p(B \mid A) mentions A and B. For each of the k values of B we add up k terms (one per value of A): k \times k = k^2 terms.
\sum_B p(C \mid B)\,p(B) mentions B and C: again k^2 terms.
\sum_C p(D \mid C)\,p(C) mentions C and D: again k^2 terms.

That is n - 1 = 3 sums of k^2 terms each, so (n-1)k^2 in total, which is O(nk^2).
With invented numbers. Suppose each variable has k = 10 values.



Chain length
Naive (k^n)
Elimination ((n-1)k^2)




n = 4
10^4 = 10{,}000
3 \times 100 = 300


n = 20
10^{20}
19 \times 100 = 1{,}900



Adding one more variable multiplies the naive cost by k but only adds k^2 to the elimination cost. That is the exponential-to-polynomial gap: n sits in the exponent for the naive table and only as a multiplier for elimination.



Elimination ordering matters, and finding the best one is hard. The complexity of variable elimination depends on the chosen order, since different orders leave different numbers of variables inside each intermediate sum. Unfortunately, finding the elimination ordering that minimizes the worst intermediate sum is NP-hard in general, so in practice orderings are chosen by heuristics (or, in this course, simply given).






TipRecap: Variable elimination





What the symbols stand for:

k: the number of values each variable can take. n: the number of variables.
O(k^n): cost grows like k^n, the size of the full joint table.
O(nk^2): cost grows like n small sums, each over two variables.

Taking the rearranged sum apart:
p(D) = \sum_C p(D \mid C) \Big(\sum_B p(C \mid B)\,\tau(B)\Big), \tau(B) = \sum_A p(A)\,p(B \mid A) = p(B).

Each \sum is moved as far right as it can go, past every factor that does not contain its variable.
The innermost sum only touches A and B, so it is a small table. Its result, p(B), then feeds the next sum.
The answer is the same as the naive sum, because we only regrouped additions and multiplications.

A teaching example with binary A \to B \to C: p(A{=}1) = 0.6, p(B{=}1 \mid A{=}1) = 0.7, p(B{=}1 \mid A{=}0) = 0.2, p(C{=}1 \mid B{=}1) = 0.9, p(C{=}1 \mid B{=}0) = 0.4.

Eliminate A: p(B{=}1) = 0.6(0.7) + 0.4(0.2) = 0.5.
Eliminate B: p(C{=}1) = 0.5(0.9) + 0.5(0.4) = 0.65.

Each step was a two-term sum. For a chain of 10 binary variables, the naive table has 2^{10} = 1024 entries, while elimination does about 10 \times 2^2 = 40 multiplications.

title: Week 3: Markov Random Fields and Exact Inference
section: Sum-product inference: unifying DAGMs and MRFs
text:
Sum-product inference: unifying DAGMs and MRFs
The chain example eliminated variables from a DAG’s conditional probabilities. Since the point of this lecture is MRFs, we need to check that the same algorithm works when the factors are clique potentials that need not sum to 1.
Variable elimination on a DAG is really the same algorithm as on an MRF, once we notice that a DAG’s conditional probability tables are themselves just a special kind of nonnegative potential. So we give every conditional probability table (or every MRF potential) one name: a nonnegative factor.
Take a small DAG on four variables X, A, B, C, and suppose we want the marginal over A, B, C: p(A,B,C) = \sum_X p(X)\,p(A\mid X)\,p(B\mid A)\,p(C\mid B,X). Rename each conditional probability table as a factor:



Factor
Conditional probability table
Variables it touches




\phi_1(X)
p(X)
X


\phi_2(A,X)
p(A\mid X)
A, X


\phi_3(A,B)
p(B\mid A)
A, B


\phi_4(X,B,C)
p(C\mid B,X)
X, B, C



The marginal becomes a sum of a product of factors: p(A,B,C) = \sum_X \phi_1(X)\,\phi_2(A,X)\,\phi_3(A,B)\,\phi_4(X,B,C). The table shows that \phi_3 does not touch X, so it can be pulled outside the sum over X: p(A,B,C) = \phi_3(A,B) \sum_X \phi_1(X)\,\phi_2(A,X)\,\phi_4(X,B,C). The remaining sum leaves a function of A, B, C only. Call it \tau: \tau(A,B,C) = \sum_X \phi_1(X)\,\phi_2(A,X)\,\phi_4(X,B,C), \qquad p(A,B,C) = \phi_3(A,B)\,\tau(A,B,C). This \tau is an intermediate factor. It is generally not any of the original conditional probability tables; it is simply whatever function of the remaining variables the sum happened to produce. This is the mechanical step that repeats at every stage of variable elimination.
Abstractly, both DAG and MRF inference reduce to the same sum-product computation:

p(x_F\mid x_E) \propto \tau(x_F,x_E) = \sum_{x_R} \prod_{C\in\mathcal{F}} \psi_C(x_C).

The symbols are:

x_F: the variables we want a distribution over.
x_E: the observed evidence.
x_R: the rest, summed out.
\mathcal{F}: the set of factors, each a group of variables C with its potential \psi_C.

The only difference between the two model types is where \mathcal{F} comes from:

DAG: one factor per node i, on the variables \{i\}\cup\text{parents}(i) (its conditional probability table).
MRF: one factor per maximal clique.







TipRecap: Sum-product inference: unifying DAGMs and MRFs





What the symbols stand for:

\phi_i or \psi_C: a factor, any nonnegative table over a few variables. Conditional probability tables and MRF potentials are both factors. (This \phi is a factor, not the feature vector \phi_C of MRFs as exponential families.)
\mathcal{F}: the set of all factors in the model.
\tau: an intermediate factor, the table left over after summing a variable out of a product of factors.

Taking the sum-product formula apart:

\prod_{C \in \mathcal{F}} \psi_C(x_C): multiply all factors to score one full setting. This is the product.
\sum_{x_R}: add those scores over the variables we do not care about. This is the sum.
The result \tau(x_F, x_E) is proportional to the posterior. For an MRF the proportionality constant is not 1, so we still divide by \sum_{x_F} \tau.

A teaching example on the MRF chain X_1 - X_2 - X_3 with \psi_{1,2}(a,b) = 3 if a = b and 1 otherwise, and \psi_{2,3}(0,0) = 1, \psi_{2,3}(0,1) = 2, \psi_{2,3}(1,0) = 4, \psi_{2,3}(1,1) = 1. We want p(x_3).

Eliminate X_1: \tau(x_2) = \sum_{x_1}\psi_{1,2}(x_1, x_2) = 3 + 1 = 4 for both values of x_2.
Eliminate X_2: \tau(x_3) = \sum_{x_2} \tau(x_2)\,\psi_{2,3}(x_2, x_3), which is 4(1) + 4(4) = 20 for x_3 = 0 and 4(2) + 4(1) = 12 for x_3 = 1.
Normalize: the total is 32 (which is Z), so p(X_3{=}1) = 12/32 = 0.375. Unlike a DAG, this last division was needed.

title: Week 3: Markov Random Fields and Exact Inference
section: Worked example: variable elimination on a Bayes net
text:
Worked example: variable elimination on a Bayes net
On the chain of Variable elimination, every intermediate sum involved at most two variables. On a graph with more branching, an intermediate factor can involve several variables, and the elimination order decides how many. The lecture’s student network shows this, using the sum-product form just stated. First, the general procedure for computing a marginal p(x_F) with nothing observed.

Recipe.

List the factors. Write the joint as a product of factors and record the factor set \mathcal{F}. For a DAG this is one conditional probability table per node; for an MRF it is one potential per maximal clique.
Pick what to sum out. Every variable outside the query x_F gets summed out. Fix an order for eliminating them (here the order is given; finding the best one is NP-hard, Variable elimination).
Eliminate one variable at a time. For the next variable in the order:

collect every factor that mentions it, whether original or intermediate;
multiply those factors and sum the variable out;
the result is a new intermediate factor \tau over the other variables those factors touched;
remove the factors you used and add \tau in their place.

Multiply what is left. Once only query variables remain, the product of the remaining factors is \tau(x_F) \propto p(x_F).
Normalize if needed. Divide by \sum_{x_F}\tau(x_F). For a DAG built from its own conditional probability tables this sum is already 1; for an MRF it is not.
Read off the cost. Let N_i be the number of variables in the product formed when eliminating variable i. The largest N_i sets the cost.




  
    
      
    
  
  A Bayes net example
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  C
  
  D
  
  I
  
  G
  
  S
  
  L
  
  J
  
  H


Figure 8. A Bayes net over Coherence C, Difficulty D, Intelligence I, Grade G, SAT S, Letter L, Job J, and Happiness H.
This graph gives the factorization p(C,D,I,G,S,L,H,J) = p(C)p(D\mid C)p(I)\,p(G\mid D,I)p(L\mid G)p(S\mid I)p(J\mid S,L)p(H\mid J,G). Reading off one factor per node (its own conditional probability table), \mathcal{F} = \big\{\{C\},\{C,D\},\{I\},\{G,D,I\},\{L,G\},\{S,I\},\{J,S,L\},\{H,J,G\}\big\}, so m=|\mathcal{F}|=8.
Suppose we want p(J), the probability of getting a job, with the elimination order C,D,I,H,G,S,L (an ordering the instructor supplies; finding an optimal one is the NP-hard problem from Variable elimination). Eliminate C first: it appears only in \psi(C) and \psi(C,D), so \sum_C \psi(C)\,\psi(C,D) = \tau(D). Eliminate D next, in \psi(G,D,I) and the new \tau(D): \sum_D \psi(G,D,I)\,\tau(D) = \tau(G,I). Eliminate I, in \psi(S,I), \psi(I), and \tau(G,I): \sum_I \psi(S,I)\,\psi(I)\,\tau(G,I) = \tau(S,G). Eliminate H, which appears only in \psi(H,G,J): \sum_H \psi(H,G,J) = \tau(G,J). Eliminate G, now present in \psi(L,G), \tau(S,G), and \tau(G,J): \sum_G \psi(L,G)\,\tau(S,G)\,\tau(G,J) = \tau(J,L,S). Eliminate S, in \psi(J,L,S) and \tau(J,L,S): \sum_S \psi(J,L,S)\,\tau(J,L,S) = \tau(J,L). Finally eliminate L: \sum_L \tau(J,L) = \tau(J). The result, \tau(J), is proportional to p(J); since Z=1 for a DAG’s own conditional probability tables (they are already properly normalized), no further rescaling is needed here, though for a general MRF the final \tau would still require dividing by \sum_{x_F}\tau(x_F) to become an actual probability.
Reading off the complexity. Each sum above is labeled by how many variables appear inside it: \sum_C has N_C=2 (namely C,D), \sum_D has N_D=3 (G,D,I), \sum_I has N_I=3 (S,I,G), \sum_H has N_H=3 (H,G,J), \sum_G has N_G=4 (L,G,S,J, the largest), \sum_S has N_S=3, and \sum_L has N_L=2. The complexity of variable elimination under a given ordering is O\big(m\,k^{N_{\max}}\big), \qquad N_{\max}=\max_i N_i, where m is the number of initial factors and k is the (assumed common) number of states per variable. Here N_{\max}=4 (achieved at the G-elimination step), so the cost of this particular ordering is O(8k^4): substantially better than enumerating the full 8-variable joint, but not as good as the chain example of Variable elimination, because this graph has a genuinely more complex dependency structure than a simple chain.






TipRecap: Worked example: variable elimination on a Bayes net





What the symbols stand for:

C, D, I, G, S, L, J, H: the eight variables of the student network (Figure 8).
\psi(\cdot): an original factor, here one conditional probability table per node.
\tau(\cdot): an intermediate factor created by an elimination step, named by the variables it still depends on.
N_i: the number of variables inside the product when variable i is eliminated. N_{\max}: the largest N_i.
m: the number of original factors (8 here). k: values per variable.

Taking the cost formula O(m\,k^{N_{\max}}) apart:

Eliminating a variable means building a table over all N_i variables in the product, which has k^{N_i} entries.
The biggest such table dominates, which gives k^{N_{\max}}.
There are about m elimination steps, which gives the factor m.

A teaching example: why the order matters. Suppose we eliminated G first instead of fifth. G appears in \psi(G, D, I), \psi(L, G), and \psi(H, J, G), so the product touches G, D, I, L, H, J: six variables. With k = 10 that one step builds a table of 10^6 entries. The lecture’s order never goes above four variables, at most 10^4 entries per step, so roughly 8 \times 10^4 in total. Enumerating the full joint would mean 10^8 entries.

title: Week 3: Markov Random Fields and Exact Inference
text:
Variable elimination with evidence
Inference as defined in Exact inference as a conditional distribution usually conditions on observed evidence x_E, but the student-network example computed a marginal with nothing observed. Reintroducing evidence changes only which variable is fixed rather than summed. The general procedure for a posterior p(x_F\mid \bar x_E), where \bar x_E are the observed values:

Recipe.

Split the variables. Sort them into the query x_F, the evidence x_E, and the rest x_R.
Clamp the evidence. Substitute the observed values \bar x_E into every factor that mentions an evidence variable. Those factors now depend only on their other variables. Evidence variables are never summed over.
Eliminate the rest. Run the recipe from Worked example: variable elimination on a Bayes net over x_R only. The result is \tau(x_F) = p(x_F, \bar x_E). A factor that sums to 1 over the variable being eliminated, such as the conditional probability table of an unobserved leaf, drops out as a 1.
Normalize. Divide by the sum over the query: p(x_F\mid \bar x_E) = \frac{\tau(x_F)}{\sum_{x_F}\tau(x_F)}. This step is needed even for a DAG, because the denominator equals p(\bar x_E), not 1.


Worked example. Take the DAG X_1 \to X_2 \to X_4, X_1 \to X_3 \to X_5 \to X_6, X_2 \to X_6 (so X_6 has two parents, X_2 and X_5), giving p(x_1,\dots,x_6) = p(x_1)p(x_2\mid x_1)p(x_3\mid x_1)p(x_4\mid x_2)p(x_5\mid x_3)p(x_6\mid x_2,x_5). Suppose X_6=\bar x_6 is observed and we want p(X_1\mid \bar x_6), so x_F=\{x_1\}, x_E=\{x_6\}, x_R=\{x_2,x_3,x_4,x_5\}. By the definition in Exact inference as a conditional distribution, p(x_1\mid \bar x_6) = \frac{p(x_1,\bar x_6)}{\sum_{x_1} p(x_1,\bar x_6)}. Computing the numerator by variable elimination in the order 5,4,3,2 (the nested sums below run from x_2 outermost to x_5 innermost) (the observed value \bar x_6 is simply substituted into p(x_6\mid x_2,x_5) wherever it appears, rather than summed over): p(x_1,\bar x_6) = p(x_1)\sum_{x_2} p(x_2\mid x_1)\sum_{x_3} p(x_3\mid x_1)\sum_{x_4} p(x_4\mid x_2)\sum_{x_5} p(x_5\mid x_3)\,p(\bar x_6\mid x_2,x_5). The innermost sum over x_5 produces a new factor depending on x_2,x_3: \sum_{x_5} p(x_5\mid x_3)\,p(\bar x_6\mid x_2,x_5) = p(\bar x_6\mid x_2,x_3).






TipQuestion: Why does summing over x5 give p(x6 | x2, x3)?





Fast test procedure. To sum out a variable x_s from a product of DAG conditionals:

Find the factors that contain x_s. These are x_s’s own table and the tables of its children.
If x_s appears in no factor except its own table, drop that table. A conditional summed over its own left-hand variable equals 1.
Collect the new factor’s variables. These are the other variables in the kept factors: the parents of x_s, the children of x_s, and the other parents of those children.
Sort by side. Query variables go on the left, along with any children of x_s. Everything else goes on the right.

The four examples below use the same procedure.
Example 1 (the question above). Summing x_5 from p(x_5\mid x_3)\,p(\bar x_6\mid x_2,x_5) keeps both factors, since x_5 is a child of x_3 and a parent of x_6. The new factor is over x_2, x_3, x_6. With x_6 as the query, the answer is p(\bar x_6\mid x_2,x_3).
Example 2: no children left. In p(x_6\mid x_2)\sum_{x_5} p(x_5\mid x_3), the only factor containing x_5 is its own table, so step 2 drops it and it sums to 1. The answer is p(x_6\mid x_2), and x_3 does not appear.
Example 3: a chain. For \sum_{x_5} p(x_5\mid x_3)\,p(x_7\mid x_5), the child x_7 has no other parents. The new factor is over x_3 and x_7, with x_7 on the left, giving p(x_7\mid x_3).
Example 4: two children. For \sum_{x_3} p(x_3\mid x_1)\,p(x_6\mid x_2,x_3)\,p(x_8\mid x_3), the variable x_3 has two children, x_6 and x_8, so both go on the left. The answer is a joint, p(x_6,x_8\mid x_1,x_2), not a product of two conditionals, because both children depend on the summed x_3. Its parents x_1 and x_2 go on the right.
MRFs. The same neighbor rule finds the variables, but a product of potentials \psi has no left or right side. The result is an unnormalized function of those variables, so write it without a bar.
The steps below prove Example 1.
The sum has a factor p(x_5\mid x_3) and a factor p(\bar x_6\mid x_2,x_5), and the claim is that adding over x_5 leaves a conditional that depends only on x_2 and x_3. The idea is to read the sum as a marginal of a joint distribution and then use the graph to simplify that joint.
Step 1: Write the target as a sum over x_5. A marginal is a sum over the variables left out of a joint. Here the variable left out is x_5, so p(\bar x_6\mid x_2,x_3) = \sum_{x_5} p(x_5,\bar x_6\mid x_2,x_3).
Step 2: Apply the chain rule to the joint. p(x_5,\bar x_6\mid x_2,x_3) = p(x_5\mid x_2,x_3)\;p(\bar x_6\mid x_2,x_3,x_5).
Step 3: Drop x_3 from the second factor. The parents of x_6 are x_2 and x_5. In a DAG, a node is independent of its other ancestors once its parents are known, so x_3 adds nothing: p(\bar x_6\mid x_2,x_3,x_5) = p(\bar x_6\mid x_2,x_5).
Step 4: Drop x_2 from the first factor. The only parent of x_5 is x_3, and x_2 is not a descendant of x_5. So once x_3 is known, x_2 tells us nothing more about x_5: p(x_5\mid x_2,x_3) = p(x_5\mid x_3). This works because the only path from x_5 to x_2 runs x_5 \leftarrow x_3 \leftarrow x_1 \rightarrow x_2, and conditioning on the middle node x_3 blocks it.
Step 5: Substitute back. Steps 2 to 4 give p(\bar x_6\mid x_2,x_3) = \sum_{x_5} p(x_5\mid x_3)\,p(\bar x_6\mid x_2,x_5), which is the identity we started from. The sum is not a cancellation. It runs over every value of x_5, weighting each by p(x_5\mid x_3), and that total is the conditional probability of \bar x_6.



The next sum, over x_4, involves only p(x_4\mid x_2), none of whose terms depend on x_4 after it is summed out (it sums to 1), so it drops out entirely: \sum_{x_4} p(x_4\mid x_2) = 1. This leaves p(x_1,\bar x_6) = p(x_1)\sum_{x_2} p(x_2\mid x_1)\sum_{x_3} p(x_3\mid x_1)\,p(\bar x_6\mid x_2,x_3). Summing x_3 next produces p(\bar x_6\mid x_1,x_2) (using \sum_{x_3}p(x_3\mid x_1)\,p(\bar x_6\mid x_2,x_3) = p(\bar x_6\mid x_1,x_2) by the product and sum rules), and then x_2: p(x_1,\bar x_6) = p(x_1)\sum_{x_2} p(x_2\mid x_1)\,p(\bar x_6\mid x_1,x_2) = p(x_1)\,p(\bar x_6\mid x_1). So the whole computation collapses to the two-factor product one would expect from a two-node chain X_1 \to X_6, even though the actual graph has six nodes; every other variable was marginalized away without ever touching a table larger than three variables at once. Normalizing gives the final answer: p(x_1\mid \bar x_6) = \frac{p(x_1)\,p(\bar x_6\mid x_1)}{\sum_{x_1} p(x_1)\,p(\bar x_6\mid x_1)}. This is Bayes’ rule from Week 1 (Worked example: a diagnostic test in Week 1), rederived as a special case of variable elimination: computing a posterior for a two-variable relationship, after algebraically marginalizing away every variable that connects them only indirectly.






TipRecap: Variable elimination with evidence





What the symbols stand for:

\bar x_E: the observed values of the evidence variables. The bar means “fixed at what we saw”.
Clamping: substituting \bar x_E into every factor that mentions an evidence variable, so that variable is no longer summed.
\tau(x_F) = p(x_F, \bar x_E): what elimination returns once evidence is clamped.

Taking the procedure apart:

Clamp first. A factor like p(\bar x_6 \mid x_2, x_5) is now a table over x_2, x_5 only.
Eliminate the rest as before. A variable whose only factor is its own table, with no children left, sums to 1 and disappears.
Normalize at the end: p(x_F \mid \bar x_E) = \tau(x_F) / \sum_{x_F} \tau(x_F). The denominator is p(\bar x_E), which is not 1.

A teaching example on X_1 \to X_2 \to X_3 with p(X_1{=}1) = 0.3, p(X_2{=}1 \mid X_1{=}1) = 0.8, p(X_2{=}1 \mid X_1{=}0) = 0.1, and any table for X_3. We observe X_2 = 1 and want p(X_1 \mid X_2{=}1).

Clamp X_2 = 1. Eliminate X_3: \sum_{x_3} p(x_3 \mid X_2{=}1) = 1, so it drops out.
\tau(X_1{=}1) = 0.3 \times 0.8 = 0.24 and \tau(X_1{=}0) = 0.7 \times 0.1 = 0.07.
Their sum, 0.31, is p(X_2{=}1). Dividing, p(X_1{=}1 \mid X_2{=}1) = 0.24 / 0.31 \approx 0.77.

title: Week 3: Markov Random Fields and Exact Inference
text:
Restricted Boltzmann machines
Variable elimination is exact but can be expensive, and every MRF query seems to need the partition function Z, itself a sum over all variables. The lecture closes with a model whose graph structure makes some queries cheap without ever computing Z. As a modern application tying together the Ising model, exponential families, and Hammersley-Clifford, consider a restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM): a special Ising model over visible variables X_1,\dots,X_k and hidden variables H_1,\dots,H_l, all in \{-1,+1\}, whose graph is bipartite: every H_i connects to every X_j, but no H_i-H_{i'} or X_j-X_{j'} edges exist at all.


  An RBM's bipartite graph
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  H1
  
  H2
  
  X1
  
  X2
  
  X3


Figure 9. An RBM’s graph: every hidden node connects to every visible node, and there are no hidden-hidden or visible-visible edges.
Writing the Ising-style distribution with per-edge potentials \psi_{X_i,H_j}(x_i,h_j) = \exp\{\frac{1}{l}\alpha_i x_i + \frac{1}{k}\beta_j h_j + J_{ij}x_ih_j\} (splitting the node biases evenly across the edges touching each node so that the product of edge potentials reproduces the full node bias), the joint is p(x_1,\dots,x_k,h_1,\dots,h_l) = \frac{1}{Z}\prod_{i=1}^k\prod_{j=1}^l \psi_{X_i,H_j}(x_i,h_j). Computing Z exactly can be expensive (it is a sum over all 2^{k+l} joint settings), but the bipartite structure lets us compute the two conditional distributions p(x\mid h) and p(h\mid x) efficiently, without ever needing Z. This is exactly what the Hammersley-Clifford theorem predicts: since there are no edges between different H_i’s, they are all mutually independent given X (every H_i-H_{i'} pair is separated by the fully-observed X, the same non-adjacent-pair rule from The Hammersley-Clifford theorem), so the joint conditional factors into a per-node product, and each factor can be computed on its own: p(h_j\mid x) = \frac{\prod_{i=1}^k \psi_{ij}(x_i,h_j)}{\prod_{i=1}^k\psi_{ij}(x_i,-1) + \prod_{i=1}^k\psi_{ij}(x_i,1)} = \sigma\Big(\beta_j + \sum_i J_{ij}x_i\Big), where \sigma(y) = \frac{e^y}{e^{-y}+e^y} = \frac{1}{1+e^{-2y}} is the sigmoid function. This gives a probabilistic reading of the sigmoid activation used in neural networks: it is exactly the conditional-probability formula that falls out of treating a layer of binary units as conditionally independent given the layer below, under an Ising-style pairwise potential.






TipRecap: Restricted Boltzmann machines





What the symbols stand for:

x_1, \dots, x_k: the visible units. h_1, \dots, h_l: the hidden units. All take values in \{-1, +1\}.
\alpha_i: the field on visible unit i. \beta_j: the field on hidden unit j.
J_{ij}: the coupling between visible unit i and hidden unit j.
\sigma(y) = 1/(1 + e^{-2y}): the sigmoid, in the form that matches \pm 1 spins.

Taking p(h_j \mid x) apart:

Given the visible units, every hidden unit is cut off from the other hidden units, so each one can be handled alone.
The terms in h_j’s exponent add to h_j\big(\beta_j + \sum_i J_{ij}x_i\big). Write y_j = \beta_j + \sum_i J_{ij}x_i for the bracket.
The probabilities of h_j = +1 and h_j = -1 are then proportional to e^{y_j} and e^{-y_j}. Normalizing gives e^{y_j}/(e^{y_j} + e^{-y_j}) = \sigma(y_j).
The \alpha_i terms are the same on top and bottom, so they cancel. So does Z.

A teaching example with one hidden unit, three visible units, \beta = 0.5, and couplings J = (1, -1, 0.5).

Visible x = (+1, +1, -1): y = 0.5 + 1 - 1 - 0.5 = 0, so p(h{=}{+1} \mid x) = \sigma(0) = 0.5.
Visible x = (+1, -1, +1): y = 0.5 + 1 + 1 + 0.5 = 3, so p(h{=}{+1} \mid x) = 1/(1 + e^{-6}) \approx 0.998.

Each visible unit that agrees with the sign of its coupling pushes the hidden unit toward +1.

title: Week 3: Markov Random Fields and Exact Inference
text:
Summary






Note



Key takeaways from Week 3:

Markov random fields (MRFs) model undirected interactions: p(\boldsymbol{x}) \propto \prod_{C\in\mathcal{C}} \psi_C(x_C) over maximal cliques \mathcal{C}. The Hammersley-Clifford theorem says this factorization is equivalent to the global Markov property, X_A\perp X_B\mid X_S whenever S separates A from B in the graph.
MRFs and DAGs are not nested: a 4-cycle’s independencies cannot be captured by any DAG, and explaining-away cannot be captured by any MRF.
MRFs are exponential families when potentials are log-linear; a minimal representation drops one redundant coordinate per clique. The Ising model and Gaussian graphical models (where K_{ij}=0 \iff X_i\perp X_j\mid X_{\text{rest}} for the precision matrix K) are the two running examples, and Gaussian MLE reduces to \hat K^{-1}=S_n, the sample covariance.
Inference is computing p(x_F\mid x_E) by marginalizing out x_R. Variable elimination does this efficiently by choosing an order and pushing sums inward; the same sum-product algorithm handles DAGs and MRFs via a shared notion of factors, and the resulting intermediate factors (\tau) are what make the computation dynamic-programming-style rather than exponential.
Restricted Boltzmann machines are a bipartite Ising model where Hammersley-Clifford guarantees the hidden units are conditionally independent given the visible ones (and vice versa), giving the sigmoid activation as a direct consequence rather than an ad hoc choice.



Next week: continuing the inference thread, as listed on the course roadmap (not written yet).

title: Week 3: Markov Random Fields and Exact Inference
text:
Quick self-check
If you can explain, in your own words, why the same variable-elimination algorithm works on both a DAG and an MRF once conditional probability tables are treated as potentials, and why a bipartite Ising model makes the hidden units of a restricted Boltzmann machine conditionally independent given the visible ones, you have understood the core of Week 3.

title: Week 3: Markov Random Fields and Exact Inference
text:
High-level overview
This section retells each part of the week in plain language and without formulas, using the lecture’s own examples. Read it before the chapter for orientation, or after it as a review.
From DAGs to undirected graphs (From DAGs to undirected graphs). Some relationships have no direction. Neighbouring pixels in an image influence each other symmetrically, and neither one causes the other. Forcing arrows onto a grid of pixels makes certain diagonal pixels look related to a pixel through explaining away, even though we only wanted each pixel tied to its four neighbours.
Markov random fields, cliques, and the factorization theorem (Markov random fields, cliques, and the factorization theorem). An MRF drops the arrows: an edge only says “these two interact”. Each group of variables that are all linked to each other (a clique) gets a compatibility score that is high for combinations that go well together, such as two neighbouring pixels sharing a colour. The scores are not probabilities, so the product of all of them is divided by one overall constant to make everything add up to 1.
The Hammersley-Clifford theorem (The Hammersley-Clifford theorem). An undirected graph can be read two ways: as a recipe for building the distribution from clique scores, or as a list of independence statements (“a variable depends only on its neighbours”). The theorem says that, as long as no combination has zero probability, the two readings describe exactly the same distributions. For the image, once we know a pixel’s neighbours, the rest of the picture tells us nothing more about that pixel.
Worked example (Worked example: cliques, factorization, and independence). Practice on a seven-node graph: find the cliques, write down the product of scores, and read off independences by checking whether the observed nodes cut one group off from another.
What MRFs can express that DAGs cannot, and vice versa (What MRFs can express that DAGs cannot, and vice versa). Neither kind of graph is strictly better. Four variables in a ring, each linked to its two neighbours, cannot be drawn as any DAG without changing what is independent. In the other direction, explaining away (rain, ballgame, traffic) cannot be drawn as any MRF.
MRFs as exponential families (MRFs as exponential families). To learn clique scores from data, we write them in Week 1’s exponential-family template, so the same fitting machinery applies.
The Ising model (The Ising model). The simplest MRF. Each variable takes one of two values (originally the up or down spin of a tiny magnet), and each edge has one number saying how strongly its two ends prefer to agree. For a black-and-white image, a positive number means neighbouring pixels tend to share a colour.
Gaussian graphical models (Gaussian graphical models). The continuous version. For bell-curve-shaped data, one matrix of numbers (the precision matrix) encodes the whole graph. A zero in position (i,j) means variables i and j have no direct link once all the others are known, so the graph can be read off by looking for zeros.
Exact inference as a conditional distribution (Exact inference as a conditional distribution). Everything so far described distributions. Now we compute with them. Inference answers questions like “given what we observed, what are the chances for this variable?”, which means adding up over every variable we neither observed nor asked about.
Variable elimination (Variable elimination). Adding up over every combination of the unobserved variables grows exponentially. Variable elimination removes them one at a time: each sum touches only the factors that involve that variable, and the result is stored for reuse. On the chain A\to B\to C\to D, finding the distribution of D means summing out A (which involves only A and B), then B, then C, so no step ever handles more than two variables. The elimination order never changes the answer, but it can change the cost enormously.
Sum-product inference (Sum-product inference: unifying DAGMs and MRFs). A DAG’s conditional probability tables and an MRF’s clique scores are both just tables of nonnegative numbers. So one algorithm (multiply the relevant tables, then sum a variable out) works on both kinds of graph.
Variable elimination on a Bayes net, with and without evidence (Worked example: variable elimination on a Bayes net, Variable elimination with evidence). The student network links, among other things, a course’s difficulty and a student’s intelligence to their grade, the grade to a recommendation letter, and the letter to a job offer. Elimination answers questions like “how likely is a job offer?” When we observe something, such as the grade, that variable is held at its observed value instead of being summed out, and the answer is renormalized at the end.
Restricted Boltzmann machines (Restricted Boltzmann machines). A layer of visible units (for example, pixels) is connected to a layer of hidden units, with no connections inside either layer. Because of that structure, once the pixels are known the hidden units are independent of each other, so each one can be computed separately in a single cheap step. The familiar sigmoid activation from neural networks falls out of this structure rather than being chosen by hand.

title: Week 3 practice: Markov random fields and exact inference
text:
Problem 1: Cliques in a house-shaped graph
Overview. These problems drill Week 3. Try each stem before opening the worked solution. The graphs, potentials, and probability tables here are invented for practice; they are not the seven-node clique example, the student network, the six-node evidence example, or the diamond graph from the lecture. Notation matches the week chapter. The exception is the final section, Tutorial questions, which restates the Week 3 tutorial’s own examples.
A Markov random field has five variables arranged like the outline of a house: a square 1\text{-}2\text{-}3\text{-}4\text{-}1 (the walls) with a roof node 5 joined to both 1 and 2. The edges are 1\text{-}2, 2\text{-}3, 3\text{-}4, 4\text{-}1, 1\text{-}5, 2\text{-}5.
Figure 1. The house graph used in Problems 1 and 2.
List every maximal clique of this graph, then write the general form of a distribution that factorizes with respect to it.

text:
A house-shaped MRF

TipWorked solution





This uses Week 3, Markov random fields, cliques, and the factorization theorem and the clique-hunting method of the worked example.
A clique needs every pair inside it connected. Start with the largest candidates. The roof gives a triangle: 1\text{-}2, 1\text{-}5, 2\text{-}5 are all edges, so \{1,2,5\} is a clique. Can it grow? Adding 3 fails (1\text{-}3 is not an edge), and adding 4 fails (2\text{-}4 is not an edge), so it is maximal.
The square has no diagonals, so no three of 1,2,3,4 are pairwise connected. The remaining edges 2\text{-}3, 3\text{-}4, 4\text{-}1 are each cliques of size two. None extends: for example \{2,3\} would need a third node adjacent to both 2 and 3, and no such node exists. The edge 1\text{-}2 is not maximal on its own, because it sits inside \{1,2,5\}.
Answer. Four maximal cliques: \{1,2,5\}, \{2,3\}, \{3,4\}, \{1,4\}. Any distribution that factorizes with respect to the house graph has the form p(\boldsymbol{x}) = \frac{1}{Z}\,\psi_{1,2,5}(x_1,x_2,x_5)\,\psi_{2,3}(x_2,x_3)\,\psi_{3,4}(x_3,x_4)\,\psi_{1,4}(x_1,x_4) for nonnegative potentials, with Z the partition function.

title: Week 3 practice: Markov random fields and exact inference
section: Problem 2: Reading independence off the house graph
text:
Problem 2: Reading independence off the house graph
Using the house graph of Problem 1, answer each question by graph separation.

Is X_5\perp X_3\mid X_2?
Is X_5\perp X_3\mid\{X_1,X_2\}?
Is X_1\perp X_3\mid\{X_2,X_4\}?
What is the Markov blanket of X_5?







TipWorked solution





This uses the global Markov property from Week 3, The Hammersley-Clifford theorem: X_A\perp X_B\mid X_S whenever every path from A to B passes through S.

Paths from 5 to 3: 5\text{-}2\text{-}3 passes through 2 and is blocked. But 5\text{-}1\text{-}4\text{-}3 never touches 2, so it stays open. One open path is enough to break separation: no, X_5\not\perp X_3\mid X_2 in general.
Node 5’s only neighbours are 1 and 2, so every path out of 5 starts by entering 1 or 2. Conditioning on both blocks them all: yes.
Node 1’s neighbours are 2, 4, and 5. Paths through 2 or 4 are blocked directly. A path through 5 must continue 5\text{-}2, since 2 is the only other neighbour of 5, so it is blocked at 2 as well: yes.
In an MRF the Markov blanket of a node is just its graph neighbours, with no co-parent correction (the contrast with DAGs drawn in §hc).

Answer. (1) No. (2) Yes. (3) Yes. (4) \{X_1, X_2\}, which is exactly why question 2 came out yes.

title: Week 3 practice: Markov random fields and exact inference
section: Problem 3: Directed, undirected, both, or neither?
text:
Problem 3: Directed, undirected, both, or neither?
For each independence pattern below, say whether it can be represented exactly by a DAG, by an MRF, by both, or by neither. Give a one-line reason.

Three variables with X\perp Y marginally, but X\not\perp Y\mid Z.
Three variables with X\perp Z\mid Y and no other independencies.
Three variables with no independencies at all, marginal or conditional.
Five variables on a ring 1\text{-}2\text{-}3\text{-}4\text{-}5\text{-}1, where each variable is conditionally independent of the two non-neighbouring variables given all the others, and no other independencies hold.







TipWorked solution





This uses Week 3, What MRFs can express that DAGs cannot, and vice versa, together with the three canonical structures from Week 2.

This is explaining away: X\to Z\leftarrow Y produces it. An MRF cannot, because in an undirected graph conditioning on more variables can only block paths, never open them, so a marginal independence can never be destroyed by conditioning.
The chain X\to Y\to Z (or the common cause X\leftarrow Y\to Z) gives it as a DAG, and the undirected chain X - Y - Z gives it as an MRF, since Y separates X from Z.
A fully connected graph encodes no independencies. As an MRF, that is the triangle; as a DAG, any ordering with all three arrows, such as X\to Y, X\to Z, Y\to Z.
The undirected 5-cycle represents it exactly: non-neighbours are separated by the rest of the ring. For a DAG, orient the five edges any way that creates no directed cycle. Some node must then have both of its ring edges pointing into it (follow arrows forward and you must stop somewhere, and that stopping node has two incoming arrows). Say that node is 3, with parents 2 and 4. The pattern requires X_2\perp X_4 given all the others, including X_3; but conditioning on the collider 3 opens the path 2\to3\leftarrow4, so the DAG makes them dependent. The same argument works for every orientation. This is the 4-cycle argument of the lecture, extended to a longer ring.

Answer. (a) DAG only. (b) Both. (c) Both. (d) MRF only.

title: Week 3 practice: Markov random fields and exact inference
text:
Problem 4: A two-spin Ising model
Two spins x_1,x_2\in\{-1,+1\} form an Ising model with a single edge potential \psi_{12}(x_1,x_2)=e^{Jx_1x_2}, where e^{J}=2. Spin 1 also has an external-field potential \psi_1(x_1)=e^{b x_1} with e^{b}=2. Spin 2 has no field.

Compute the unnormalized weight of each of the four configurations, and the partition function Z.
Compute P(x_1=x_2), P(x_1=+1), and P(x_2=+1).
Without the field on spin 1, what is P(x_1=x_2)? Explain why the field did or did not change it.







TipWorked solution





This uses Week 3, The Ising model.
The edge potential is e^{J}=2 when the spins agree and e^{-J}=\tfrac12 when they disagree. The field gives spin 1 a factor e^{b}=2 when it is +1 and e^{-b}=\tfrac12 when it is -1. Multiply the two for each configuration:

So Z = 4 + 1 + \tfrac14 + 1 = 6.25.
P(x_1=x_2) = (4+1)/6.25 = 0.8. P(x_1=+1) = (4+1)/6.25 = 0.8. P(x_2=+1) = (4+\tfrac14)/6.25 = 0.68. The field acts only on spin 1, yet spin 2 also leans toward +1, because the coupling passes the preference along the edge.
For part 3, drop the field: weights become 2, \tfrac12, \tfrac12, 2, so Z=5 and P(x_1=x_2)=4/5=0.8, unchanged. The reason: for either fixed value of x_1, the field multiplies the agreeing and disagreeing configurations by the same factor, so the conditional chance of agreement given x_1 is always 2/(2+\tfrac12)=0.8. The field moves where the spins point; only the coupling J controls how often they agree.
Answer. Weights 4, 1, \tfrac14, 1 and Z=6.25. P(x_1=x_2)=0.8, P(x_1=+1)=0.8, P(x_2=+1)=0.68. Without the field, P(x_1=x_2) is still 0.8.

title: Week 3 practice: Markov random fields and exact inference
text:
Problem 5: A star-shaped precision matrix
A zero-mean Gaussian over (X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4) has precision matrix K=\Sigma^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}4&-1&-1&-1\\-1&2&0&0\\-1&0&2&0\\-1&0&0&2\end{bmatrix}.

Draw the Gaussian graphical model.
Is X_2\perp X_3\mid\{X_1,X_4\}?
Is X_2\perp X_3\mid X_1 (conditioning on X_1 alone)?
Is X_2\perp X_3\mid X_4?
Is X_2\perp X_3 marginally?







TipWorked solution





This uses Week 3, Gaussian graphical models and the separation rule of §hc.

Edges sit where off-diagonal entries of K are nonzero: K_{12}, K_{13}, K_{14}. The graph is a star with centre 1 and leaves 2, 3, 4.
K_{23}=0, which is exactly the statement X_2\perp X_3\mid X_{\text{rest}}: yes.
The precision-matrix rule speaks only about conditioning on everything else, so switch to graph separation. In a star, every path between two leaves passes through the centre, so \{1\} separates 2 from 3: yes.
Conditioning on 4 leaves the path 2\text{-}1\text{-}3 open: no.
Marginal independence is read from \Sigma, not K. With nothing conditioned on, the path 2\text{-}1\text{-}3 is open, so we should expect dependence. Inverting K confirms it: \Sigma_{23}=0.1\neq 0. A zero in K does not produce a zero in \Sigma.

Answer. (1) Star centred at 1. (2) Yes. (3) Yes. (4) No. (5) No: \Sigma_{23}=0.1.

title: Week 3 practice: Markov random fields and exact inference
section: Problem 6: Elimination order on a star
text:
Problem 6: Elimination order on a star
An MRF has a centre variable C joined to four leaves L_1,L_2,L_3,L_4, with one pairwise potential per edge: \psi(C,L_1),\dots,\psi(C,L_4), so m=4 factors. Every variable has k states. We want p(L_1).
Compare two variable elimination orders:

Order A: C, then L_2, L_3, L_4.
Order B: L_2, L_3, L_4, then C.

For each order, give the variables involved in each sum, N_{\max}, and the complexity O(m\,k^{N_{\max}}).






TipWorked solution





This uses Week 3, Variable elimination and the complexity bookkeeping of the Bayes-net worked example.
Order A. C appears in all four potentials, so summing it out first touches every variable at once: \sum_C \psi(C,L_1)\,\psi(C,L_2)\,\psi(C,L_3)\,\psi(C,L_4) = \tau(L_1,L_2,L_3,L_4). That sum involves 5 variables. Eliminating L_2 then sums \tau over L_2 with 4 variables inside, L_3 with 3, and L_4 with 2. So N_{\max}=5 and the cost is O(4k^5).
Order B. Each leaf appears in one potential only: \sum_{L_2}\psi(C,L_2) = \tau_2(C), with 2 variables inside, and the same for L_3 and L_4. Finally \sum_C \psi(C,L_1)\,\tau_2(C)\,\tau_3(C)\,\tau_4(C) = \tau(L_1), again with only 2 variables inside. So N_{\max}=2 and the cost is O(4k^2).
Eliminating the hub first glued all its neighbours into one large intermediate factor; eliminating the leaves first never created a factor over more than one variable. The star is a tree, and this leaves-inward pattern is the starting point of Week 4.
Answer. Order A: N_{\max}=5, O(4k^5). Order B: N_{\max}=2, O(4k^2). Both give the same p(L_1), since summation order does not change the answer.

title: Week 3 practice: Markov random fields and exact inference
section: Problem 7: Elimination with evidence on a three-node chain
text:
Problem 7: Elimination with evidence on a three-node chain
A Bayesian network A\to B\to C has binary variables with

p(A=1)=0.3,
p(B=1\mid A=1)=0.8 and p(B=1\mid A=0)=0.1,
p(C=1\mid B=1)=0.9 and p(C=1\mid B=0)=0.2.

We observe C=1. Use variable elimination to compute p(A=1\mid C=1).






TipWorked solution





This uses Week 3, Variable elimination with evidence and the definition of inference in §inference.
Here x_F=\{A\}, x_E=\{C\}, x_R=\{B\}. The evidence value is plugged in, not summed over: p(a, C=1) = p(a)\sum_b p(b\mid a)\,p(C=1\mid b).
Eliminate B first. The inner sum is a new factor depending only on a: \tau(a) = \sum_b p(b\mid a)\,p(C=1\mid b) = p(C=1\mid a). For a=1: 0.8\cdot0.9 + 0.2\cdot0.2 = 0.72+0.04 = 0.76. For a=0: 0.1\cdot0.9 + 0.9\cdot0.2 = 0.09+0.18 = 0.27.
Multiply by the prior on A: p(A=1, C=1) = 0.3\cdot0.76 = 0.228 and p(A=0, C=1) = 0.7\cdot0.27 = 0.189.
Normalize over A: p(A=1\mid C=1) = \frac{0.228}{0.228+0.189} = \frac{0.228}{0.417}\approx 0.547.
As in the lecture’s evidence example, eliminating the middle variable collapses the computation to Bayes’ rule on the two-node relationship A\to C, with the derived likelihood p(C=1\mid a).
Answer. p(A=1\mid C=1)\approx 0.547, up from the prior 0.3.

title: Week 3 practice: Markov random fields and exact inference
section: Problem 8: What an RBM can compute without Z
text:
Problem 8: What an RBM can compute without Z
A restricted Boltzmann machine has three visible units X_1,X_2,X_3 and two hidden units H_1,H_2, all in \{-1,+1\}, with every hidden unit joined to every visible unit and no other edges.

Why is p(h_1,h_2\mid x) = p(h_1\mid x)\,p(h_2\mid x)?
Is the marginal p(h_1,h_2) also a product p(h_1)\,p(h_2) in general? Why or why not?
Which of p(h_1\mid x), p(x,h), and p(h) can be computed without knowing the partition function Z?







TipWorked solution





This uses Week 3, Restricted Boltzmann machines and the separation rule of §hc.

There is no H_1\text{-}H_2 edge, and every path between them runs through some visible unit. Observing all of X blocks every such path, so H_1\perp H_2\mid X by the global Markov property, and the conditional factors.
Not in general. With X unobserved, paths like H_1\text{-}X_1\text{-}H_2 are open, so summing out the visible units typically couples the hidden units. Separation needs the separating set to be observed.
p(h_1\mid x) is a ratio in which Z cancels: the week chapter’s formula gives \sigma(\beta_1+\sum_i J_{i1}x_i) with Week 3’s \sigma(y)=1/(1+e^{-2y}). In contrast, p(x,h) is the product of potentials divided by Z, and p(h) is a sum of those joint probabilities, so both need Z.

Answer. (1) X separates the hidden units. (2) No: summing out X couples them. (3) Only p(h_1\mid x) avoids Z.
crumbs: 7  Week 3 practice: Markov random fields and exact inference

title: Week 3 practice: Markov random fields and exact inference
text:
Marginalization in factorized models
These problems drill summing a variable out of a product of factors, which is the core step of variable elimination and of every message-passing algorithm later in the course. All numbers are invented.

Problem 9: Summing out a shared variable
Two factors over binary variables are given as tables, rows indexed by the first argument and columns by the second (value 0 first): f(a,b)=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&1\end{pmatrix}, \qquad g(b,c)=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&4\end{pmatrix}. Compute the new factor \tau(a,c)=\sum_bf(a,b)\,g(b,c) as a 2\times2 table.






TipWorked solution





This is the elementary step of Week 3, Variable elimination: multiply the factors that mention b, then sum b out. The result depends only on the variables left over, a and c.
For each of the four (a,c) pairs, add the two terms b=0 and b=1:

\tau(0,0)=f(0,0)g(0,0)+f(0,1)g(1,0)=1\cdot2+2\cdot1=4
\tau(0,1)=f(0,0)g(0,1)+f(0,1)g(1,1)=1\cdot1+2\cdot4=9
\tau(1,0)=f(1,0)g(0,0)+f(1,1)g(1,0)=3\cdot2+1\cdot1=7
\tau(1,1)=f(1,0)g(0,1)+f(1,1)g(1,1)=3\cdot1+1\cdot4=7

Row a of f meets column c of g, and the shared index b is summed: this is exactly the matrix product FG. Summing out a variable shared by two pairwise factors is always a matrix multiplication.
Answer. \tau=\begin{pmatrix}4&9\\7&7\end{pmatrix}.





Problem 10: Push the sum inward
Let every variable have k states, and consider h(a)=\sum_b\sum_cf(a,b)\,g(b,c).

Computed naively (for each a, sum the product over all (b,c) pairs), how many multiplications does h take?
Rewrite h(a) by pushing \sum_c inside past f. How many multiplications now?
Evaluate h with the tables of Problem 9.







TipWorked solution





This is the “push the sum inward” move of Week 3, Variable elimination.

There are k values of a and k^2 pairs (b,c), with one multiplication per term: k^3 in total.
f(a,b) does not mention c, so it moves outside the inner sum: h(a)=\sum_bf(a,b)\Big[\sum_cg(b,c)\Big]=\sum_bf(a,b)\,s(b). Computing s(b) takes only additions. The outer sum takes one multiplication per (a,b) pair: k^2 in total, a factor of k saved.
s(0)=2+1=3 and s(1)=1+4=5. Then h(0)=1\cdot3+2\cdot5=13 and h(1)=3\cdot3+1\cdot5=14. As a check, these are the row sums of \tau from Problem 9.

Answer. k^3 naively, k^2 after pushing the sum in; h=(13,\ 14).





Problem 11: The partition function and marginals of a three-node MRF
An MRF on the chain x_1-x_2-x_3, with every x_i\in\{0,1\}, has potentials \psi_{12}(x_1,x_2)=\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \psi_{23}(x_2,x_3)=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}, so the first edge favours agreement and the second favours disagreement. Compute the partition function Z, the marginal p(x_2), and the pairwise marginal p(x_1,x_3).






TipWorked solution





This uses Week 3, Variable elimination on an MRF, as in Week 3, Sum-product inference.
Z by eliminating the ends. For each x_2, sum out x_1 and x_3 separately, since no factor contains both: Z=\sum_{x_2}\Big[\sum_{x_1}\psi_{12}(x_1,x_2)\Big]\Big[\sum_{x_3}\psi_{23}(x_2,x_3)\Big]. Each column of \psi_{12} sums to 4 and each row of \psi_{23} sums to 3, so both values of x_2 contribute 4\times3=12, and Z=24.
p(x_2). The same bracketed product, before summing over x_2, is the unnormalized marginal: (12,12)/24, so p(x_2) is uniform.
p(x_1,x_3). Now x_2 is the variable summed out, which is Problem 9’s matrix product: \sum_{x_2}\psi_{12}(x_1,x_2)\,\psi_{23}(x_2,x_3)=\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}5&7\\7&5\end{pmatrix}. Dividing by Z=24 gives p(x_1,x_3). The entries sum to 24, as they must.
x_1 and x_3 share no edge, yet they are dependent: they disagree with probability 14/24 rather than 1/2. Agreement along the first edge and disagreement along the second combine into disagreement between the ends.
Answer. Z=24; p(x_2)=(\tfrac12,\tfrac12); p(x_1,x_3)=\tfrac{1}{24}\begin{pmatrix}5&7\\7&5\end{pmatrix}.





Problem 12: Evidence: normalize last
In the MRF of Problem 11, we observe x_3=1. Compute p(x_1\mid x_3=1) without using Z.






TipWorked solution





This follows Week 3, Variable elimination with evidence: fix the observed variable instead of summing it, eliminate the rest, and normalize at the very end.
With x_3=1 fixed, summing out x_2 gives the x_3=1 column of the table from Problem 11: \tau(x_1)=(7,\ 5) for x_1=0,1. These are proportional to p(x_1,x_3{=}1), and the constant \tfrac1Z cancels when we normalize over x_1: p(x_1=0\mid x_3=1)=\frac{7}{7+5}=\frac{7}{12}, \qquad p(x_1=1\mid x_3=1)=\frac{5}{12}.
Answer. p(x_1\mid x_3=1)=(\tfrac{7}{12},\ \tfrac{5}{12}).





Problem 13: Which axis gets summed?
With the arrays of Problem 9 stored as f = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 1]]) and g = np.array([[2, 1], [1, 4]]), what does this line produce, and which variable has been eliminated?
tau = (f[:, :, None] * g[None, :, :]).sum(axis=1)






TipWorked solution





This is Problem 9 written with array broadcasting.

f[:, :, None] has shape (2, 2, 1) and axes (a,b,\cdot).
g[None, :, :] has shape (1, 2, 2) and axes (\cdot,b,c).
Their product broadcasts to shape (2, 2, 2) with axes (a,b,c), and entry [a, b, c] equals f(a,b)\,g(b,c).
.sum(axis=1) sums over the middle axis, which is b.

So tau[a, c] =\sum_bf(a,b)g(b,c), a (2, 2) array equal to f @ g. Lining up each factor’s variables on its own axis, multiplying, and summing the axis of the eliminated variable is how variable elimination is usually implemented.
Answer. array([[4, 9], [7, 7]]); b was eliminated.





Problem 14: Summing out creates new dependencies
A star-shaped MRF has a centre x_2 joined to three leaves x_1,x_3,x_4, with one pairwise potential per edge. Sum out x_2. What does the graph of the resulting marginal over (x_1,x_3,x_4) look like, and why?






TipWorked solution





This uses Week 3, Variable elimination together with Week 3, The Hammersley-Clifford theorem.
All three potentials mention x_2, so eliminating it multiplies all three and sums: \tau(x_1,x_3,x_4)=\sum_{x_2}\psi_{21}(x_2,x_1)\,\psi_{23}(x_2,x_3)\,\psi_{24}(x_2,x_4). This new factor involves all three leaves at once, and in general it does not split into a product of pairwise pieces. The marginal is p(x_1,x_3,x_4)\propto\tau(x_1,x_3,x_4), a single factor over all three, so its graph needs \{x_1,x_3,x_4\} as a clique: every pair of leaves is now joined.
Before elimination, the leaves were independent given x_2, because x_2 separated them. Summing x_2 out removes the separator, and the leaves become dependent through it. In variable elimination, these new edges are what make an intermediate factor larger than any original one.
Answer. A triangle: every pair of leaves becomes adjacent, because the factor created by eliminating x_2 involves all three leaves.
crumbs: 7  Week 3 practice: Markov random fields and exact inference

title: Week 3 practice: Markov random fields and exact inference
text:
Tutorial questions
The questions below are the Week 3 tutorial’s examples, restated as questions. They use the tutorial’s own graphs and models, and each is also worked in the week chapter; each solution says where.

Tutorial question 1: Hammersley-Clifford on a chain
Take the chain X-Y-Z. Its graphical model consists of all distributions that factorize as f(x,y,z)=\alpha(x,y)\,\beta(y,z). Show that, when \alpha>0 and \beta>0 everywhere, this is equivalent to X\perp Z\mid Y. Use the characterization: X\perp Z\mid Y if and only if f(x\mid y,z) does not depend on z.






TipWorked solution





This is the chain example of Week 3, The Hammersley-Clifford theorem.
Independence implies the factorization. If X\perp Z\mid Y, then f(x\mid y,z)=f(x\mid y), so f(x,y,z)=f(y,z)\,f(x\mid y,z)=f(x\mid y)\,f(y,z). This has the required form with \alpha(x,y)=f(x\mid y) and \beta(y,z)=f(y,z).
The factorization implies independence. If f=\alpha\beta, summing out x gives f(y,z)=\big(\sum_x\alpha(x,y)\big)\beta(y,z). Dividing, f(x\mid y,z)=\frac{\alpha(x,y)\,\beta(y,z)}{\big(\sum_{x'}\alpha(x',y)\big)\beta(y,z)}=\frac{\alpha(x,y)}{\sum_{x'}\alpha(x',y)}. The \beta factor cancels (positivity makes the division safe), and what remains does not depend on z.
Answer. Both directions hold, so for positive factors “factorizes over the cliques \{X,Y\},\{Y,Z\}” and “X\perp Z\mid Y” describe the same distributions.





Tutorial question 2: The Gaussian log-likelihood in the precision matrix
Observe x_1,\dots,x_n i.i.d. from an m-variate Gaussian with mean 0 (centre the data first) and precision matrix K=\Sigma^{-1}. The log-density is \log f(x;K)=-\frac m2\log(2\pi)+\frac12\log\det K-\frac12x^\top Kx.

Show that, up to constants, \ell_n(K)=\frac n2\big(\log\det K-\mathrm{tr}(KS_n)\big), where S_n=\frac1n\sum_ix_ix_i^\top.
Using \nabla\log\det K=K^{-1} and \nabla\,\mathrm{tr}(KS_n)=S_n, find the maximizer.







TipWorked solution





This is the derivation in Week 3, Gaussian graphical models.

Summing the log-density over the data and dropping -\frac{nm}{2}\log(2\pi), \ell_n(K)=\frac n2\log\det K-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^nx_i^\top Kx_i. A scalar equals its own trace, and the trace is unchanged by cycling a product, so x_i^\top Kx_i=\mathrm{tr}(Kx_ix_i^\top). By linearity, \sum_i\mathrm{tr}(Kx_ix_i^\top)=\mathrm{tr}\big(K\sum_ix_ix_i^\top\big)=n\,\mathrm{tr}(KS_n).
The gradient is \frac n2\big(K^{-1}-S_n\big). Setting it to zero gives K^{-1}=S_n. Since \log\det K is strictly concave and \mathrm{tr}(KS_n) is linear, this stationary point is the unique maximizer (when S_n is invertible).

Answer. \hat K=S_n^{-1}, equivalently \hat\Sigma=S_n.





Tutorial question 3: A binary chain MRF as an exponential family
Take binary variables on the chain X_1-X_2-X_3 with p(x_1,x_2,x_3\mid\theta)=\frac{1}{Z(\theta)}\,\psi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2\mid\theta_{1,2})\,\psi_{2,3}(x_2,x_3\mid\theta_{2,3}).

Let \theta_{1,2}\in\mathbb{R}^4 list \log\psi_{1,2} at (0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1). Find \phi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2) with \log\psi_{1,2}=\theta_{1,2}^\top\phi_{1,2}, and write p as an exponential family. What is Z(\theta) in this parameterization?
Why is this representation not minimal, and how do we make it minimal?







TipWorked solution





This is the worked example in Week 3, MRFs as exponential families.

Let \phi_{1,2} be the indicator vector of which of the four configurations occurred: \phi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2)=\big((1-x_1)(1-x_2),\ (1-x_1)x_2,\ x_1(1-x_2),\ x_1x_2\big)^\top. Exactly one entry is 1, so \theta_{1,2}^\top\phi_{1,2} picks out the right log-potential. Defining \phi_{2,3} and \theta_{2,3} the same way, p(x_1,x_2,x_3\mid\theta)=\exp\big\{\theta_{1,2}^\top\phi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2)+\theta_{2,3}^\top\phi_{2,3}(x_2,x_3)-\log Z(\theta)\big\}, an exponential family with sufficient statistics (\phi_{1,2},\phi_{2,3}). Following the tutorial, the potentials in this parameterization are taken to be normalized already, so Z(\theta)=1 and A(\theta)=0.
The four entries of \phi_{1,2} always sum to 1, so the statistics lie in a hyperplane. With \theta restricted so that Z(\theta)=1, A\equiv0 on that set, so \nabla A=0 there cannot equal \mathbb{E}_\theta T(X). For the unrestricted A=\log Z the identity holds; what non-minimality really costs is identifiability, since different \theta give the same distribution. The fix is to drop the first coordinate and measure the others relative to it: \bar\theta_{1,2}=\big(\theta^{(1)},\,\theta^{(2)},\,\theta^{(3)}\big), \qquad \theta^{(1)}=\log\psi_{1,2}(0,1)-\log\psi_{1,2}(0,0), \theta^{(2)}=\log\psi_{1,2}(1,0)-\log\psi_{1,2}(0,0), \qquad \theta^{(3)}=\log\psi_{1,2}(1,1)-\log\psi_{1,2}(0,0), \bar\phi_{1,2}=\begin{pmatrix}(1-x_1)x_2\\ x_1(1-x_2)\\ x_1x_2\end{pmatrix}, and similarly for the (2,3) edge. Since \log\psi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2)=\log\psi_{1,2}(0,0)+\bar\theta_{1,2}^\top\bar\phi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2) for every configuration, p(x_1,x_2,x_3)=\exp\big\{\bar\theta_{1,2}^\top\bar\phi_{1,2}+\bar\theta_{2,3}^\top\bar\phi_{2,3}+\log\psi_{1,2}(0,0)\,\psi_{2,3}(0,0)\big\}, so A(\bar\theta)=-\log\psi_{1,2}(0,0)\,\psi_{2,3}(0,0). The tutorial writes this without the minus sign. The minus sign is needed: A(\bar\theta)=\log\sum_xe^{\bar\theta^\top\bar\phi(x)} is at least 0 because the all-zeros configuration contributes e^0=1, while \psi_{1,2}(0,0)\,\psi_{2,3}(0,0)=p(0,0,0)\le1 has a nonpositive log.

Answer. (1) Indicator features with Z=1. (2) The indicators sum to 1; dropping one coordinate per edge gives a minimal family with A(\bar\theta)=-\log\big(\psi_{1,2}(0,0)\,\psi_{2,3}(0,0)\big), which must then be written in terms of \bar\theta_{1,2} and \bar\theta_{2,3}.





Tutorial question 4: Variable elimination with evidence
The DAG with edges x_1\to x_2, x_1\to x_3, x_2\to x_4, x_3\to x_5, x_2\to x_6, x_5\to x_6 factorizes as p(x_1,\dots,x_6)=p(x_1)\,p(x_2\mid x_1)\,p(x_3\mid x_1)\,p(x_4\mid x_2)\,p(x_5\mid x_3)\,p(x_6\mid x_2,x_5). We observe X_6=\bar x_6. Compute p(x_1\mid\bar x_6) by variable elimination, eliminating x_5, then x_4, x_3, x_2.






TipWorked solution





This is the worked example of Week 3, Variable elimination with evidence.
Here x_F=\{x_1\}, x_E=\{x_6\}, x_R=\{x_2,x_3,x_4,x_5\}, and p(x_1\mid\bar x_6)=p(x_1,\bar x_6)\big/\sum_{x_1}p(x_1,\bar x_6). Push each sum inward past the factors that do not mention its variable: p(x_1,\bar x_6)=p(x_1)\sum_{x_2}p(x_2\mid x_1)\sum_{x_3}p(x_3\mid x_1)\sum_{x_4}p(x_4\mid x_2)\sum_{x_5}p(x_5\mid x_3)\,p(\bar x_6\mid x_2,x_5).

Eliminate x_5: \sum_{x_5}p(x_5\mid x_3)\,p(\bar x_6\mid x_2,x_5)=p(\bar x_6\mid x_2,x_3). This result does not involve x_4, so it moves outside the x_4 sum.
Eliminate x_4: \sum_{x_4}p(x_4\mid x_2)=1. A leaf that is neither queried nor observed drops out.
Eliminate x_3: \sum_{x_3}p(x_3\mid x_1)\,p(\bar x_6\mid x_2,x_3)=p(\bar x_6\mid x_1,x_2).
Eliminate x_2: \sum_{x_2}p(x_2\mid x_1)\,p(\bar x_6\mid x_1,x_2)=p(\bar x_6\mid x_1).

Answer. p(x_1\mid\bar x_6)=\frac{p(x_1)\,p(\bar x_6\mid x_1)}{\sum_{x_1}p(x_1)\,p(\bar x_6\mid x_1)}, Bayes’ rule on the two-node relationship x_1\to x_6, after everything in between has been summed out.





Tutorial question 5: Conditionals of a restricted Boltzmann machine
A restricted Boltzmann machine has visible units X_1,\dots,X_k and hidden units H_1,\dots,H_l, all in \{-1,1\}, on the complete bipartite graph between them: p(x,h)\propto\exp\Big\{\sum_i\alpha_ix_i+\sum_j\beta_jh_j+\sum_{i=1}^k\sum_{j=1}^lJ_{ij}x_ih_j\Big\}.

Write p(x,h) as \frac1Z\prod_{i,j}\psi_{X_i,H_j}(x_i,h_j).
Show that p(h_j=1\mid x)=\sigma\big(\beta_j+\sum_iJ_{ij}x_i\big) with \sigma(y)=1/(1+e^{-2y}), and that the H_j are independent given X.







TipWorked solution





This is Week 3, Restricted Boltzmann machines.

Share each single-node term evenly across the edges that touch it. x_i has l edges and h_j has k: \psi_{X_i,H_j}(x_i,h_j)=\exp\Big\{\tfrac1l\alpha_ix_i+\tfrac1k\beta_jh_j+J_{ij}x_ih_j\Big\}. Multiplying over all k\times l pairs recovers each \alpha_ix_i once (l copies of \frac1l), each \beta_jh_j once, and every coupling term.
With x fixed, p(h\mid x)\propto\prod_j\big[\prod_i\psi_{X_i,H_j}(x_i,h_j)\big] is a product of separate functions of each h_j. That makes the H_j independent given X, as Hammersley-Clifford predicts: X separates the hidden units. Normalizing one factor over h_j\in\{-1,1\}, the \alpha terms cancel and, with a_j=\beta_j+\sum_iJ_{ij}x_i, p(h_j=1\mid x)=\frac{e^{a_j}}{e^{-a_j}+e^{a_j}}=\frac{1}{1+e^{-2a_j}}=\sigma(a_j). Z never appears, because it cancels in the ratio. The same argument gives p(x\mid h).

Answer. p(h_j=1\mid x)=\sigma(\beta_j+\sum_iJ_{ij}x_i), and p(h\mid x)=\prod_jp(h_j\mid x).

title: Week 4: Message Passing and Monte Carlo
text:
Latent variables and the TrueSkill model
Overview. Week 3 ended with variable elimination: to compute a conditional p(x_F\mid x_E) in a graphical model, sum out the remaining variables x_R one at a time, pushing each sum inward past every factor that does not mention it. This lecture takes that algorithm in two directions. The first half starts from a model where exact inference is out of reach, the TrueSkill model for ranking game players, and then shows that on a tree variable elimination can be rewritten as messages passed between neighbouring nodes. Two sweeps of messages give every node’s marginal at once (belief propagation). Running the same updates on a graph with cycles gives loopy belief propagation, an approximation with few guarantees that is still useful in practice; the tutorial uses it to denoise a binary image. The second half changes strategy entirely: instead of summing over a distribution, we draw random samples from it. We cover ancestral sampling, simple Monte Carlo estimation of expectations, and two tools for distributions we can only evaluate up to a constant: importance sampling and rejection sampling.
Skipped: the title slide. The two agenda slides (slides 2 and 19) became the paragraph above.
Some variables in a model are never observed, yet the model depends on them. What do we do with such a variable?
If an inference question never asks about a latent variable z, we can simply marginalize it out (integrate over it, or sum if it is discrete), exactly as Week 3 summed out the remaining variables x_R (Exact inference as a conditional distribution in Week 3). In other problems the latent variables are the very thing we want to learn about. Clustering is one example, and the course returns to latent variables when it covers Gaussian mixtures.
The lecture’s running example of the second kind is TrueSkill, a ranking system for players of competitive games. The goal is to infer each player’s skill from observing who beats whom.
The function \sigma here is the standard logistic function: it maps any real number into (0,1), equals \tfrac12 at 0, and approaches 1 as its argument grows. So two players of equal skill each win half the time, and the larger the skill gap z_i - z_j, the more likely the stronger player wins. Week 3’s restricted Boltzmann machine section (Restricted Boltzmann machines in Week 3) used the same letter for \sigma(y) = 1/(1+e^{-2y}), which has an extra factor of 2 because those units took values in \{-1,+1\}. In this chapter \sigma always means the standard version, 1/(1+e^{-y}).
Treating the games as independent given the skills, the joint distribution of all skills and all T game outcomes is the prior times one factor per game:
p(z_1,\dots,z_N,\text{game } 1,\dots,\text{game } T) = \Big[\prod_{i=1}^N p(z_i)\Big]\Big[\prod_{\text{games}} p(i \text{ beats } j\mid z_i,z_j)\Big].
Why the posterior is hard. Once we observe some games, the skills are no longer independent, even for two players who have never played each other. This is Week 2’s explaining-away structure (Conditional independence: three canonical structures in Week 2): a game outcome is a common child of the two players’ skills, so observing it couples them. If A beat B, then learning that B is strong makes it more likely that A is strong too. A chain of games (A played B, B played C) then couples A and C through B. As a result, even the exact posterior over just two players requires integrating over every other player’s skill:
p(z_1,z_2\mid\text{games}) = \int\!\cdots\!\int p(z_1,z_2,z_3,\dots,z_N\mid\text{games})\,dz_3\cdots dz_N.
This is an (N-2)-dimensional integral with no closed form. The rest of the first half builds a tool, message passing, that computes approximate posteriors of this kind.
