title: Week 4: Message Passing and Monte Carlo
text:
Comparing the sampling methods






TipQuestion: What do the hat, the tilde and the word proposal mean?





Three pieces of notation come up in every method in this section.

The hat on \hat\Phi. A hat marks an estimate computed from samples. \Phi is the true expectation, and \hat\Phi is what the sample average or weighted average gives us. The hat is not a property of the density.
The tilde on \tilde p. A tilde marks an unnormalized density: a formula we can evaluate, but which does not integrate to 1. The true density is p = \tilde p / Z_p, where Z_p is the constant that makes it integrate to 1. The tilde version has the same shape as p, just scaled. The tilde goes on \tilde p, \tilde q and \tilde w, but not on p itself, which is already normalized.
The proposal q. A proposal is a distribution we choose and can sample from, and use in place of p when we cannot sample p directly. It is written with the same tilde convention: \tilde q is its unnormalized form, with q = \tilde q / Z_q. A good proposal covers p (so q > 0 wherever p > 0) and has roughly the same shape. Importance sampling draws from q and reweights. Rejection sampling draws from q and accepts or rejects using an envelope c\tilde q.

What the tilde tells you. A tilde means the formula is known but its normalizing constant may not be. \tilde p and \tilde q are what we can evaluate. p and q are normalized, so they integrate to 1 and give real probabilities. The same split applies to the weights:

\tilde w_r = \tilde p(x^{(r)})/\tilde q(x^{(r)}) is what we compute. It is not normalized. Its average over draws estimates Z_p/Z_q, so it is not a probability.
w_r = \tilde w_r / \sum_{r'}\tilde w_{r'} is normalized. The w_r sum to 1, and the estimator \sum_r w_r\,\phi(x^{(r)}) uses them.

When to use which.

Use the tilde when the constant is unknown or cancels: in algorithms, such as the rejection test u \le \tilde p(x) and the envelope c\tilde q \ge \tilde p, where Z_p and Z_q never need to be computed.
Use the plain form when the constant matters: stating the target \Phi = \mathbb{E}_p[\phi], quoting the acceptance rate Z_p/(cZ_q), or reporting a probability.
Do not compare a tilde value with a plain one. A value \tilde p(x) = 3 says nothing about p(x) by itself. Only ratios carry over: \tilde p(x)/\tilde p(y) = p(x)/p(y).




The four methods in this half of the lecture are easy to blur together, so it helps to sort them by two questions. Which problem does the method solve: drawing samples (Problem 1) or estimating an expectation (Problem 2)? And what does it need from us before it can run?










Method
Solves
Needs
Produces
Struggles when




Ancestral sampling (Ancestral sampling)
Problem 1
a DAG whose conditionals we can sample, in topological order
exact, independent samples from p
we condition on observed descendants, or the model is not a DAG of normalized conditionals


Simple Monte Carlo (Simple Monte Carlo)
Problem 2
samples from p itself
an unbiased estimate of \Phi with variance \mathrm{var}[\phi]/R
we have no way to sample p


Importance sampling (Importance sampling)
Problem 2
\tilde p to evaluate; a proposal q to sample and evaluate
a weighted estimate of \Phi, plus an estimate of Z_p/Z_q; no samples from p
q rarely visits where p has mass, so a few large weights dominate


Rejection sampling (Rejection sampling)
Problem 1
\tilde p to evaluate; a proposal q; a constant c with c\tilde q \ge \tilde p everywhere
exact samples from p
the dimension grows, since the acceptance rate Z_p/(cZ_q) shrinks exponentially



Read as a decision: if we can sample p directly (ancestral sampling is one way), use simple Monte Carlo on those samples. If we can only evaluate \tilde p, choose importance sampling when an expectation is all we need, and rejection sampling when we need the samples themselves and the problem is low-dimensional. The three examples below use invented numbers, one for each branch.






TipExample 1: When to use ancestral sampling with simple Monte Carlo





In plain terms: when the model is a chain of “this causes that” steps and each step is a probability table we can roll against, we can generate exact samples cheaply. Then we just count.
Take a three-node chain x_1 \to x_2 \to x_3 of binary variables with p(x_1{=}1) = 0.3, p(x_2{=}1 \mid x_1{=}1) = 0.9, p(x_2{=}1 \mid x_1{=}0) = 0.2, p(x_3{=}1 \mid x_2{=}1) = 0.8, and p(x_3{=}1 \mid x_2{=}0) = 0.1. We want \mathbb{P}(x_3{=}1), which is \mathbb{E}_p[\phi] for the indicator \phi(x) = \mathbf{1}_{\{x_3=1\}}.

Ancestral sampling draws x_1, then x_2 given x_1, then x_3 given x_2. Suppose five samples come out with x_3 = 1, 0, 0, 1, 0.
Simple Monte Carlo averages the indicator: \hat\Phi = 2/5 = 0.4.
The exact answer, for checking, is \mathbb{P}(x_2{=}1) = 0.3(0.9) + 0.7(0.2) = 0.41, so \mathbb{P}(x_3{=}1) = 0.41(0.8) + 0.59(0.1) = 0.387.

Why not the others: nothing here is unnormalized, so there is no Z_p to dodge. Importance sampling would only add weights that correct for a mismatch we do not have, and rejection sampling would throw away draws that ancestral sampling keeps. If we instead observed x_3 and wanted p(x_1 \mid x_3), ancestral sampling would no longer apply directly, because it only samples forward from parents to children.









TipExample 2: When to use importance sampling





In plain terms: when we can score how plausible each value is but cannot draw from that distribution, and all we want is an average, we can draw from something easy and reweight. Every draw gets used.
A coin has unknown bias \theta, with a uniform prior on [0, 1]. We see two heads and one tail. The posterior is known only up to a constant: \tilde p(\theta) = \theta^2(1-\theta). We want the posterior mean \mathbb{E}_p[\theta].
Use the prior as the proposal, q(\theta) = 1 on [0, 1], with \tilde q = 1. Then the weight \tilde p / \tilde q is just the likelihood of the data at each draw. Four draws from q:



\theta^{(r)}
0.2
0.5
0.7
0.9




\tilde w_r = \theta^2(1-\theta)
0.032
0.125
0.147
0.081



\hat\Phi = \frac{0.2(0.032) + 0.5(0.125) + 0.7(0.147) + 0.9(0.081)}{0.032 + 0.125 + 0.147 + 0.081} = \frac{0.2447}{0.385} \approx 0.64.
The exact posterior mean is \int_0^1 \theta^3(1-\theta)\,d\theta \,\big/ \int_0^1 \theta^2(1-\theta)\,d\theta = \frac{1/20}{1/12} = 0.6. The average weight 0.385/4 \approx 0.096 also estimates Z_p/Z_q = Z_p = 1/12 \approx 0.083, the probability of the observed data.
Why not the others: we cannot sample the posterior directly, so simple Monte Carlo on its own is out, and ancestral sampling does not condition on observed data. Rejection sampling would work in one dimension, but it discards some draws and needs a bound c. Since we only want an average, importance sampling uses every draw and gives Z_p for free.









TipExample 3: When to use rejection sampling





In plain terms: when we need actual values drawn from the distribution (to plot them, or to feed them into another simulation), and the problem is low-dimensional with a known ceiling on \tilde p, we can propose values and keep only the ones that pass a fair test.
Keep the coin posterior \tilde p(\theta) = \theta^2(1-\theta) from Example 2, but now suppose we want a set of exact posterior draws of \theta, for instance to simulate the next ten flips under each draw. Importance sampling cannot give us that, because its draws come from q and only the weights carry p.
The peak of \tilde p is at \theta = 2/3, where \tilde p = 4/27 \approx 0.148. With the uniform proposal \tilde q = 1, the constant c = 4/27 gives an envelope at least as high as \tilde p everywhere. Draw \theta from q, then u uniformly from [0, 4/27]:

\theta = 0.7, u = 0.10: \tilde p(0.7) = 0.147 and 0.10 \le 0.147, so accept.
\theta = 0.2, u = 0.05: \tilde p(0.2) = 0.032 and 0.05 > 0.032, so reject.

The acceptance rate is Z_p/(cZ_q) = (1/12)/(4/27) = 0.5625, so a bit over half of the proposals become exact posterior samples.
Why not the others, and where this breaks: ancestral sampling and simple Monte Carlo again need samples from p that we do not have. The catch is dimension. With twenty independent coins of this kind and the matching product envelope, the acceptance rate becomes 0.5625^{20} \approx 10^{-5}, about one acceptance per hundred thousand proposals. At that point rejection sampling is no longer practical, and we need methods that do not rely on a global envelope.

title: Week 4: Message Passing and Monte Carlo
text:
Summary






Note



Key takeaways from Week 4:

Latent variables and TrueSkill. TrueSkill models each player’s skill as a latent variable with p(i\text{ beats }j\mid z_i,z_j)=\sigma(z_i-z_j). Observing games couples the skills (explaining away), so the exact posterior needs a high-dimensional integral.
Message passing on trees. On a tree, eliminating from the leaves inward is optimal, and the intermediate factors become messages m_{j\to i}(x_i)=\sum_{x_j}\psi_j\psi_{ij}\prod_{k\ne i}m_{k\to j}. A node’s normalized belief b(x_i)\propto\psi_i\prod_j m_{j\to i} is its exact marginal.
Belief propagation. Two passes (leaves to root, root to leaves) compute every marginal on a tree. On graphs with cycles, loopy BP iterates the same updates from uniform messages; it gives approximate, often over-confident beliefs, may not converge, and is stabilized by normalization and momentum. Replacing the sum with a max gives max-product BP, whose max-marginals yield the MAP estimate.
Image denoising. A noisy binary image’s posterior is an Ising MRF with edge potentials e^{Jx_sx_t} and node potentials e^{\beta y_sx_s}, \beta=\tfrac12\log\frac{1-\epsilon}{\epsilon}, and loopy BP approximates its pixel marginals.
Monte Carlo. Ancestral sampling draws from a DAG in topological order. Simple Monte Carlo estimates \mathbb{E}_p[\phi] by a sample average that is unbiased with variance \mathrm{var}[\phi]/R, independent of dimension. When p is known only up to Z, importance sampling reweights samples from a proposal q by \tilde p/\tilde q, and rejection sampling accepts proposals that fall under \tilde p beneath an envelope c\tilde q, at an acceptance rate Z_p/(cZ_q) that collapses in high dimensions.



Next week: per the lecture’s closing slide, methods for generating samples from a particular distribution, continuing the sampling thread.

title: Week 4: Message Passing and Monte Carlo
text:
High-level overview
This section retells each part of the week in plain language and without formulas, using the lecture’s own examples. Read it before the chapter for orientation, or after it as a review.
Latent variables and TrueSkill (Latent variables and the TrueSkill model). Some quantities matter but are never observed. In TrueSkill, each player has a hidden skill, and all we see is who beat whom. The stronger player is more likely to win, but upsets happen. One game links the two players’ skills: if A beat B, then A is strong, or B is weak, or both. With many players and games, finding everyone’s skill exactly requires a huge integral, which motivates the rest of the week.
Trees and elimination order (Trees and elimination order). On a tree (a graph with no loops), variable elimination is easy: always remove a leaf first. Removing a leaf touches only its one neighbour, so no large intermediate table ever appears.
Worked example: elimination becomes message passing (Worked example: elimination on a tree becomes message passing). On a five-node tree, eliminating from the leaves inward means each step produces a small summary that one node hands to its neighbour. These summaries are the messages.
Messages and beliefs (Messages and beliefs). A message from node j to node i is j’s summary of everything on its side of the tree, phrased as “how well each value of i fits with what I know”. A node’s belief combines its own local evidence with every message it receives. On a tree, that belief is exactly the correct probability for the node.
Belief propagation on trees (Belief propagation on trees). To get every node’s probabilities, not just one node’s, send messages inward to a root and then back out again. Each message is computed once and reused, so all the answers together cost about twice as much as a single one.
Loopy belief propagation (Loopy belief propagation). A graph with loops has no leaves to start from. Loopy BP starts every message at “no opinion” and keeps updating until things settle. The answers are approximate and tend to be overconfident, because evidence travelling around a loop gets counted more than once, and sometimes the updates never settle at all.
Max-product BP and MAP inference (Max-product BP and MAP inference). Sometimes we want the single best overall explanation rather than a probability for each variable. Replacing “add up the possibilities” with “keep the best possibility” in every message gives that best explanation.
Image denoising with loopy BP (Tutorial example: image denoising with loopy BP). A black-and-white Mona Lisa passes through a channel that flips some pixels at random. Cleaning it up balances two pulls on each pixel: stay close to the colour that was received, and agree with the neighbours, since real images have large smooth regions. Loopy BP balances these pulls across the whole grid, so isolated flipped pixels get pulled back to match their surroundings.
Sampling from an unnormalized density (Sampling from an unnormalized density). The second half switches strategy: instead of computing sums, draw random examples and average over them. The catch is that we often know a distribution only up to an unknown scaling constant. We can say one point is twice as likely as another, but not the actual probability of either.
Ancestral sampling (Ancestral sampling). In a DAG, sampling is easy: sample the variables without parents first, then each child given its parents’ values, and so on down the graph. For the weather chain, first decide whether the pressure is low, then whether it rains given the pressure, then the traffic given the rain.
What sampling is for (What sampling is for). Two separate jobs. The first is to produce random examples that follow the distribution. The second is to estimate an average, such as an expected value, under it.
Simple Monte Carlo (Simple Monte Carlo). If we can draw examples, we estimate an average by averaging over them. To estimate a fair die’s average roll, roll it many times and take the mean. The estimate is right on average, and its typical error shrinks as samples are added (four times as many samples halve it), however many dimensions the problem has.
Why the normalizing constant is hard (Why the normalizing constant is hard). The lecture’s lake picture: we want the average plankton concentration in a lake, and from a boat we can measure the depth and the plankton at any spot. If a few narrow, very deep canyons hold much of the water, randomly chosen spots rarely land on them, and we badly misjudge the total. High-dimensional distributions behave like this, with most of the probability in tiny regions. Checking every point on a grid is no escape, because the number of grid points multiplies with every added dimension.
Importance sampling (Importance sampling). When we cannot sample from the distribution we care about, we sample from an easier one and correct the mismatch with weights. A point the easy distribution produces too often gets a small weight, and a point it produces too rarely gets a large one. The weighted average then estimates the average we wanted, and the unknown scaling constants cancel. It works only if the easy distribution covers the important regions. If it misses a canyon, a few huge weights dominate the answer.
Rejection sampling (Rejection sampling). Choose an easy distribution that, once scaled up, lies above the target everywhere. Propose points from it and keep each one with a chance equal to the target’s height divided by the cover’s height at that point. The points we keep are exact samples from the target. In high dimensions, though, almost every proposal is rejected.
Comparing the sampling methods (Comparing the sampling methods). Every method above depends on an easy distribution that resembles the target, and such a distribution is very hard to find in high dimensions. Week 5’s Markov chain methods avoid needing one.

title: Week 4 practice: Message passing and Monte Carlo
text:
Problem 1: The log-prior of independent skills
Three players have independent normal priors z_i\sim\mathcal N(0,1). Two candidate skill settings are stored as the rows of a 2\times3 array:
\begin{pmatrix}0&1&-2\\0.5&0.5&0.5\end{pmatrix}.

Compute the log-prior \log p(z_1,z_2,z_3) for each row.
Why is the joint log-prior a sum, and along which axis of this array does that sum run? What shape is the result?







TipWorked solution





This uses the prior in the TrueSkill definition of Week 4, Latent variables and the TrueSkill model.
The standard normal log-density is \log\mathcal N(z;0,1)=-\tfrac12\log(2\pi)-\tfrac12z^2, and \tfrac12\log(2\pi)\approx0.9189. Because the priors are independent, \log p(z_1,z_2,z_3)=\sum_{i=1}^3\log\mathcal N(z_i;0,1)=-3\cdot\tfrac12\log(2\pi)-\tfrac12\big(z_1^2+z_2^2+z_3^2\big). Each of the three players contributes one -0.9189, so the constant part is -3(0.9189)=-2.7568 for every row.

Row 1: the squares are 0^2,1^2,(-2)^2=0,1,4, so -2.7568-\tfrac12(0+1+4)=-2.7568-2.5=-5.257. Row 2: the squares are 3\times0.5^2=3\times0.25=0.75, so -2.7568-\tfrac12(0.75)=-3.132.
Independence makes the joint prior a product \prod_ip(z_i), and the log of a product is a sum of logs. Each row is one setting of all players, so the sum runs across the players within a row (axis 1, the column axis), leaving one number per row: shape (2,). Summing down the columns instead would add the same player’s log-density across two different settings, which is not the log of any probability in the model.

Row 2 scores higher because all three skills sit near the prior mean of 0; row 1 pays for the player at -2.
Answer. -5.257 and -3.132. A sum because of independence, taken across players (axis 1), giving shape (2,).





Problem 2: Logs of sums without overflow
Double-precision floats overflow above about 1.8\times10^{308}, so e^{a} is stored as infinity once a exceeds roughly 709 (arithmetic overflow).

Compute \log\big(e^{1000}+e^{998}\big) by hand, without ever forming e^{1000}.
The function \mathrm{logaddexp}(u,v)=\log(e^u+e^v) is computed with the same trick. Write \log(1+e^{a}) using it. What does the naive formula log(1 + exp(a)) return at a=800, and what is the correct value to many digits?







TipWorked solution





This supports evaluating the logistic function of Week 4, Latent variables and the TrueSkill model in log space.

Factor out the largest exponential (the LogSumExp trick). With m=\max(a,b), \log\big(e^{a}+e^{b}\big)=\log\big(e^{m}(e^{a-m}+e^{b-m})\big)=m+\log\big(e^{a-m}+e^{b-m}\big). Every exponent on the right is \le0, so nothing can overflow. Substituting a=1000, b=998, m=1000: \log\big(e^{1000}+e^{998}\big)=1000+\log\big(e^{0}+e^{-2}\big)=1000+\log(1.1353)=1000.1269. The only exponential left to evaluate is e^{-2}, which is harmless.
Since 1=e^0, \log(1+e^{a})=\mathrm{logaddexp}(0,a). Naively, exp(800) overflows to infinity and the log of infinity is infinity. Factoring out e^{a} instead gives 800+\log(1+e^{-800}), and e^{-800} is so small that the answer is 800 to all printed digits. For very negative a the same trick avoids the opposite problem, where e^{a} underflows toward 0 and the log goes to -\infty.

Answer. (1) \approx1000.1269. (2) \log(1+e^a)=\mathrm{logaddexp}(0,a); the naive formula returns infinity at a=800, the true value is 800 (to double precision).





Problem 3: Looking up skills game by game
Four players have skills z = np.array([0.5, -1.0, 2.0, 0.0]). Five games are stored one per row as (winner index, loser index):
games = np.array([[2, 0],
                  [0, 1],
                  [3, 1],
                  [2, 3],
                  [1, 0]])
What does z[games[:, 0]] - z[games[:, 1]] evaluate to, and what does each entry mean in the model?






TipWorked solution





This sets up the “one factor per game” product of Week 4, Latent variables and the TrueSkill model.

games[:, 0] is the winner column [2, 0, 3, 2, 1], and indexing z with an integer array returns one entry per index: z[games[:, 0]] is [2.0, 0.5, 0.0, 2.0, -1.0].
games[:, 1] is [0, 1, 1, 3, 0], so z[games[:, 1]] is [0.5, -1.0, -1.0, 0.0, 0.5].
The elementwise difference has shape (5,), one entry per game.

Each entry is z_{\text{winner}}-z_{\text{loser}}, the argument of \sigma in that game’s likelihood factor. Positive entries are games the stronger player won. The last entry, -1.5, is an upset: player 1 beat a player rated higher, so its factor \sigma(-1.5)\approx0.18 is small. Player indices may repeat across rows, which is how several games between the same pair, or one player in many games, are handled with no loop.
Answer. array([ 1.5,  1.5,  1. ,  2. , -1.5]): the winner-minus-loser skill gap for each game.





Problem 4: A two-player posterior up to a constant
Two players A and B have independent priors z_A,z_B\sim\mathcal N(0,1) and the course’s TrueSkill likelihood p(A\text{ beats }B\mid z_A,z_B)=\sigma(z_A-z_B). They play four games: A wins three and B wins one.

Write \log p(z_A,z_B,\text{games}).
Evaluate it, dropping the constant -\log(2\pi), at (z_A,z_B)=(0,0), (0.5,-0.5), and (1.5,0.5). Which is most probable under the posterior?
Why can we draw the posterior’s contour lines from \log p(z_A,z_B,\text{games}) without ever computing p(\text{games})?
Change variables to d=z_A-z_B and s=z_A+z_B. Show that the likelihood depends only on d, and that the prior factorizes into a function of d times a function of s. What does that say about what the games can teach us?







TipWorked solution





This uses the joint distribution in Week 4, Latent variables and the TrueSkill model and the unnormalized-density setting of Sampling from an unnormalized density.

Prior times one factor per game, with games independent given the skills: \log p=-\log(2\pi)-\tfrac12\big(z_A^2+z_B^2\big) {}+3\log\sigma(z_A-z_B)+\log\sigma(z_B-z_A).
Since \sigma(y)=1/(1+e^{-y}), \log\sigma(y)=-\log(1+e^{-y}). Write d=z_A-z_B, so the likelihood part is 3\log\sigma(d)+\log\sigma(-d) and the prior part (without the constant) is -\tfrac12(z_A^2+z_B^2). The values we need are \log\sigma(0)=-\log2=-0.6931, \log\sigma(1)=-\log(1+e^{-1})=-0.3133, and \log\sigma(-1)=-\log(1+e)=-1.3133.

(0,0): d=0, likelihood 3(-0.6931)+(-0.6931)=-2.7726, prior -\tfrac12(0+0)=0; total -2.773.
(0.5,-0.5): d=1, likelihood 3(-0.3133)-1.3133=-2.2530, prior -\tfrac12(0.25+0.25)=-0.25; total -2.503.
(1.5,0.5): d=1 again, so the same likelihood -2.2530, prior -\tfrac12(2.25+0.25)=-1.25; total -3.503.

(0.5,-0.5) is the most probable of the three.
p(z_A,z_B\mid\text{games})=p(z_A,z_B,\text{games})/p(\text{games}), and the denominator does not depend on (z_A,z_B). Dividing by a constant, or subtracting a constant in log space, shifts every height by the same amount, so the level sets are the same curves; only their labels change.
The likelihood is a function of z_A-z_B=d alone. For the prior, z_A=\tfrac{s+d}{2} and z_B=\tfrac{s-d}{2}, so z_A^2+z_B^2=\tfrac14\big[(s+d)^2+(s-d)^2\big]=\tfrac12\big(s^2+d^2\big), and the prior is proportional to e^{-d^2/4}\,e^{-s^2/4}. (The change of variables also brings a constant Jacobian factor, which does not affect the shape.) The posterior is therefore \big[e^{-d^2/4}\times\text{likelihood}(d)\big]\times e^{-s^2/4}: the games update our belief about the skill difference, while the belief about the sum stays exactly at the prior. Part 2 shows this: (0.5,-0.5) and (1.5,0.5) share d=1 and get the same likelihood, and only the prior separates them.

Answer. (2) -2.773, -2.503, -3.503; (0.5,-0.5) is highest. (3) The normalizer is a constant shift. (4) Likelihood in d only, prior \propto e^{-d^2/4}e^{-s^2/4}, so data inform d and leave s at its prior.

title: Week 4 practice: Message passing and Monte Carlo
text:
Trees and elimination order
Practice for Trees and elimination order.

Problem 5: Why leaves go first
A tree has a hub node h joined to five leaves a,b,c,d,e, and nothing else. Every variable takes k=4 values. The MRF has one potential per node and one per edge, nothing is observed, and we want the normalizer Z by variable elimination.

Suppose we sum out the hub x_h first. Which factors does that sum touch, and over how many variables is the intermediate factor it produces? How many entries does that factor have?
Now sum out the five leaves first, one at a time, and the hub last. Over how many variables is each intermediate factor, and how many entries does it have?
Roughly how many multiply-adds does each order cost? Compare the leaf-first count with the O(nk^2) rate from the week chapter.







TipWorked solution





This uses Week 4, Trees and elimination order.

Every edge potential mentions x_h, so the sum over x_h has to wrap \psi_h and all five edge potentials \psi_{ha},\dots,\psi_{he}. What is left after summing is a function of all five leaves at once, \tau(x_a,x_b,x_c,x_d,x_e), with 4^5=1024 entries. This is the “intermediate factor over many variables” the week chapter warns about.
Summing out a leaf, say x_a, touches only \psi_a(x_a) and \psi_{ha}(x_h,x_a), because no other factor mentions x_a. The result \tau_a(x_h)=\sum_{x_a}\psi_a(x_a)\,\psi_{ha}(x_h,x_a) is a function of x_h alone: 4 entries. The same holds for every leaf. After all five, the hub’s sum \sum_{x_h}\psi_h(x_h)\prod_\ell\tau_\ell(x_h) is a single number.
Hub first: \tau has 4^5=1024 entries, and each entry is a sum of 4 terms (one per value of x_h), so filling it takes about 1024\times4=4^6=4096 multiply-adds, before we even start on the leaves. Leaves first: each \tau_\ell has 4 entries, each a sum of 4 terms, so 16 per leaf and 80 for the five, plus 4 for the hub’s final sum. That is about 84, in line with nk^2=6\cdot16=96. No step ever involved more than two variables at once.

Answer. (1) A factor over all five leaves, 4^5=1024 entries. (2) Each leaf leaves a factor over x_h only, 4 entries. (3) About 4096 against about 84: leaves first is the cheap order.

Problem 6: Pushing sums inward on a different tree
A four-node tree has edges 1\text{-}2, 2\text{-}3, 2\text{-}4, so node 2 is the centre. All variables are binary, x_i\in\{0,1\}. Nodes 1 and 4 are observed, and we want p(x_3\mid\bar x_1,\bar x_4). With the evidence plugged in, the potentials are:



Potential
Value at 0
Value at 1




\psi_2(x_2)
2
1


\psi_3(x_3)
1
3


\psi_{12}(\bar x_1,x_2), as a function of x_2
3
1


\psi_{24}(x_2,\bar x_4), as a function of x_2
1
2



The observed node potentials are plain numbers, \psi_1(\bar x_1)=2 and \psi_4(\bar x_4)=1. The edge between the two unobserved nodes is \psi_{23}(x_2,x_3)=2 when x_2=x_3 and 1 otherwise.

Name the evidence x_E, the query x_F, and the variables x_R that get summed out.
Write p(x_3\mid\bar x_1,\bar x_4) as a normalized sum over x_2, then group the factors into m_{1\to2}(x_2), m_{4\to2}(x_2), and m_{2\to3}(x_3).
Compute the three messages, the unnormalized belief \tilde b(x_3), and p(x_3=1\mid\bar x_1,\bar x_4).







TipWorked solution





This uses Week 4, Worked example: elimination on a tree becomes message passing. The shape differs from the lecture’s tree: here the one summed-out node sits in the middle, between both pieces of evidence and the query.

x_E=\{x_1,x_4\}, x_F=\{x_3\}, x_R=\{x_2\}.
The joint is the product of all seven potentials. Summing out x_2 and normalizing over x_3: p(x_3\mid\bar x_1,\bar x_4)=\frac{1}{Z^E}\,\psi_3(x_3)\sum_{x_2}\psi_2(x_2)\,\psi_{23}(x_2,x_3) {}\times\big[\psi_1(\bar x_1)\psi_{12}(\bar x_1,x_2)\big]\big[\psi_4(\bar x_4)\psi_{24}(x_2,\bar x_4)\big]. The first bracket involves only x_2: it is m_{1\to2}(x_2). The second is m_{4\to2}(x_2). The whole sum over x_2 is a function of x_3 alone, which is m_{2\to3}(x_3).
Observed senders plug in their value, so m_{1\to2}=2\cdot(3,\ 1)=(6,\ 2),\qquad m_{4\to2}=1\cdot(1,\ 2)=(1,\ 2). Node 2 multiplies its own potential by both incoming messages, one number per value of x_2: 2\cdot6\cdot1=12 at x_2=0 and 1\cdot2\cdot2=4 at x_2=1. Then it multiplies by the edge and sums out x_2: m_{2\to3}(0)=12\cdot2+4\cdot1=28,\qquad m_{2\to3}(1)=12\cdot1+4\cdot2=20. The belief is \tilde b(x_3)=\psi_3(x_3)\,m_{2\to3}(x_3)=(28,\ 60), so Z^E=88 and p(x_3=1\mid\bar x_1,\bar x_4)=\frac{60}{88}=\frac{15}{22}\approx0.682. As a check, listing the four terms of the sum directly gives 24+4=28 at x_3=0 and 36+24=60 at x_3=1. The messages did the same sum in pieces.

Answer. (1) x_E=\{x_1,x_4\}, x_F=\{x_3\}, x_R=\{x_2\}. (3) m_{1\to2}=(6,2), m_{4\to2}=(1,2), m_{2\to3}=(28,20), \tilde b=(28,60), p(x_3=1\mid\bar x_1,\bar x_4)=15/22\approx0.682.

title: Week 4 practice: Message passing and Monte Carlo
text:
Messages and beliefs
Practice for Messages and beliefs.

Problem 7: Sum-product on a three-node star
Three binary spins x_1,x_2,x_3\in\{+1,-1\} form a star with centre x_2: the edges are 1\text{-}2 and 2\text{-}3. The potentials are

\psi_1(+1)=1, \psi_1(-1)=2, and \psi_2=\psi_3=1;
\psi_{12}(x_1,x_2)=3 if x_1=x_2 and 1 otherwise;
\psi_{23}(x_2,x_3)=2 if x_2=x_3 and 1 otherwise.

We observe \bar x_3=+1.

Compute m_{1\to2}(x_2) and m_{3\to2}(x_2), then the belief b(x_2)=p(x_2\mid\bar x_3).
Check part 1 by writing out the unnormalized joint \tilde p(x_1,x_2,\bar x_3) for all four settings of (x_1,x_2).
To get b(x_1), which extra message is needed? Compute it and the belief.







TipWorked solution





This uses the message and belief definitions in Week 4, Messages and beliefs, including the rule for an observed sender.

Node 1 is an unobserved leaf, so it sums over its own value: m_{1\to2}(+1)=\psi_1(+1)\cdot3+\psi_1(-1)\cdot1=3+2=5, m_{1\to2}(-1)=\psi_1(+1)\cdot1+\psi_1(-1)\cdot3=1+6=7. Node 3 is observed, so its value is plugged in rather than summed: m_{3\to2}(x_2)=\psi_3(+1)\,\psi_{23}(x_2,+1), which is 2 at x_2=+1 and 1 at x_2=-1. The belief multiplies both in with \psi_2=1: \tilde b(x_2)=(5\cdot2,\ 7\cdot1)=(10,\ 7),\qquad b(x_2)=\big(\tfrac{10}{17},\ \tfrac{7}{17}\big)\approx(0.588,\ 0.412). The observation x_3=+1 pulls x_2 toward +1, while node 1’s preference for -1 pulls the other way through a stronger edge. The observation wins, narrowly.
\tilde p(x_1,x_2,\bar x_3)=\psi_1(x_1)\,\psi_{12}(x_1,x_2)\,\psi_{23}(x_2,+1):










(x_1,x_2)
(+1,+1)
(-1,+1)
(+1,-1)
(-1,-1)




\tilde p
1\cdot3\cdot2=6
2\cdot1\cdot2=4
1\cdot1\cdot1=1
2\cdot3\cdot1=6



Summing over x_1 gives 10 at x_2=+1 and 7 at x_2=-1, the same as \tilde b(x_2). The messages did this sum in pieces.
Node 1 has one neighbour, node 2, so it needs m_{2\to1}. Node 2 multiplies in what it heard from its other neighbour, node 3, and sums out x_2: m_{2\to1}(+1)=3\cdot2+1\cdot1=7,\qquad m_{2\to1}(-1)=1\cdot2+3\cdot1=5. Then \tilde b(x_1)=(\psi_1(+1)\cdot7,\ \psi_1(-1)\cdot5)=(7,\ 10), so b(x_1)\approx(0.412,\ 0.588). The table agrees: 6+1=7 at x_1=+1 and 4+6=10 at x_1=-1.

Answer. (1) m_{1\to2}=(5,7), m_{3\to2}=(2,1), b(x_2)=(10/17,\ 7/17). (2) The table sums to the same (10,7). (3) m_{2\to1}=(7,5), b(x_1)=(7/17,\ 10/17).





Problem 8: What goes into a message
Node j in a tree-shaped MRF has three neighbours: i, k, and l.

Write m_{j\to i}(x_i) out in full. Which incoming messages appear in it, and which one is left out?
Now suppose x_j is observed with value \bar x_j. The messages m_{k\to j} and m_{l\to j} still appear in the formula. As functions of x_i, how do they affect m_{j\to i}? What does that say about how much node i learns from the far side of j?
A classmate says the message (0.2,\ 0.9) must be a bug because its entries do not sum to 1. Are they right?
Leaf j is unobserved, with \psi_j=(1,1) and binary edge potential \psi_{ij}=2 when x_i=x_j and 1 otherwise. Compute m_{j\to i}. What does it tell node i?







TipWorked solution





This uses the message definition and the remarks after it in Week 4, Messages and beliefs.

m_{j\to i}(x_i)=\sum_{x_j}\psi_j(x_j)\,\psi_{ij}(x_i,x_j)\,m_{k\to j}(x_j)\,m_{l\to j}(x_j). The messages from k and l appear. The message m_{i\to j} is left out, because node i already knows what it sent.
With x_j fixed, the formula becomes \psi_j(\bar x_j)\,\psi_{ij}(x_i,\bar x_j)\,m_{k\to j}(\bar x_j)\,m_{l\to j}(\bar x_j). The two incoming messages are each evaluated at one value, so they are just numbers: they scale the whole message by a constant and do not change its shape as a function of x_i. After normalizing, m_{j\to i} depends only on \psi_{ij}(x_i,\bar x_j). So node i learns nothing from beyond j once x_j is observed, which is the graph-separation picture of conditional independence in an MRF.
No. A message is a nonnegative score per state, like a potential, not a probability distribution. Only the ratio 0.9/0.2=4.5 matters, and rescaling never changes a normalized belief.
m_{j\to i}(x_i)=\sum_{x_j}\psi_{ij}(x_i,x_j) gives 2+1=3 at both values of x_i. The message is flat, so it multiplies every belief entry by the same 3 and tells node i nothing. A leaf with no preference and a symmetric edge has no opinion to pass on.

Answer. (1) m_{k\to j} and m_{l\to j} appear; m_{i\to j} is excluded. (2) They become constants, so the far side has no effect on node i. (3) No: messages need not sum to 1. (4) (3,\ 3), a flat message carrying no information.

title: Week 4 practice: Message passing and Monte Carlo
text:
Belief propagation on trees
Practice for Belief propagation on trees.

Problem 9: Scheduling messages on a tree
An undirected graph has six nodes and the edges 1\text{-}2,\quad 2\text{-}3,\quad 2\text{-}4,\quad 4\text{-}5,\quad 4\text{-}6.

Check that the graph is a tree and list its leaves. Would it still be a tree if we added the edge 1\text{-}3?
How many messages does belief propagation send in total?
Which messages can be computed before any other message exists?
Which incoming messages must node 4 hold before it can send m_{4\to2}? Which must node 2 hold before it can send m_{2\to1}?
With node 2 as the root, list the messages of the inward pass and of the outward pass.







TipWorked solution





This uses the tree definition in Week 4, Trees and elimination order and the two-pass schedule in Belief propagation on trees.

Every node is reachable from node 2 (1, 3, 4 directly; 5, 6 through 4), so the graph is connected. A connected graph on 6 nodes with no cycles has exactly 5 edges, and this one has 5, so it has no cycles and is a tree. The leaves, the nodes with exactly one neighbour, are 1, 3, 5, and 6. Adding 1\text{-}3 closes the cycle 1\text{-}2\text{-}3\text{-}1, so the graph would no longer be a tree.
One message in each direction along each edge: 2|\mathcal E|=2\cdot5=10.
A node can send to i once it has heard from every neighbour other than i. A leaf has no other neighbours, so the product in the message formula is empty and it can send right away: m_{1\to2}, m_{3\to2}, m_{5\to4}, m_{6\to4}. Nodes 2 and 4 each have at least two neighbours they have not yet heard from, so they must wait.
N(4)\setminus\{2\}=\{5,6\}, so node 4 needs m_{5\to4} and m_{6\to4}. N(2)\setminus\{1\}=\{3,4\}, so node 2 needs m_{3\to2} and m_{4\to2}. The second of these itself waited on nodes 5 and 6, which is how m_{2\to1} ends up summarizing the whole subtree on node 2’s side.
Inward: m_{1\to2}, m_{3\to2}, m_{5\to4}, m_{6\to4}, then m_{4\to2}. Outward: m_{2\to1}, m_{2\to3}, m_{2\to4}, then m_{4\to5}, m_{4\to6}. That is 5+5=10 messages, matching part 2.

Answer. (1) A tree with leaves 1, 3, 5, 6; adding 1\text{-}3 makes a cycle. (2) 10. (3) The four leaf messages. (4) Node 4 needs messages from 5 and 6; node 2 needs messages from 3 and 4. (5) As listed above.





Problem 10: Why not just run elimination once per node?
A chain x_1\text{-}x_2\text{-}\cdots\text{-}x_n has n variables with k states each. Computing one message costs about k^2 multiply-adds (a sum over k values for each of k values).

How many messages does belief propagation send to get every marginal? About how many multiply-adds is that?
Instead, run variable elimination separately for each node, with that node as the query. One run costs about (n-1)k^2. What is the total for all n runs?
Evaluate both totals for n=100 and k=10.
Which work does the separate-runs approach repeat? Name two runs that share a message.







TipWorked solution





This uses Week 4, Belief propagation on trees.

A chain with n nodes is a tree with n-1 edges, and BP sends one message in each direction along each edge: 2(n-1) messages, about 2(n-1)k^2 multiply-adds.
n runs at (n-1)k^2 each: about n(n-1)k^2.
BP: 2\cdot99\cdot100=19{,}800. Separate runs: 100\cdot99\cdot100=990{,}000. The ratio is n/2=50.
The run with query x_5 computes m_{1\to2},m_{2\to3},m_{3\to4},m_{4\to5} from the left. The run with query x_6 computes those same four messages and then m_{5\to6}. Every left-to-right message is recomputed in every run whose query lies to its right, and likewise from the other side. BP computes each of the 2(n-1) distinct messages once and lets every node reuse them.

Answer. (1) 2(n-1) messages, about 2(n-1)k^2. (2) About n(n-1)k^2. (3) 19{,}800 against 990{,}000. (4) The queries x_5 and x_6 share m_{1\to2},\dots,m_{4\to5}.

title: Week 4 practice: Message passing and Monte Carlo
text:
Loopy belief propagation
Practice for Loopy belief propagation.

Problem 11: True or false on loopy BP
Say whether each statement is true or false, with a one-line reason.

On a tree, running the loopy BP updates until they stop changing gives the exact marginals.
On a graph with cycles, loopy BP always converges if we run enough iterations.
With plain updates (no momentum), rescaling each new message so that it sums to 1 does not change the normalized beliefs.
On a graph with cycles, loopy BP beliefs are often more peaked than the true marginals.
Setting \alpha=1 in the momentum update gives back the plain update.
If a node’s message to i also multiplied in the message i had sent it, beliefs on a tree would still be exact.







TipWorked solution





This uses Week 4, Loopy belief propagation and the exclusion rule in Messages and beliefs.

True. On a tree the message updates are the same as BP, and the lecture states loopy BP is exact on trees.
False. The lecture says it may not converge at all, and messages can oscillate.
True. Each update is a sum of products that is linear in every incoming message, so a constant factor on one message passes through as a constant factor on later messages and beliefs. Normalizing the belief removes it, as in the three-node chain example. With momentum, scale does matter: blending (1-\alpha)\,m^{\text{old}}+\alpha\,[\text{update}] weights the two vectors by their sizes as well as by \alpha. That is one reason to normalize before blending.
True. Evidence that leaves a node along one edge of a cycle can return along another and be multiplied in again, like hearing your own rumour back.
True. (1-1)\,m^{\text{old}}+1\cdot[\text{update}]=[\text{update}].
False. Take the chain x_1\text{-}x_2. The modified message would be m_{2\to1}(x_1)=\sum_{x_2}\psi_2(x_2)\,\psi_{12}(x_1,x_2)\,m_{1\to2}(x_2), and m_{1\to2}(x_2)=\sum_{x_1'}\psi_1(x_1')\,\psi_{12}(x_1',x_2) is built from node 1’s own potential. The belief b(x_1)\propto\psi_1(x_1)\,m_{2\to1}(x_1) would then count node 1’s evidence once directly and a second time after a round trip through node 2. Worse, each message would need the other before it could be computed, so on a tree the schedule could never start. The exclusion k\ne i is what stops a node’s own information from being counted twice.

Answer. True, false, true, true, true, false.





Problem 12: One message, by hand
In a denoising MRF with node potentials \psi_j(x_j)=e^{\beta y_jx_j} and edge potentials \psi_{ij}(x_i,x_j)=e^{Jx_ix_j}, take \beta=0.7 and an edge j\text{-}i with coupling J=0.4. Pixels take values \pm1, with +1 for white and -1 for black (this convention holds for all the denoising problems below). Pixel j is observed black, y_j=-1. Its three other neighbours currently send it these messages, written \big(m(+1),\ m(-1)\big):
(0.6,\ 0.4), \qquad (0.7,\ 0.3), \qquad (0.45,\ 0.55).

Compute the unnormalized message m_{j\to i}(x_i) for x_i=+1 and x_i=-1.
Normalize it.
The old message was (0.5,\ 0.5). Apply the momentum update with step size \alpha=0.6.







TipWorked solution





This uses the update rule of Week 4, Loopy belief propagation with the potentials of the denoising example. The message is m_{j\to i}(x_i)=\sum_{x_j\in\{+1,-1\}}\psi_j(x_j)\,\psi_{ij}(x_i,x_j)\prod_{k\in N(j)\setminus\{i\}}m_{k\to j}(x_j), and we build it from the inside out.
Step 1: product of incoming messages, one number per state of x_j. x_j=+1:\ 0.6\cdot0.7\cdot0.45=0.189, \qquad x_j=-1:\ 0.4\cdot0.3\cdot0.55=0.066.
Step 2: node potential. Substituting \beta=0.7, y_j=-1 into \psi_j(x_j)=e^{\beta y_jx_j}: \psi_j(+1)=e^{0.7(-1)(+1)}=e^{-0.7} and \psi_j(-1)=e^{0.7(-1)(-1)}=e^{0.7}. The observation pulls x_j toward black.
Step 3: sum over x_j for each x_i. The edge potential is \psi_{ij}=e^{Jx_ix_j}, which is e^{0.4} when x_i,x_j agree and e^{-0.4} when they disagree. Node and edge potentials multiply, so their exponents add: \psi_j(x_j)\,\psi_{ij}(x_i,x_j)=e^{\beta y_jx_j+Jx_ix_j}. For example, at x_i=x_j=+1 the exponent is 0.7(-1)(+1)+0.4(+1)(+1)=-0.7+0.4. Each line below has the x_j=+1 term first and the x_j=-1 term second: m_{j\to i}(+1)=e^{-0.7+0.4}(0.189)+e^{0.7-0.4}(0.066) =0.7408(0.189)+1.3499(0.066)=0.1400+0.0891=0.2291, m_{j\to i}(-1)=e^{-0.7-0.4}(0.189)+e^{0.7+0.4}(0.066) =0.3329(0.189)+3.0042(0.066)=0.0629+0.1983=0.2612.
Normalize. The total is 0.4903, giving (0.4673,\ 0.5327).
Momentum. m^{\text{new}}=(1-\alpha)\,m^{\text{old}}+\alpha\,[\text{update}]: 0.4\,(0.5,\ 0.5)+0.6\,(0.4673,\ 0.5327)=(0.4804,\ 0.5196).
Notice the tug of war. Two of the three neighbours lean white, which shows up as the larger product at x_j=+1, but the black observation multiplies the x_j=-1 branch by e^{0.7}/e^{-0.7}\approx4. The message ends up leaning slightly black. In code, the same three steps are an elementwise product, a 2\times2 table of edge-times-node potentials, and a sum over one axis, as in Week 3 practice, Problem 13.
Answer. Unnormalized (0.2291,\ 0.2612); normalized (0.4673,\ 0.5327); after momentum (0.4804,\ 0.5196).





Problem 13: What the step size does
Loopy BP on a cycle can oscillate. Take a toy version: a single message (p,\ 1-p) whose freshly computed update is always the flipped vector (1-p,\ p). Start from p=0.8 and apply the momentum update m^{\text{new}}=(1-\alpha)\,m^{\text{old}}+\alpha\,[\text{update}].

Trace p for three iterations with \alpha=1, \alpha=0.5, and \alpha=0.25.
Write p^{\text{new}}-\tfrac12 in terms of p^{\text{old}}-\tfrac12 and explain the three behaviours.







TipWorked solution





This uses the momentum trick in Week 4, Loopy belief propagation.

The first entry updates as p^{\text{new}}=(1-\alpha)p+\alpha(1-p).

\alpha=1 (plain replacement): 0.8\to0.2\to0.8\to0.2. It never settles.
\alpha=0.5: 0.5\,(0.8)+0.5\,(0.2)=0.5, then 0.5 forever.
\alpha=0.25: 0.75p+0.25(1-p)=0.25+0.5p, so 0.8\to0.65\to0.575\to0.5375.

Subtracting \tfrac12 from both sides, p^{\text{new}}-\tfrac12=(1-2\alpha)\big(p^{\text{old}}-\tfrac12\big). The distance from the fixed point \tfrac12 is multiplied by 1-2\alpha each iteration. At \alpha=1 the factor is -1: same size, opposite sign, a permanent oscillation. At \alpha=0.5 it is 0 and the oscillation dies in one step. At \alpha=0.25 it is \tfrac12, so the distance halves each time with no sign flips.

Real BP updates are not this simple map, so no single step size zeroes out oscillation in general. The general point survives: blending in the old message shrinks the jump each iteration, which damps oscillation. The price is that when the plain updates would have converged anyway, a small \alpha makes each iteration move less.
Answer. \alpha=1: 0.2, 0.8, 0.2. \alpha=0.5: 0.5, 0.5, 0.5. \alpha=0.25: 0.65, 0.575, 0.5375. The deviation from \tfrac12 scales by 1-2\alpha per step.

Max-product BP and MAP inference
Practice for Max-product BP and MAP inference.

Problem 14: Max-product against the most likely state of each node
Two spins x_1,x_2\in\{+1,-1\} share one edge, with node potentials equal to 1 and edge potential




x_2=+1
x_2=-1




x_1=+1
4
1


x_1=-1
3
3




Run sum-product: compute both messages, both beliefs, and the setting (\tilde x_1,\tilde x_2) that picks the more likely state of each node separately. What is its probability?
Run max-product and read off \hat x_i=\arg\max_{x_i}b(x_i). What is the probability of (\hat x_1,\hat x_2)?
Explain the difference in one or two sentences.







TipWorked solution





This uses Week 4, Max-product BP and MAP inference.
The normalizer is Z=4+1+3+3=11, so the joint probabilities are the table entries divided by 11.

Each node has one neighbour and node potentials are 1, so the message formula reduces to m_{2\to1}(x_1)=\sum_{x_2}\psi_{12}(x_1,x_2) (a row sum of the table) and m_{1\to2}(x_2)=\sum_{x_1}\psi_{12}(x_1,x_2) (a column sum): m_{2\to1}(+1)=4+1=5,\qquad m_{2\to1}(-1)=3+3=6, m_{1\to2}(+1)=4+3=7,\qquad m_{1\to2}(-1)=1+3=4. The belief is b(x_i)\propto\psi_i(x_i)\,m_{j\to i}(x_i) with \psi_i=1, so each belief is its incoming message normalized: b(x_1)=(5,6)/11=(5/11,\ 6/11) and b(x_2)=(7,4)/11=(7/11,\ 4/11). Node by node, \tilde x_1=-1 and \tilde x_2=+1. The pair (-1,+1) has probability 3/11\approx0.273.
Max-product takes the largest term instead: m_{2\to1}(+1)=\max(4,1)=4,\qquad m_{2\to1}(-1)=\max(3,3)=3, m_{1\to2}(+1)=\max(4,3)=4,\qquad m_{1\to2}(-1)=\max(1,3)=3. With \psi_i=1 the max-marginals are the messages themselves: b(x_1)=m_{2\to1}=(4,\ 3) and b(x_2)=m_{1\to2}=(4,\ 3). Both peak at +1, so (\hat x_1,\hat x_2)=(+1,+1), with probability 4/11\approx0.364. This is the largest entry in the table, so it is the MAP estimate.
A sum-product belief adds up every configuration with x_1 in a given state. x_1=-1 wins that total (3+3 against 4+1) without containing the single best configuration. A max-product belief scores only the best configuration in each state, so reading those off node by node gives the best joint setting.

Answer. (1) b(x_1)=(5/11,6/11), b(x_2)=(7/11,4/11); the node-by-node choice is (-1,+1), probability 3/11. (2) Max-product gives (+1,+1), probability 4/11, the MAP estimate. (3) Summed totals and best single configurations can disagree.





Problem 15: Max-product on a three-node chain
Binary variables x_1\text{-}x_2\text{-}x_3, each in \{0,1\}, have node potentials \psi_1=(2,\ 1) (values at 0 and 1) and \psi_2=\psi_3=1. The edge potentials are

\psi_{12}(x_1,x_2)=3 if x_1=x_2 and 1 otherwise;
\psi_{23}(x_2,x_3) given by the table below.

Run max-product: compute all four messages and the three max-marginals b(x_1), b(x_2), b(x_3). Read off (\hat x_1,\hat x_2,\hat x_3).
Check part 1 by listing \tilde p(x_1,x_2,x_3) for all eight configurations. What is the probability of the MAP setting?
What do the largest entries of the three max-marginals have in common, and why?







TipWorked solution





This uses Week 4, Max-product BP and MAP inference. Write each message as (value at 0, value at 1).

Each message is the sum-product formula with \max in place of \sum. m_{1\to2}(x_2)=\max_{x_1}\psi_1(x_1)\,\psi_{12}(x_1,x_2):\quad(\max(6,1),\ \max(2,3))=(6,\ 3), m_{3\to2}(x_2)=\max_{x_3}\psi_{23}(x_2,x_3):\quad(\max(1,4),\ \max(2,2))=(4,\ 2). The other two messages each use the one message the sender received from its other side: m_{2\to3}(x_3)=\max_{x_2}\psi_{23}(x_2,x_3)\,m_{1\to2}(x_2):\quad(\max(6,6),\ \max(24,6))=(6,\ 24), m_{2\to1}(x_1)=\max_{x_2}\psi_{12}(x_1,x_2)\,m_{3\to2}(x_2):\quad(\max(12,2),\ \max(4,6))=(12,\ 6). The max-marginal at each node is its own potential times all incoming messages, b(x_i)=\psi_i(x_i)\prod_jm_{j\to i}(x_i). Since \psi_2=\psi_3=1, only node 1 has a potential to multiply in: b(x_1)=\psi_1\cdot m_{2\to1}=(2\cdot12,\ 1\cdot6)=(24,\ 6), b(x_2)=m_{1\to2}\cdot m_{3\to2}=(6\cdot4,\ 3\cdot2)=(24,\ 6), and b(x_3)=m_{2\to3}=(6,\ 24). So (\hat x_1,\hat x_2,\hat x_3)=(0,0,1).

The largest entry is 24 at (0,0,1), matching part 1. The total is Z=55, so the MAP setting has probability 24/55\approx0.436.
Each one is 24, the score of the MAP configuration. A max-marginal b(x_i) scores the best configuration with node i in state x_i, and the best configuration overall has every node in some state, so it shows up as the top entry at every node. The table confirms the other entries too: the best configuration with x_3=0 scores 6, which is b(x_3=0).

section: Tutorial example: image denoising with loopy BP
text:
Tutorial example: image denoising with loopy BP
Practice for Tutorial example: image denoising with loopy BP.

Problem 16: Who talks to whom on a 3×3 grid
A 3\times3 binary image is flattened into a vector of n=9 pixels in row-major order, so node s sits in row \lfloor s/3\rfloor and column s \bmod 3:
\begin{matrix}0&1&2\\3&4&5\\6&7&8\end{matrix}
Use the 4-neighbour rule: with m=3, node s has right neighbour s+1 unless (s+1)\bmod m=0, left neighbour s-1 unless s\bmod m=0, lower neighbour s+m if s+m<n, and upper neighbour s-m if s-m\ge0.

List the neighbours of node 0 (a corner), node 1 (an edge), and node 4 (the centre).
Messages are stored in an array messages of shape (2, 9, 9), where messages[:, j, i] is the message from node j to node i, entry 0 is the value at x_i=+1 and entry 1 the value at x_i=-1. Which slice holds m_{4\to1}?
When node 4 computes its message to node 1, which slices does it multiply together? Is the edge 4\text{-}1 horizontal or vertical?







TipWorked solution





This uses the message definition in Week 4, Messages and beliefs and the grid model of the denoising example.

Node 0: column 0 has no left neighbour and row 0 has no upper one, leaving \{1,3\}. Node 1: right 2, left 0, lower 4, no upper, so \{0,2,4\}. Node 4: all four exist, \{1,3,5,7\}. Corners have 2 neighbours, edges 3, interior pixels 4.
The sender is the middle index and the receiver the last, so m_{4\to1} is messages[:, 4, 1]: messages[0, 4, 1] is m_{4\to1}(+1) and messages[1, 4, 1] is m_{4\to1}(-1).
The product runs over k\in N(4)\setminus\{1\}=\{3,5,7\}, and each factor is a message into node 4: messages[:, 3, 4], messages[:, 5, 4], messages[:, 7, 4]. The message messages[:, 1, 4] is left out, because node 4 does not echo back what node 1 told it. Nodes 4 and 1 share column 1 and sit in adjacent rows, so the edge is vertical.

Answer. (1) N(0)=\{1,3\}, N(1)=\{0,2,4\}, N(4)=\{1,3,5,7\}. (2) messages[:, 4, 1]. (3) The incoming messages from 3, 5, and 7 (second index = sender, third = 4); the edge is vertical.





Problem 17: From messages to a pixel decision
A pixel i in the same model (\beta=0.7, +1 white, -1 black) is observed white, y_i=+1. After message passing, its four neighbours send
(0.3,\ 0.7), \qquad (0.4,\ 0.6), \qquad (0.35,\ 0.65), \qquad (0.6,\ 0.4).

Compute the unnormalized belief \tilde b(x_i) and the normalized belief b(x_i).
Using the rule \hat x_i=\arg\max_{x_i}b(x_i), what colour is the denoised pixel?
Suppose the last message had been stored unnormalized as (6,\ 4). Does anything in part 2 change?







TipWorked solution





This uses the belief formula of Week 4, Messages and beliefs and the decision rule at the end of the denoising example.

The belief is \tilde b(x_i)=\psi_i(x_i)\prod_{j\in N(i)}m_{j\to i}(x_i). Substituting \beta=0.7, y_i=+1 into \psi_i(x_i)=e^{\beta y_ix_i} gives \psi_i(+1)=e^{0.7}=2.0138 and \psi_i(-1)=e^{-0.7}=0.4966. Unlike a message, a belief multiplies in every neighbour’s message, with no exclusion: \prod_jm_{j\to i}(+1)=0.3\cdot0.4\cdot0.35\cdot0.6=0.0252, \prod_jm_{j\to i}(-1)=0.7\cdot0.6\cdot0.65\cdot0.4=0.1092. So \tilde b=(2.0138\cdot0.0252,\ 0.4966\cdot0.1092)=(0.0507,\ 0.0542), and dividing by the total 0.1050 gives b=(0.483,\ 0.517).
b(-1)>b(+1), so \hat x_i=-1: black. Three of four neighbours lean black strongly enough to outvote both the white observation and the one neighbour leaning white, which is how the model corrects a pixel the channel likely flipped.
No. Multiplying one message by 10 multiplies both entries of \tilde b by 10, and normalizing removes it. This is the scaling argument of the week chapter’s three-node chain example.

Answer. \tilde b\approx(0.0507,\ 0.0542), b\approx(0.483,\ 0.517); the pixel is set to black; rescaling a message changes nothing.





Problem 18: Observation strength against coupling

A binary symmetric channel flips each pixel with probability \epsilon. Compute \beta=\tfrac12\log\frac{1-\epsilon}{\epsilon} for \epsilon=0.1 and \epsilon=0.25.
An interior pixel i is observed black (y_i=-1; as before, +1 is white and -1 black). To isolate the trade-off, suppose its four neighbours are known to be white (+1), so each sends the message m(x_i)=e^{Jx_i} (one shared coupling J on all four edges). Find the ratio b(+1)/b(-1), and the condition on J under which the pixel’s belief favours white.
Evaluate that threshold for both values of \epsilon from part 1.







TipWorked solution





This uses the observation model and the posterior of Week 4, Tutorial example: image denoising.

\epsilon=0.1: \beta=\tfrac12\log9=\log3\approx1.099. \epsilon=0.25: \beta=\tfrac12\log3\approx0.549. Noisier observations deserve less trust, and \beta shrinks accordingly.
The node potential gives e^{-\beta} at x_i=+1 and e^{\beta} at x_i=-1. Each neighbour message gives e^{J} versus e^{-J}, four times over. So \frac{b(+1)}{b(-1)}=\frac{e^{-\beta}\,e^{4J}}{e^{\beta}\,e^{-4J}}=e^{8J-2\beta}. The belief favours white exactly when 8J>2\beta, that is J>\beta/4.
\epsilon=0.1: J>0.275. \epsilon=0.25: J>0.137.

The inequality is a vote. The observation contributes 2\beta toward black, and each agreeing neighbour contributes 2J toward white. With noisier data a weaker coupling is enough to outvote the observation. The inequality has no way of knowing whether the black pixel is noise or a genuine one-pixel detail of the image: it treats both the same.
Answer. (1) \beta\approx1.099 and 0.549. (2) b(+1)/b(-1)=e^{8J-2\beta}; white wins when J>\beta/4. (3) J>0.275 and J>0.137.

title: Week 4 practice: Message passing and Monte Carlo
text:
Sampling from an unnormalized density
Practice for Sampling from an unnormalized density.

Problem 19: What needs Z and what does not

A model on a huge state space can evaluate \tilde p but not Z. For four particular states it reports \tilde p(s_1)=6, \tilde p(s_2)=2, \tilde p(s_3)=0.5, \tilde p(s_4)=6. For each question, say whether it can be answered without Z, and answer it if so.

How many times more probable is s_1 than s_3?
Which of s_1,s_2 is more probable?
Is p(s_1)>0.01?
What is p(s_1)+p(s_4)?

In the denoising posterior p(x\mid y)\propto\exp\{J\sum_{s\sim t}x_sx_t+\beta\sum_sy_sx_s\}, take J=0.5 and \beta=1. Pixel s has x_s=+1 (white), four neighbours all equal to +1, and observation y_s=-1 (black). Let x' be the same image with only x_s flipped to -1. Find p(x\mid y)/p(x'\mid y).







TipWorked solution





This uses Week 4, Sampling from an unnormalized density and the posterior of the denoising example.

Since p=\tilde p/Z, any ratio of probabilities cancels Z, and any single probability needs it.

No Z needed: 6/0.5=12 times.
No Z needed: s_1, three times as probable.
Needs Z. p(s_1)=6/Z, and without Z that could be anything.
Needs Z: it is 12/Z. We can say s_1 and s_4 are equally probable, but not how much of the total they hold.

The ratio is \exp\{E(x)-E(x')\} where E is the exponent. Every term that does not involve pixel s is the same in both images and cancels, along with Z. The terms that involve s are x_s\big(J\sum_{t\in N(s)}x_t+\beta y_s\big), and flipping x_s flips their sign, so E(x)-E(x')=2x_s\Big(J\sum_{t\in N(s)}x_t+\beta y_s\Big)=2\,(0.5\cdot4-1)=2. The ratio is e^2\approx7.39. Agreeing with four white neighbours outweighs disagreeing with the black observation. The calculation looked at five pixels and never touched Z, which is a sum over all 2^n images.

Answer. (1a) 12. (1b) s_1. (1c) and (1d) need Z. (2) e^2\approx7.39.

text:
Ancestral sampling
Practice for Ancestral sampling.

Problem 20: Ancestral sampling by hand
A DAG over binary variables A,B,C,D\in\{0,1\} has edges A\to B, A\to C, B\to D, C\to D, with

p(A=1)=0.3;
p(B=1\mid A=0)=0.2, p(B=1\mid A=1)=0.7;
p(C=1\mid A=0)=0.6, p(C=1\mid A=1)=0.1;
p(D=1\mid B,C)=0.1,\ 0.5,\ 0.5,\ 0.9 for (B,C)=(0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1).

To sample a binary variable with p(\text{variable}=1)=\theta, draw u uniform on [0,1] and set the variable to 1 if u<\theta.

Which of these are valid topological orders? (a) A,B,C,D (b) A,C,B,D (c) B,A,C,D (d) A,D,B,C.
Visit the nodes in order A,B,C,D using the uniforms 0.25,\ 0.81,\ 0.05,\ 0.47. What sample do you get, and what is its probability under the joint?
Can this procedure give a sample from p(A\mid D=1) directly? Why or why not?







TipWorked solution





This uses Week 4, Ancestral sampling.


and (b) are valid: A comes before both its children, and D comes after both its parents. Swapping B and C is fine because neither is a parent of the other. (c) puts B before its parent A, and (d) puts D before its parents B and C, so both are invalid.

Each step uses the conditional with the parents set to values already drawn.

A: 0.25<0.3, so A=1.
B: p(B=1\mid A=1)=0.7 and 0.81\ge0.7, so B=0.
C: p(C=1\mid A=1)=0.1 and 0.05<0.1, so C=1.
D: p(D=1\mid B=0,C=1)=0.5 and 0.47<0.5, so D=1.

The sample is (A,B,C,D)=(1,0,1,1). A DAG’s joint factorizes as p(A)\,p(B\mid A)\,p(C\mid A)\,p(D\mid B,C), so its probability is the product of the four factors used, each read at the values drawn: p(A=1)\,p(B=0\mid A=1)\,p(C=1\mid A=1)\,p(D=1\mid B=0,C=1)=0.3\cdot(1-0.7)\cdot0.1\cdot0.5=0.0045. The second factor is 0.3 because B came out 0, so we need 1-p(B=1\mid A=1).
No. D is drawn last, from its parents, so its value is an output of the procedure, not something we can fix in advance. Nothing in the procedure sets D=1 and then updates A. The lecture notes that ancestral sampling draws from the joint with nothing observed and does not directly give conditional samples.

Answer. (1) (a) and (b). (2) (1,0,1,1), probability 0.0045. (3) No: the observed variable is a child, drawn last.

text:
What sampling is for
Practice for What sampling is for.

Problem 21: Picking the test function
A random variable takes values x\in\{0,1,2,3\} with probabilities p=(0.1,\ 0.4,\ 0.3,\ 0.2). For each question, write the test function \phi whose expectation answers it, then compute the exact answer.

The mean of x.
The variance of x.
\mathbb P(x\ge2).
\mathbb P(x\text{ is odd and }x\ge2).
Apply the variance recipe of part 2 to the test function of part 3. What do you get, and why is the formula so short?







TipWorked solution





This uses Week 4, What sampling is for.

\phi_1(x)=x: \Phi_1=0(0.1)+1(0.4)+2(0.3)+3(0.2)=1.6.
The lecture’s recipe adds a second test function \phi_2(x)=x^2: \Phi_2=0^2(0.1)+1^2(0.4)+2^2(0.3)+3^2(0.2)=0+0.4+1.2+1.8=3.4, so the variance is \Phi_2-\Phi_1^2=3.4-1.6^2=3.4-2.56=0.84. Once the mean is known, the single test function \phi(x)=(x-1.6)^2 gives the same answer directly: 2.56(0.1)+0.36(0.4)+0.16(0.3)+1.96(0.2)=0.84.
The indicator function \phi(x)=\mathbf 1_{\{x\ge2\}}: its expectation is 0.3+0.2=0.5.
\phi(x)=\mathbf 1_{\{x\text{ odd}\}}\cdot\mathbf 1_{\{x\ge2\}}. A product of indicators is 1 only when both events hold, so it is the indicator of the intersection, here \{3\}: the answer is 0.2.
An indicator only takes the values 0 and 1, so it equals its own square, and \Phi_2=\Phi_1=0.5. The variance is 0.5-0.5^2=0.25, the familiar p(1-p). This is the quantity that sets how many samples a probability estimate needs.

Answer. (1) 1.6. (2) 0.84. (3) 0.5. (4) 0.2. (5) 0.25=p(1-p), because an indicator squared is itself.

Suppose some sampler has produced eight draws from a joint posterior over two players’ skills (z_i,z_j):

Estimate \mathbb P(z_i\ge z_j\mid\text{games}).
Estimate the posterior mean and standard deviation of z_i.
If the draws were independent, roughly how uncertain is the estimate in part 1?







TipWorked solution





This uses Week 4, What sampling is for and Simple Monte Carlo.

A probability is the expectation of an indicator function: \mathbb P(z_i\ge z_j)=\mathbb E\big[\mathbf 1_{\{z_i\ge z_j\}}\big]. The simple Monte Carlo estimate is the fraction of samples where the event holds. Row by row the indicator is 1,0,1,1,0,0,1,1, so the estimate is 5/8=0.625.
Mean: average the test function \phi_1=z_i over the draws. The z_i row sums to 1.2+0.4+1.5+0.9+0.3+1.1+1.8+0.7=7.9, so \hat\Phi_1=7.9/8=0.9875. For the spread, use the second test function \phi_2=z_i^2. The squares are 1.44,\ 0.16,\ 2.25,\ 0.81,\ 0.09,\ 1.21,\ 3.24,\ 0.49, summing to 9.69, so \hat\Phi_2=9.69/8=1.2113, so the variance estimate is \hat\Phi_2-\hat\Phi_1^2=1.2113-0.9752=0.2361 and the standard deviation is 0.486.
The indicator has variance p(1-p), so with independent draws \mathrm{var}[\hat\Phi]=p(1-p)/R\approx0.625\cdot0.375/8=0.029, a standard deviation of about 0.17. Eight samples cannot pin the probability down. The 1/R rate assumes independent draws; samplers that produce each draw from the previous one give correlated samples, and then the error shrinks more slowly than this formula says.

Answer. (1) 0.625. (2) Mean 0.9875, standard deviation \approx0.486. (3) About \pm0.17 (one standard deviation) for independent draws.

text:
Simple Monte Carlo
Practice for Simple Monte Carlo.

Problem 23: How many samples?

A test function has \mathrm{var}[\phi(x)]=9 under p. How many independent samples does simple Monte Carlo need for the standard deviation of \hat\Phi to be at most 0.1? At most 0.05?
We want \mathbb P(x\in A) to within a standard deviation of 0.01, using the indicator function as the test function. Show that \mathrm{var}[\mathbf 1_{\{x\in A\}}]\le\tfrac14 and find an R that is enough whatever the true probability is. How many would suffice if we knew the probability was about 0.1?







TipWorked solution





This uses the variance formula in Week 4, Simple Monte Carlo.

\mathrm{var}[\hat\Phi]=\mathrm{var}[\phi]/R=9/R. A standard deviation of 0.1 means variance 0.01, so R\ge900. Halving the standard deviation to 0.05 means variance 0.0025, so R\ge3600. Halving the error costs four times the samples.
The indicator is 1 with probability p and 0 otherwise, so its variance is p(1-p), a parabola with its maximum \tfrac14 at p=\tfrac12. We need p(1-p)/R\le0.01^2. Using the bound, R\ge0.25/0.0001=2500 is enough whatever p is. If p\approx0.1, then p(1-p)=0.09 and R\ge900 suffices.

Answer. (1) 900 and 3600. (2) p(1-p)\le\tfrac14; R=2500 always suffices, R=900 if p\approx0.1.





Problem 24: An estimator small enough to list completely
A biased coin gives x=1 with probability 0.3 and x=0 otherwise. We estimate \Phi=\mathbb E[x]=0.3 by simple Monte Carlo with \phi(x)=x and only R=2 independent draws.

List every possible pair of draws, its probability, and the value of \hat\Phi.
From that list, compute \mathbb E[\hat\Phi] and \mathrm{var}[\hat\Phi]. Compare them with \Phi and with \mathrm{var}[\phi(x)]/R.
What is the probability that \hat\Phi equals 0.3 exactly? Does that contradict part 2?
Suppose a bug made the second draw a copy of the first. What is \mathrm{var}[\hat\Phi] now?







TipWorked solution





This uses the unbiasedness and variance results of Week 4, Simple Monte Carlo.

Zero: \hat\Phi can only be 0, 0.5, or 1. No contradiction. Unbiased means the estimates are right on average over repetitions, not that any one estimate is right. The variance measures how far a typical estimate lands from \Phi.
With a copy, \hat\Phi=\tfrac12(x+x)=x, so \mathrm{var}[\hat\Phi]=0.21, no better than one draw. The 1/R in the formula came from adding the variances of independent terms; a copied draw adds no new information.

section: Why the normalizing constant is hard
text:
Why the normalizing constant is hard
Practice for Why the normalizing constant is hard.

Problem 25: Counting grid points
A grid with 50 points per axis is used to approximate Z by adding up \tilde p at every grid point.

How many grid points are there for D=3 and for D=10?
If one evaluation of \tilde p takes a nanosecond, how long does each grid take?







TipWorked solution





This uses the grid example in Week 4, Why the normalizing constant is hard.

50^3=125{,}000 points for D=3 and 50^{10}\approx9.8\times10^{16} for D=10. The grid grows exponentially with D (the curse of dimensionality).
Time is (number of points) × 10^{-9} s. D=3: 125{,}000\times10^{-9}=1.25\times10^{-4} s, about 0.1 milliseconds. D=10: 9.8\times10^{16}\times10^{-9}=9.8\times10^{7} seconds, and dividing by about 3.15\times10^{7} seconds per year gives roughly three years. A 10\times10 binary image already has D=100.

Compare the sample counts in Problem 23: they do not mention D at all. The catch is that they assume we can already draw samples from p.
Answer. (1) 125{,}000 and about 9.8\times10^{16}. (2) About 0.1 ms against about three years.





Problem 26: The canyon a boat never finds
On the unit cube [0,1]^D, a density puts 90% of its mass inside the small corner cube [0,\tfrac12]^D and spreads the other 10% thinly over the rest. We know nothing about where the mass is, so we place “boat” locations uniformly at random in the cube, as in the lecture’s lake picture.

What fraction f of the cube’s volume is the corner cube, for D=1, D=10, and D=30?
With R=1000 uniform draws, what is the probability that none lands in the corner cube, for D=10 and D=30?
We estimate Z=\int\tilde p by the average of \tilde p over the uniform draws (the cube has volume 1). If no draw lands in the corner cube, roughly what will the estimate be, compared with the true Z? Would anything in the output warn us?







TipWorked solution





This uses the lake analogy in Week 4, Why the normalizing constant is hard.

f=(\tfrac12)^D: 0.5 for D=1, 1/1024\approx9.8\times10^{-4} for D=10, and (\tfrac12)^{30}\approx9.3\times10^{-10} for D=30.
Each draw misses with probability 1-f, independently, so all miss with probability (1-f)^{R} with R=1000. For small f, \log(1-f)\approx-f, so (1-f)^R\approx e^{-Rf}. For D=10, Rf=1000/1024\approx0.977 and the probability is about e^{-0.977}\approx0.38. For D=30, Rf=1000\times9.3\times10^{-10}=9.3\times10^{-7}, so e^{-Rf}\approx1-Rf=1-9.3\times10^{-7}: essentially certain.
The average of \tilde p is a simple Monte Carlo estimate of \int\tilde p under the uniform distribution. If every draw misses the corner, the draws only see the thin 10% part, so the estimate comes out near 0.1\,Z, ten times too small. Nothing in the output flags this: the sampled values look perfectly ordinary, because the method never visited the place where it went wrong. This is the narrow, deep canyon from the lecture, holding most of the water and almost never visited.

Answer. (1) 0.5, about 10^{-3}, about 10^{-9}. (2) About 0.38 and essentially 1. (3) Near 0.1\,Z, with no warning sign.

title: Week 4 practice: Message passing and Monte Carlo
text:
Importance sampling
Practice for Importance sampling.

Problem 27: Importance sampling with an unnormalized target
A target on \{1,2,3,4\} is known only up to a constant: \tilde p=(1,\ 2,\ 4,\ 1). The proposal is uniform, \tilde q(x)=1 for every x. Five draws from q come out as 1,\quad 3,\quad 3,\quad 2,\quad 4.

Compute the importance weights \tilde w_r and the normalized weights w_r.
Estimate \mathbb E_p[x] and compare it with the exact value.
Estimate Z_p/Z_q and compare it with the exact value.
Suppose instead \tilde q=(1,\ 1,\ 0.05,\ 1). What weight would a draw of x=3 get, and why is that a problem?







TipWorked solution





This uses Week 4, Importance sampling.

\tilde w_r=\tilde p(x^{(r)})/\tilde q(x^{(r)})=\tilde p(x^{(r)}) here, giving 1,4,4,2,1. They sum to 12, so w_r=\tfrac1{12},\tfrac4{12},\tfrac4{12},\tfrac2{12},\tfrac1{12}.
The self-normalized estimate is \sum_r x^{(r)}w_r=(1\cdot1+3\cdot4+3\cdot4+2\cdot2+4\cdot1)/12=33/12=2.75. Exactly, Z_p=\sum_x\tilde p(x)=1+2+4+1=8 and \mathbb E_p[x]=(1\cdot1+2\cdot2+3\cdot4+4\cdot1)/8=21/8=2.625. Five samples land fairly close.
The average weight estimates Z_p/Z_q: 12/5=2.4. Exactly, Z_p=8 and Z_q=4, so the ratio is 2. Neither normalizer was needed to form the estimate in part 2; the ratio cancels in the self-normalized form.
\tilde w=4/0.05=80, against at most 2 for the other values. The proposal rarely visits x=3, which holds half of p’s mass, so a run either misses it (and underestimates \mathbb E_p[x]) or hits it once and lets that one sample dominate the sum. This is the poor-coverage failure the week chapter warns about.

Answer. (1) \tilde w=(1,4,4,2,1), w=(1,4,4,2,1)/12. (2) 2.75 against 2.625. (3) 2.4 against 2. (4) Weight 80: one rare draw dominates.





Problem 28: Choosing between two proposals
A target on \{1,2,3\} is p=(0.1,\ 0.1,\ 0.8), and we want \Phi=\mathbb E_p[x]. In this small example we know p and q exactly, so we can use the middle form of the week chapter’s derivation, \hat\Phi=\frac1R\sum_r\phi(x^{(r)})\,p(x^{(r)})/q(x^{(r)}), with x^{(r)}\sim q.

Compute \Phi.
For proposal A, uniform q=(\tfrac13,\tfrac13,\tfrac13), and proposal B, q=(0.2,\ 0.2,\ 0.6): compute the weights p/q, check that \mathbb E_q[\phi\,p/q]=\Phi, and compute the variance of one term \phi(x)\,p(x)/q(x) under q.
How many samples does each proposal need for a standard deviation of 0.1?
Proposal C is q=(0.5,\ 0.5,\ 0). What does the estimate converge to?







TipWorked solution





This uses Week 4, Importance sampling together with the variance formula of Simple Monte Carlo.

\Phi=1(0.1)+2(0.1)+3(0.8)=2.7.
Write g(x)=\phi(x)\,p(x)/q(x) for one term.

A: weights p/q=(0.3,\ 0.3,\ 2.4), so g=(0.3,\ 0.6,\ 7.2). Then \mathbb E_q[g]=(0.3+0.6+7.2)/3=8.1/3=2.7 and \mathbb E_q[g^2]=(0.09+0.36+51.84)/3=52.29/3=17.43, so \mathrm{var}_q[g]=17.43-2.7^2=10.14.
B: weights (0.5,\ 0.5,\ 1.333), so g=(0.5,\ 1,\ 4). Then \mathbb E_q[g]=0.1+0.2+2.4=2.7 and \mathbb E_q[g^2]=0.05+0.2+9.6=9.85, so \mathrm{var}_q[g]=2.56.

Both are unbiased. A rarely visits x=3, where most of p sits, and pays with a large weight there.
\mathrm{var}[\hat\Phi]=\mathrm{var}_q[g]/R\le0.01 needs R\ge1014 for A and R\ge256 for B. The proposal that resembles p is four times cheaper.
C never proposes x=3, so every term is 1(0.2) or 2(0.2) and the estimate converges to \tfrac12(0.2+0.4)=0.3, not 2.7. More samples do not help: a proposal must put mass wherever p does, or that part of p is invisible.

Answer. (1) 2.7. (2) Variances 10.14 (A) and 2.56 (B). (3) About 1014 and 256. (4) 0.3: C misses x=3 entirely.

title: Week 4 practice: Message passing and Monte Carlo
text:
Rejection sampling
Practice for Rejection sampling.

Problem 29: Rejection sampling, and what dimension does to it
Take \tilde p(x)=x(1-x) on [0,1] and the uniform proposal q(x)=1 on [0,1], so \tilde q=q and Z_q=1.

Find Z_p and the smallest valid c. What is the acceptance rate?
With that c, decide accept or reject for these (x,u) pairs, where u was drawn uniform on [0,\ c\,\tilde q(x)]: (0.2,\ 0.10), (0.9,\ 0.12), (0.5,\ 0.24), (0.05,\ 0.03), (0.7,\ 0.22).
What happens to the acceptance rate with c=0.5? What goes wrong with c=0.2?
Now take D independent copies: \tilde p(\mathbf x)=\prod_{d=1}^Dx_d(1-x_d) on the unit cube, with a uniform proposal on the cube. Find the acceptance rate for D=10 and D=100, and the expected number of proposals per accepted sample.







TipWorked solution





This uses Week 4, Rejection sampling, including the acceptance-rate formula at the end of that section.

Z_p=\int_0^1(x-x^2)\,dx=\tfrac12-\tfrac13=\tfrac16. The envelope must satisfy c\cdot1\ge x(1-x) everywhere. The maximum of x(1-x) is \tfrac14 at x=\tfrac12, so the smallest valid c is \tfrac14. The acceptance rate is Z_p/(cZ_q)=\tfrac16/\tfrac14=\tfrac23.
Accept when u\le\tilde p(x):

\tilde p(0.2)=0.16\ge0.10: accept.
\tilde p(0.9)=0.09<0.12: reject.
\tilde p(0.5)=0.25\ge0.24: accept.
\tilde p(0.05)=0.0475\ge0.03: accept.
\tilde p(0.7)=0.21<0.22: reject.

The accepted samples are 0.2, 0.5, 0.05.
c=0.5 is still a valid envelope, but the rate becomes \tfrac16/\tfrac12=\tfrac13: half as many acceptances for the same work. c=0.2 is invalid because 0.2<\tilde p(x) near x=\tfrac12. There every u is at most 0.2, so every proposal is accepted, and the accepted samples follow \min(\tilde p(x),\,0.2) rather than \tilde p. The peak is flattened and the samples are no longer from p.
Each factor x_d(1-x_d) depends on its own coordinate only, so the product is maximized by putting every x_d=\tfrac12: the maximum is (\tfrac14)^D, and the smallest c is (\tfrac14)^D. For the same reason the integral over the cube splits into a product of one-dimensional integrals, Z_p=\int_{[0,1]^D}\prod_{d=1}^Dx_d(1-x_d)\,d\mathbf x=\prod_{d=1}^D\int_0^1x_d(1-x_d)\,dx_d=\big(\tfrac16\big)^D, and the uniform proposal has Z_q=1. The rate is (\tfrac23)^D.

D=10: (\tfrac23)^{10}\approx0.0173, about 58 proposals per accepted sample.
D=100: (\tfrac23)^{100}\approx2.5\times10^{-18}, about 4\times10^{17} proposals per accepted sample.

Each dimension multiplies the rate by \tfrac23, so it decays exponentially with D. This is the lecture’s reason for presenting rejection sampling as a one-dimensional tool.

Answer. (1) Z_p=\tfrac16, c=\tfrac14, rate \tfrac23. (2) Accept, reject, accept, accept, reject. (3) Rate \tfrac13; c=0.2 is not an envelope and gives samples from the wrong distribution. (4) (\tfrac23)^D: about 0.017 at D=10, about 2.5\times10^{-18} at D=100.





Problem 30: Rejection sampling with a non-uniform proposal
A target on \{1,2,3\} has \tilde p=(1,\ 3,\ 2). The proposal is q=(0.5,\ 0.25,\ 0.25), with \tilde q=q and Z_q=1. Given a proposed x, u is drawn uniformly from [0,\ c\,\tilde q(x)] as in the week chapter’s algorithm.

Find the smallest valid c.
With that c, compute the probability of accepting each x, and the probability of proposing x and accepting it. Show that the accepted draws follow p, and find the overall acceptance rate two ways.
Repeat the acceptance rate for the proposal q=(0.2,\ 0.4,\ 0.4). Why is it higher?







TipWorked solution





This uses Week 4, Rejection sampling, including the proof that accepted samples follow p.

We need c\,q(x)\ge\tilde p(x) at every x, so c\ge\max(1/0.5,\ 3/0.25,\ 2/0.25)=\max(2,12,8)=12. The envelope is 12q=(6,\ 3,\ 3).
Given x, acceptance has probability \tilde p(x)/(c\,\tilde q(x)): \Big(\tfrac16,\ 1,\ \tfrac23\Big). Multiplying by q(x) gives the probability of proposing x and accepting it: \Big(\tfrac1{12},\ \tfrac3{12},\ \tfrac2{12}\Big). These add to \tfrac6{12}=\tfrac12, the acceptance rate. Dividing by it gives the distribution of accepted draws, (\tfrac16,\ \tfrac12,\ \tfrac13), which is exactly p=\tilde p/6. The formula agrees: Z_p/(cZ_q)=6/12=\tfrac12.
Now c\ge\max(1/0.2,\ 3/0.4,\ 2/0.4)=\max(5,\ 7.5,\ 5)=7.5, so the rate is 6/7.5=0.8. The constant c is set by the worst ratio \tilde p/q. The first proposal spent half its mass on x=1, where p is small, and starved x=2, which forced a large c. A proposal shaped more like p needs a smaller envelope and wastes fewer draws.

Answer. (1) c=12. (2) Acceptance (\tfrac16,1,\tfrac23) given x; joint (\tfrac1{12},\tfrac3{12},\tfrac2{12}); accepted draws follow (\tfrac16,\tfrac12,\tfrac13)=p; rate \tfrac12. (3) Rate 0.8.
