title: Midterm practice: Weeks 1–6
text:
Section 2: Graphical models

Problem 2.1: From a factorization to a DAG
Draw the DAG for
p(A,B,C,D,E,F)=p(A)\,p(B)\,p(C\mid A,B)\,p(D\mid C)\,p(E\mid C)\,p(F\mid D,E).
If every variable is binary, how many parameters do the conditional probability tables need, compared with the full joint?






TipWorked solution





This reteaches Week 2, Directed graphical models.
A DAG factorizes as \prod_ip(x_i\mid\text{parents}(x_i)), so we read each factor backwards: whatever sits behind the bar in p(\,\cdot\mid\cdot\,) is a parent, and each parent gets an arrow into the child.

p(A), p(B): no parents.
p(C\mid A,B): arrows A\to C and B\to C.
p(D\mid C), p(E\mid C): arrows C\to D and C\to E.
p(F\mid D,E): arrows D\to F and E\to F.



  
  The DAG for Problem 2.1
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
    
    
  
  
    ABC
    DEF
  


Figure 1. The DAG for Problem 2.1. Each arrow comes from one variable behind a conditioning bar.
Parameter count. A binary node with K parents needs one number per parent configuration, 2^K. Here A and B have K=0 (1 each), C has K=2 (4), D and E have K=1 (2 each), and F has K=2 (4). The full joint over 6 binary variables needs 2^6-1.
Answer. Arrows A\to C, B\to C, C\to D, C\to E, D\to F, E\to F. The tables need 1+1+4+2+2+4=14 parameters, against 63 for the full joint.
The full joint, for comparison. The full joint makes no independence assumptions. The chain rule conditions each variable on every variable before it in a fixed ordering:
p(A,B,C,D,E,F)=p(A)\,p(B\mid A)\,p(C\mid A,B)\,p(D\mid A,B,C)\,p(E\mid A,B,C,D)\,p(F\mid A,B,C,D,E).
The DAG factorization is this same equation with the conditioning sets cut down by the missing arrows: p(B\mid A)\to p(B), p(D\mid A,B,C)\to p(D\mid C), p(E\mid A,B,C,D)\to p(E\mid C), and p(F\mid A,\dots,E)\to p(F\mid D,E). Counting the full joint factor by factor gives 1+2+4+8+16+32=63=2^6-1.
What a parameter is here. A parameter is a free number the model needs before it can assign probabilities. Fitting a model means choosing those numbers, usually from data. Counting parameters means counting how many numbers we have to choose, once any constraint that fixes the others is accounted for.
The conditional probability tables. A conditional probability table (CPT) lists p(\text{child}\mid\text{parents}) for every configuration of the parents. For a binary child, each row needs only one number, \theta=p(\text{child}=1\mid\text{parents}), because p(\text{child}=0\mid\text{parents})=1-\theta is then fixed. For p(C\mid A,B) the CPT has one row for each of the four parent configurations:










(A,B)
(0,0)
(0,1)
(1,0)
(1,1)




p(C=1\mid A,B)
\theta_{C\mid 00}
\theta_{C\mid 01}
\theta_{C\mid 10}
\theta_{C\mid 11}



So p(C\mid A,B) has 4 parameters. Each row has its own free number, and the rows do not constrain each other. Setting p(C=1\mid A=1,B=1)=0.3 forces p(C=0\mid A=1,B=1)=0.7, because that row sums to 1 for that fixed (A,B). It says nothing about p(C=1\mid A=0,B=0), p(C=1\mid A=0,B=1), or p(C=1\mid A=1,B=0), which each need their own number. The other factors follow the same rule:

p(A) and p(B): one free number each, p(A=1) and p(B=1).
p(D\mid C) and p(E\mid C): two rows each (one per value of C), so 2 parameters each.
p(F\mid D,E): four rows (one per value of (D,E)), so 4 parameters.

The total is 1+1+4+2+2+4=14.
The full joint. Without the factorization, the joint is one table with a row for every configuration of the six variables. With six binary variables there are 2^6=64 configurations, and each has a probability. The 64 probabilities must sum to 1, so we can choose any 63 freely and the last one is forced to equal 1 minus their sum. The full joint therefore has 2^6-1=63 parameters.
In general, n binary variables give 2^n configurations and one sum-to-1 constraint, so the full joint has 2^n-1 parameters. A CPT row follows the same logic in a smaller space: a binary child with K binary parents has 2^K rows, and each row’s single free number is the one left after its own sum-to-1 constraint. This is why the DAG needs only 14 numbers to describe a distribution that the full joint would describe with 63.
Counting the same full joint through the chain rule also gives 63. Each conditional table row contributes one free number after its sum-to-1 constraint, and 1+2+4+8+16+32=63. The -1 is the same constraint in both views.
Takeaways.

Read a DAG off a factorization backwards: every variable behind a conditioning bar is a parent, with an arrow into the child.
A binary node with K binary parents costs 2^K parameters, one free number per CPT row.
The full joint over n binary variables costs 2^n-1. The missing arrows are what shrink the count (here from 63 to 14).






Problem 2.2: From potentials to an MRF
Draw the Markov random field for
p(A,B,C,D,E,F)\propto\phi_{ABC}(A,B,C)\,\phi_{CD}(C,D)\,\phi_{DE}(D,E)\,\phi_{CE}(C,E)\,\phi_{EF}(E,F),
then list its maximal cliques. Is there a maximal clique that has no potential of its own?






TipWorked solution





This reteaches Week 3, Markov random fields, cliques, and the factorization theorem.
In an MRF two variables share an edge exactly when they appear together in some factor. So each potential becomes a set of edges joining all its arguments:

\phi_{ABC}: edges A\text{-}B, A\text{-}C, B\text{-}C (a triangle).
\phi_{CD}, \phi_{DE}, \phi_{CE}, \phi_{EF}: one edge each.



  The MRF for Problem 2.2
  
  
    
    
    
  
  
    
    
  
  
    ABC
    DEF
  


Figure 2. The MRF for Problem 2.2. The shaded triangle \{C,D,E\} is a maximal clique built from three pairwise potentials.
A maximal clique is a fully connected set that cannot be enlarged. \{A,B,C\} is fully connected, and adding D fails because A\text{-}D is missing. \{C,D,E\} is fully connected too: C\text{-}D, D\text{-}E, and C\text{-}E are all present, even though each came from a different pairwise potential. \{E,F\} cannot be extended because F has only one neighbour.
The graph cannot distinguish “three pairwise potentials on C,D,E” from “one potential on all three”. Both give the same picture. This is why Week 3 says a graph corresponds to the family that factorizes over its maximal cliques: the pairwise version is a special case of a single \psi_{CDE}.
Answer. Edges AB, AC, BC, CD, CE, DE, EF. Maximal cliques \{A,B,C\}, \{C,D,E\}, \{E,F\}. Yes: \{C,D,E\} has no three-way potential, only three pairwise ones.
Takeaways.

Equation to graph has one answer: join every pair of variables that share a factor.
Graph to equation has more than one valid answer. The default reading is one potential per maximal clique, the most general family the graph allows.
Pairwise potentials around a triangle are a special case of one potential on the whole triangle. Their product is a function of all three variables, but not every three-way function splits into pairwise pieces. So an equation can carry more structure than its graph shows.






Problem 2.3: Markov blankets, directed and undirected

In the DAG of Problem 2.1, give the Markov blanket of D and of C.
In the MRF of Problem 2.2, give the Markov blanket of C and of the set \{A,B\}.
In one sentence, what is the Markov blanket of a set of variables A?







TipWorked solution





This reteaches the opening of Week 3, From DAGs to undirected graphs and the global Markov property in The Hammersley-Clifford theorem.
1. DAG rule: the blanket is parents, children, and co-parents (the other parents of each child). Co-parents are needed because a child is a collider between its parents: observing the child opens the path between them.

D: parent C; child F; F’s other parent is E. Blanket \{C,E,F\}.
C: parents A,B; children D,E. D’s only parent is C, and so is E’s, so there are no co-parents. Blanket \{A,B,D,E\}.

2. MRF rule: the blanket is the set of neighbours, because conditioning on the neighbours separates a node from everything else in the graph.

C: neighbours A,B,D,E. Blanket \{A,B,D,E\}.
\{A,B\}: the neighbours of A are B,C and those of B are A,C. Removing the members of the set itself leaves \{C\}. Every path from A or B to the rest of the graph goes through C.

3. The Markov blanket of a set A is the smallest set S of other variables such that x_A is conditionally independent of all remaining variables given x_S.
Answer. (1) \{C,E,F\} and \{A,B,D,E\}. (2) \{A,B,D,E\} and \{C\}. (3) The smallest set that, once observed, makes A independent of everything else.
Takeaways.

DAG blanket: parents, children, and co-parents. Co-parents are needed because observing a child (a collider) couples its parents.
MRF blanket: just the neighbours. For a set of nodes, take all their neighbours and remove the set itself.
Check which graph type the question uses before applying a rule. Co-parents are the part most often forgotten.






Problem 2.4: How many BP passes?
A tree-shaped MRF has six nodes and edges 1\text{-}2, 2\text{-}3, 2\text{-}4, 4\text{-}5, 4\text{-}6.

We want only the marginal of x_4, and we choose node 4 as the root. How many passes, in which direction? List the messages in a valid order.
We want only the marginal of x_4, but node 1 is the root. How many passes now?
How many messages does it take to get every node’s marginal?







TipWorked solution





This reteaches Week 4, Belief propagation on trees.
The belief at a node needs one message from every neighbour: b(x_i)\propto\psi_i(x_i)\prod_{j\in N(i)}m_{j\to i}(x_i). A node may send to a neighbour only after hearing from all of its other neighbours.
1. With x_4 as the root, the inward pass ends with every neighbour of node 4 sending to it. That is all node 4’s belief needs, so one pass from the leaves to the root is enough. A valid order: m_{1\to2} and m_{3\to2} (leaves first), then m_{2\to4} (node 2 has now heard from 1 and 3); m_{5\to4} and m_{6\to4} can go at any time. That is 5 messages, one per edge.
2. With node 1 as the root, the inward pass ends at node 1. Node 4 sends m_{4\to2} during that pass but never receives m_{2\to4}, which carries the information from nodes 1 and 3. So node 4’s belief is still missing a message: we need two passes, leaves to root and then root to leaves.
3. Each of the 5 edges carries one message in each direction, so 2|\mathcal{E}|=10 messages give all six marginals.
Answer. (1) One pass, leaves to root, 5 messages. (2) Two passes: leaves to root, then root to leaves. (3) 10 messages.
Takeaways.

A belief needs one message from every neighbour, and a node sends to a neighbour only after hearing from all its other neighbours.
If the node we want is the root, one inward pass is enough. Otherwise, or when we want every marginal, we also need an outward pass.
All marginals on a tree cost 2|\mathcal{E}| messages: one per edge in each direction.






Problem 2.5: Running the passes with numbers
Take the tree from Problem 2.4 (edges 1\text{-}2, 2\text{-}3, 2\text{-}4, 4\text{-}5, 4\text{-}6) with binary variables x_i\in\{0,1\}. Every edge has the potential
\psi_{ij}(x_i,x_j)=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}
(2 when the two values agree, 1 when they differ). The node potentials, written as (\psi_i(0),\psi_i(1)), are \psi_1=(1,3), \psi_5=(2,1), and (1,1) for nodes 2, 3, 4, and 6. We observe \bar x_3=1.

With node 4 as the root, compute every message of the inward pass: m_{1\to2}, m_{3\to2}, m_{2\to4}, m_{5\to4}, and m_{6\to4}.
Compute p(x_4\mid\bar x_3).
Which extra message does p(x_2\mid\bar x_3) need? Compute it and the marginal.







TipWorked solution





This reteaches Week 4, Messages and beliefs. Section 7 runs the same calculation on a different tree.
A message from j to i multiplies j’s own potential, the edge potential, and the messages j has received from its other neighbours, then sums out x_j:
m_{j\to i}(x_i)=\sum_{x_j}\psi_j(x_j)\,\psi_{ij}(x_i,x_j)\prod_{k\in N(j)\setminus\{i\}}m_{k\to j}(x_j).
We write each message as a vector (m(0),\,m(1)).
1. The inward pass. Following the order from Problem 2.4, leaves first.

m_{1\to2}: node 1 is an unobserved leaf, so we sum over its two values. At x_2=0: 1\cdot2+3\cdot1=5. At x_2=1: 1\cdot1+3\cdot2=7. So m_{1\to2}=(5,7), leaning toward 1 because \psi_1 does.
m_{3\to2}: node 3 is observed at 1, so there is no sum, only the terms at x_3=1: m_{3\to2}(x_2)=\psi_3(1)\,\psi_{23}(x_2,1)=(1,2).
m_{5\to4}: at x_4=0: 2\cdot2+1\cdot1=5. At x_4=1: 2\cdot1+1\cdot2=4. So m_{5\to4}=(5,4), leaning toward 0.
m_{6\to4}: node 6 has a flat potential, so both entries are 1\cdot2+1\cdot1=3. The message (3,3) is flat and carries no preference.

Node 2 has now heard from its other neighbours, 1 and 3, so it can send to 4. First multiply the incoming messages at each value of x_2: \psi_2\,m_{1\to2}\,m_{3\to2}=(1\cdot5\cdot1,\ 1\cdot7\cdot2)=(5,14). Then apply the edge and sum out x_2:

x_4=0: \;2\cdot5+1\cdot14=24.
x_4=1: \;1\cdot5+2\cdot14=33.

So m_{2\to4}=(24,33)\propto(8,11).
2. Belief at the root. Node 4 has heard from all three neighbours:
\tilde b(x_4)=\psi_4(x_4)\,m_{2\to4}(x_4)\,m_{5\to4}(x_4)\,m_{6\to4}(x_4)=\big(24\cdot5\cdot3,\ 33\cdot4\cdot3\big)=(360,\ 396).
Where the normalizer comes from. The tilde marks an unnormalized belief. Each entry \tilde b(x_4) is the product of all the potentials, with x_3 clamped to 1, summed over every other unobserved variable (x_1,x_2,x_5,x_6). That is \tilde p(x_4,\bar x_3), the unnormalized joint of x_4 and the evidence. To turn it into a conditional we divide by its sum over the values of x_4, because p(x_4\mid\bar x_3)=\frac{\tilde p(x_4,\bar x_3)}{\sum_{x_4'}\tilde p(x_4',\bar x_3)}. The global partition function Z cancels between top and bottom, so we never need it. Here the sum is 360+396=756, and dividing each entry by it gives p(x_4\mid\bar x_3)=\Big(\tfrac{360}{756},\ \tfrac{396}{756}\Big)=\Big(\tfrac{10}{21},\ \tfrac{11}{21}\Big), after cancelling the common factor 36 (360=36\cdot10, 396=36\cdot11, 756=36\cdot21). The two entries add to 1, which is the check that we normalized correctly.
The pull toward 1 from the evidence and \psi_1 slightly outweighs the pull toward 0 from \psi_5.
3. A node that is not the root. Node 2’s belief needs a message from each of its neighbours 1, 3, and 4. The inward pass produced m_{1\to2} and m_{3\to2} but sent m_{2\to4} the wrong way, so we need m_{4\to2}, the first message of the outward pass. Node 4 sends it after hearing from 5 and 6:
\psi_4\,m_{5\to4}\,m_{6\to4}=(5\cdot3,\ 4\cdot3)=(15,12)\propto(5,4), then

x_2=0: \;2\cdot5+1\cdot4=14.
x_2=1: \;1\cdot5+2\cdot4=13.

So m_{4\to2}\propto(14,13). The belief is
\tilde b(x_2)=\psi_2(x_2)\,m_{1\to2}(x_2)\,m_{3\to2}(x_2)\,m_{4\to2}(x_2)=\big(5\cdot1\cdot14,\ 7\cdot2\cdot13\big)=(70,\ 182).
The normalizer is found the same way: add the two entries, 70+182=252, and divide each by the sum. Cancelling the common factor 14 (70=14\cdot5, 182=14\cdot13, 252=14\cdot18) gives p(x_2\mid\bar x_3)=\big(\frac5{18},\frac{13}{18}\big). Node 2 sits next to the evidence, so it leans toward 1 more strongly than node 4 does.






Note



Why 252 and not 756? Without any rescaling, every node’s unnormalized belief sums to the same number, \sum_{x_1,x_2,x_4,x_5,x_6}\tilde p(x_1,x_2,\bar x_3,x_4,x_5,x_6), the total weight of all configurations consistent with the evidence. We got 756 at node 4. At node 2 we got 252 because we rescaled (15,12) to (5,4), dropping a factor of 3; the unrescaled message would be m_{4\to2}=(42,39), giving \tilde b(x_2)=(210,546), which sums to 756. Rescaling a message by a constant rescales the belief by that constant and the normalizer by the same constant, so the normalized marginal is unchanged. That is why we may write messages “up to proportionality” (\propto) and why each node’s normalizer is simply whatever its own entries sum to.


Answer. (1) m_{1\to2}=(5,7), m_{3\to2}=(1,2), m_{2\to4}=(24,33)\propto(8,11), m_{5\to4}=(5,4), m_{6\to4}=(3,3). (2) p(x_4\mid\bar x_3)=(\frac{10}{21},\frac{11}{21}). (3) m_{4\to2}\propto(14,13); p(x_2\mid\bar x_3)=(\frac5{18},\frac{13}{18}).
Takeaways.

Compute messages in the order Problem 2.4 allows: a node sends only after hearing from all its other neighbours. Multiply what arrived first, then apply the edge and sum.
At the root, one inward pass gives the belief. Any other node needs one outward message from its parent toward the root.
An observed leaf sends its node and edge potentials evaluated at the observed value, with no sum. A leaf with a flat potential sends a flat message, which changes no belief.
Check a small answer by brute force: summing the unnormalized joint over all configurations consistent with the evidence must give the same marginal.






Problem 2.6: Who chooses the root?
Keep the tree and numbers of Problem 2.5. Each part below answers one question about the root.

Can we pick any root? Suppose we root the tree at node 1 instead of node 4, run the inward pass to node 1, and then send the outward messages needed for x_4. Write the formula for m_{2\to4} under this schedule. Is it the same message as in Problem 2.5, and is p(x_4\mid\bar x_3) the same?
Why would we ever root somewhere else? We have already run the inward pass to node 1, because last time we wanted p(x_1\mid\bar x_3). Now we want p(x_4\mid\bar x_3). How many messages does it cost to start over with node 4 as the root? How many new messages if we keep the stored ones?
Can there be two roots? We want both p(x_1\mid\bar x_3) and p(x_4\mid\bar x_3). Count the messages if the root is node 4, then if it is node 1. Why can one inward pass not end at both nodes?
Do we need a root at all? Apply only the rule “a node sends to a neighbour once it has heard from all its other neighbours”, starting from the leaves. Which messages get computed, and where does a root appear?







TipWorked solution





This reteaches Week 4, Belief propagation on trees.
The key fact for every part: the graph is undirected and has no root. The root is a bookkeeping choice we make to schedule the messages, and the formula for a message never mentions it.
1. Any root works. Under root 1, m_{2\to4} is sent during the outward pass, after node 2 has heard from 1 and 3:
m_{2\to4}(x_4)=\sum_{x_2}\psi_2(x_2)\,\psi_{24}(x_2,x_4)\,m_{1\to2}(x_2)\,m_{3\to2}(x_2).
This is the same formula with the same inputs, m_{1\to2}=(5,7) and m_{3\to2}=(1,2), so it gives the same (24,33). The messages m_{5\to4} and m_{6\to4} are also unchanged, so p(x_4\mid\bar x_3)=(\frac{10}{21},\frac{11}{21}) again. On a tree, every root gives the same exact marginals; only the order and the number of messages change.
2. Reuse is the reason to root elsewhere. Starting over with root 4 costs 5 messages. The inward pass to node 1 already stored m_{3\to2}, m_{5\to4}, m_{6\to4}, m_{4\to2}, and m_{2\to1}. Node 4’s belief needs m_{2\to4}, m_{5\to4}, and m_{6\to4}. Only m_{2\to4} is missing, and it needs m_{1\to2}, which is also missing. So reuse costs 2 new messages, not 5. In practice the root is often fixed by an earlier query, or by the order in which data arrives (an HMM’s forward pass roots the chain at the latest time step), not by the node we want now.
3. One root, but more than one marginal.

Root 4: the inward pass costs 5 messages and gives x_4. For x_1 we need m_{2\to1}, which needs m_{4\to2}: 2 more. Total 7.
Root 1: the inward pass costs 5 and gives x_1. For x_4 we need m_{1\to2} and m_{2\to4}: 2 more. Total 7.

The totals match. The path from 1 to 4 runs through edges 1\text{-}2 and 2\text{-}4, and both beliefs need messages along that path in both directions. One pass sends each edge’s message in one direction only, so it cannot end at both nodes. That is why a pass has exactly one root, and why a second node costs extra messages along the path between them.
4. No root is needed. With the “heard from all other neighbours” rule, the leaves 1, 3, 5, and 6 send first. Node 2 can then send to 4 (it has heard from 1 and 3), and node 4 can send to 2 (it has heard from 5 and 6). After that, nodes 2 and 4 can send back to the leaves. All 2|\mathcal{E}|=10 messages get computed and every node gets its marginal, with no root ever named. The root only matters when we want fewer than all the marginals and are deciding which messages to skip.
Answer. (1) Yes, any node can be the root: m_{2\to4}=(24,33) and p(x_4\mid\bar x_3)=(\frac{10}{21},\frac{11}{21}) as before. (2) 5 to start over, 2 with reuse. (3) 7 either way; one pass sends each edge’s message in only one direction, so it has one root. (4) All 10 messages, with no root required.
Takeaways.

The root is our scheduling choice, not part of the model. Any root gives the same exact marginals on a tree.
If we want one marginal from scratch, root at that node. We root elsewhere when messages are already stored, or when the order in which data arrives fixes it.
A pass has one root because it sends each edge’s message in only one direction. Each extra marginal costs the messages along the path back from the root.
For every marginal, skip the root: run the “heard from all other neighbours” rule until all 2|\mathcal{E}| messages are sent.

title: Midterm practice: Weeks 1–6
text:
Section 3: Decision theory

Problem 3.1: A uniform loss against a gamble
A screening lab has a backlog and two options.

Option A: run every pending scan again. The total delay this causes is uniformly distributed between 20 and 40 hours.
Option B: release the backlog as is. With probability p nothing goes wrong (delay 0); with probability 1-p a batch must be redone later, costing 120 hours.


For which values of p does Option A have the smaller expected delay?
With p=0.9, how large would the failure cost in Option B have to be (instead of 120) for the two options to tie?







TipWorked solution





This reteaches Week 2, Expected loss: when the outcome is random, compare actions by their expected loss.
Expected loss of A. The delay is \mathrm{Uniform}[20,40]. A uniform distribution on [a,b] has mean \frac{a+b}{2}, so \mathbb{E}[L_A]=\frac{20+40}{2}=30.
Expected loss of B. Two outcomes, weighted by their probabilities: \mathbb{E}[L_B]=0\cdot p+120\cdot(1-p)=120(1-p).
1. A wins when 30<120(1-p). Dividing by 120 gives \frac14<1-p, so p<\frac34.
2. Replace 120 by L and set the two expectations equal: 30=L(1-0.9)=0.1L, so L=300.
Answer. (1) p<0.75. (2) L=300 hours.
Takeaways.

When the outcome is random, compare actions by expected loss. A uniform distribution on [a,b] has mean \frac{a+b}{2}.
A tie-point question reduces to setting the two expected losses equal and solving for the unknown.






Problem 3.2: A loss matrix moves the threshold
In the cancer-screening setting, missing a cancer costs 9, a false alarm costs 1, and a correct decision costs 0. Write p=p(\mathcal{C}_{\text{cancer}}\mid x).

Write the expected cost of deciding “cancer” and of deciding “normal” as functions of p.
Above what value of p should we decide “cancer”?
One image has p=0.15. What does the discriminant rule decide, and what would the plain misclassification rule decide?
With a reject threshold \theta=0.8, another image has posteriors (0.3,\ 0.7). What happens?







TipWorked solution





This reteaches Week 2, The discriminant rule and the reject option.
The discriminant rule decides the j minimizing \sum_kL_{kj}\,p(\mathcal{C}_k\mid x): for each candidate decision, add up the cost of each possible truth weighted by its posterior.
1. Deciding cancer is only costly if the truth is normal (probability 1-p, cost 1). Deciding normal is only costly if the truth is cancer (probability p, cost 9):
\text{cost(cancer)}=1\cdot(1-p), \qquad \text{cost(normal)}=9p.
2. Decide cancer when 1-p<9p, that is 1<10p, so p>\frac1{10}. This is the general threshold \frac{L_{\text{FA}}}{L_{\text{FA}}+L_{\text{miss}}}=\frac{1}{1+9}.
3. At p=0.15: cost(cancer) =0.85 and cost(normal) =1.35, so the rule decides cancer. The misclassification rule compares posteriors directly; 0.85>0.15, so it decides normal. The loss matrix makes the rare but expensive mistake worth avoiding.
4. The reject option applies when the largest posterior is below \theta. Here \max(0.3,\,0.7)=0.7<0.8, so we decline to decide and send the case for further testing.
Answer. (1) 1-p and 9p. (2) p>0.1. (3) Cancer under the loss matrix, normal under the misclassification rule. (4) Reject.
Takeaways.

For each candidate decision, add the cost of each possible truth weighted by its posterior, then pick the smallest total.
With two classes the threshold is \frac{L_{\text{FA}}}{L_{\text{FA}}+L_{\text{miss}}}. An expensive miss pushes the threshold down.
The reject option looks at the largest posterior, not at the costs.






Problem 3.3: Where the joint densities cross
A single feature x has class-conditional densities p(x\mid\mathcal{C}_1)=\mathcal{N}(x;0,1) and p(x\mid\mathcal{C}_2)=\mathcal{N}(x;2,1).

With equal priors, what decision rule minimizes the misclassification rate?
Now p(\mathcal{C}_1)=\frac23 and p(\mathcal{C}_2)=\frac13. Find the new boundary.
An exam figure shows two curves labelled p(x,\mathcal{C}_1) and p(x,\mathcal{C}_2). Where is the boundary? What changes if the curves were labelled p(x\mid\mathcal{C}_k) instead?







TipWorked solution





This reteaches Week 2, Misclassification rate.
The misclassification rate is minimized by assigning each x to the class with the larger joint p(x,\mathcal{C}_k)=p(x\mid\mathcal{C}_k)\,p(\mathcal{C}_k), so the boundary \hat x solves p(\hat x,\mathcal{C}_1)=p(\hat x,\mathcal{C}_2).
1. With equal priors the priors cancel, and the two unit-variance Gaussians are mirror images about the midpoint of their means. The boundary is \hat x=1: decide \mathcal{C}_1 if x<1, otherwise \mathcal{C}_2.
2. Write out the equal-joint condition. The factor \frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}} appears on both sides and cancels:
\tfrac23\,e^{-x^2/2}=\tfrac13\,e^{-(x-2)^2/2}.
Take logs: \ln2-\frac{x^2}2=-\frac{(x-2)^2}2. Rearranging,
\ln 2=\frac{x^2-(x-2)^2}{2}=\frac{4x-4}{2}=2x-2.
So \hat x=1+\frac{\ln2}{2}\approx1.35. The more common class \mathcal{C}_1 gets a larger region: the boundary moves toward \mathcal{C}_2’s mean.
3. If the curves are the joints, the boundary is where they intersect: decide \mathcal{C}_1 on the side where its curve is higher. If they are class-conditionals, the crossing point is only correct when the priors are equal; otherwise multiply each curve by its prior first, as in part 2.
Answer. (1) \mathcal{C}_1 for x<1. (2) \hat x=1+\frac{\ln2}2\approx1.35. (3) At the crossing of the joint curves; class-conditional curves must be weighted by the priors first.
Takeaways.

Minimizing the misclassification rate compares the joints p(x\mid\mathcal{C}_k)\,p(\mathcal{C}_k), not the class-conditionals.
With equal variances, a larger prior moves the boundary away from that class’s mean, giving the class a larger region.
Read figure labels carefully. Joint curves cross at the boundary; class-conditional curves cross at the boundary only when the priors are equal.

title: Midterm practice: Weeks 1–6
text:
Section 4: Monte Carlo
A transit model outputs samples from P(L_1,\dots,L_T\mid\text{data}), where L_t=1 if a bus route runs late on day t. We draw N i.i.d. samples, each a vector of T binary values (l^{(i)}_1,\dots,l^{(i)}_T), for i=1,\dots,N.

Problem 4.1: Writing estimators with indicators
Write a Monte Carlo estimator for each quantity, using the indicator \mathbf{1}(E).

The probability that the route runs late on at least one day.
The probability that it runs late on both day 2 and day 5.
The expected number of late days.
The probability that it runs late on day 5, given that it ran late on days 2 and 3.
The probability that it runs late on day 3, given that it was not late on day 1.







TipWorked solution





This reteaches Week 4, What sampling is for and Simple Monte Carlo.
Every target is an expectation \Phi=\mathbb{E}[\phi(L)], and the simple Monte Carlo estimator averages the test function over the samples: \hat\Phi=\frac1N\sum_i\phi(l^{(i)}). A probability is the expectation of an indicator, P(E)=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}(E)], so it is estimated by the fraction of samples in which E happens.
1. “At least one late day” fails only when every day is on time, so either form works:
\hat P=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbf{1}\Big(\textstyle\sum_t l^{(i)}_t\ge1\Big)=1-\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbf{1}\big(l^{(i)}_1=0,\dots,l^{(i)}_T=0\big).
2. The other days are left free, so the indicator only checks days 2 and 5:
\hat P=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbf{1}\big(l^{(i)}_2=1,\ l^{(i)}_5=1\big).
3. This is not a probability. The test function is the count of late days, \phi(l)=\sum_tl_t:
\hat\Phi=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{t=1}^T l^{(i)}_t.
4. A conditional probability is a ratio, P(E\mid F)=\frac{P(E\cap F)}{P(F)}. Estimate both and divide; the \frac1N factors cancel:
\hat P=\frac{\sum_i\mathbf{1}\big(l^{(i)}_2=1,\ l^{(i)}_3=1,\ l^{(i)}_5=1\big)}{\sum_i\mathbf{1}\big(l^{(i)}_2=1,\ l^{(i)}_3=1\big)}.
This is the fraction of samples meeting the condition in which day 5 is also late.
5. Same pattern with F=\{l_1=0\}:
\hat P=\frac{\sum_i\mathbf{1}\big(l^{(i)}_1=0,\ l^{(i)}_3=1\big)}{\sum_i\mathbf{1}\big(l^{(i)}_1=0\big)}.
Answer. The five estimators above. The rule: probabilities are averages of indicators, other expectations are averages of their test function, and conditionals are ratios of two indicator sums.
Takeaways.

Every target is an expectation. A probability is the expectation of an indicator, so we estimate it by the fraction of samples in which the event happens.
A conditional probability is a ratio of two indicator sums, and the \frac1N factors cancel.
"At least one" is often easier to write as 1 minus "none".






Problem 4.2: Variance and how many samples

Suppose the true probability in 4.1 part 2 is q. What is the variance of that estimator?
If q=0.1, how many samples make its standard deviation at most 0.01?
If we know nothing about q, how many samples guarantee a standard deviation of at most 0.01?
In 4.1 part 4, suppose only 5% of samples have late buses on both days 2 and 3. Roughly how many samples does the ratio estimator actually use?







TipWorked solution





This reteaches the variance calculation in Week 4, Simple Monte Carlo.
The general result is \mathrm{var}[\hat\Phi]=\frac1N\mathrm{var}[\phi(x)], because the N independent terms add their variances and the \frac1N in front is squared.
1. An indicator with success probability q is a Bernoulli variable with variance q(1-q). So \mathrm{var}[\hat P]=\frac{q(1-q)}{N}.
2. With q=0.1, q(1-q)=0.09, so the standard deviation is \frac{0.3}{\sqrt N}. We need \frac{0.3}{\sqrt N}\le0.01, so \sqrt N\ge30 and N\ge900.
3. q(1-q) is largest at q=\frac12, where it equals \frac14. The worst case standard deviation is \frac{0.5}{\sqrt N}\le0.01, so \sqrt N\ge50 and N\ge2500.
4. The ratio estimator only learns about day 5 from samples where the condition holds. About 0.05N samples enter the numerator and denominator, so its effective sample size is about 0.05N: conditioning on a rare event makes the estimate much noisier.
Answer. (1) \frac{q(1-q)}{N}. (2) N\ge900. (3) N\ge2500. (4) About 0.05N.
Takeaways.

\mathrm{var}[\hat\Phi]=\frac1N\mathrm{var}[\phi], so the standard deviation falls like \frac1{\sqrt N}: halving the error costs four times the samples.
For a probability the variance is \frac{q(1-q)}N, largest at q=\frac12. Use that worst case when q is unknown.
A conditional estimate only uses the samples that meet the condition, so a rare condition shrinks the effective sample size.






Problem 4.3: Importance sampling by hand
A target on \{1,2,3,4\} is known only up to a constant: \tilde p=(1,1,2,4). The proposal is uniform, \tilde q=(1,1,1,1). Four draws from q come out as 4,4,3,1.

Compute the importance weights.
Estimate \mathbb{E}_p[x] with the self-normalized estimator, and compare with the exact value.
What does the average weight estimate, and what is its true value?







TipWorked solution





This reteaches Week 4, Importance sampling.
We cannot sample from p, so we sample from q and reweight each sample by how much more likely it is under p: \tilde w_r=\tilde p(x^{(r)})/\tilde q(x^{(r)}). Because both are unnormalized, we divide by the sum of the weights, which cancels the unknown constants.
1. With \tilde q=1 everywhere, the weight is just \tilde p(x): draws 4,4,3,1 get weights 4,4,2,1. Their sum is 11.
2. With \phi(x)=x,
\hat\Phi=\frac{\sum_r\phi(x^{(r)})\,\tilde w_r}{\sum_r\tilde w_r}=\frac{4\cdot4+4\cdot4+3\cdot2+1\cdot1}{11}=\frac{39}{11}\approx3.55.
The exact value uses Z_p=1+1+2+4=8: \mathbb{E}_p[x]=\frac{1\cdot1+2\cdot1+3\cdot2+4\cdot4}{8}=\frac{25}{8}\approx3.13. Four draws is a small sample, and none landed on 2, so the estimate is off; it converges as the number of draws grows.
3. The average weight estimates Z_p/Z_q. Here it is \frac{11}{4}=2.75, while the truth is \frac{8}{4}=2, since Z_q=1+1+1+1=4.
Answer. (1) 4,4,2,1. (2) \frac{39}{11}\approx3.55 against the exact \frac{25}{8}. (3) Z_p/Z_q: estimated 2.75, true 2.
Takeaways.

Each importance weight is \tilde p/\tilde q at the draw. Self-normalizing by the sum of the weights cancels the unknown constants.
The average weight estimates Z_p/Z_q.
The estimator converges as the number of draws grows, but a handful of draws can be far off.






Problem 4.4: Rejection sampling’s acceptance rate
Target \tilde p(x)=x(1-x) on [0,1]; proposal uniform on [0,1] with \tilde q(x)=1.

What is the smallest valid constant c?
What fraction of proposals is accepted?
Two rounds produce (x,u)=(0.2,\ 0.1) and (0.9,\ 0.2). Which are accepted?
If we had used c=1 instead, would the accepted samples still come from p? What changes?







TipWorked solution





This reteaches Week 4, Rejection sampling.
Rejection sampling needs an envelope c\,\tilde q(x)\ge\tilde p(x) everywhere. We draw x\sim q, draw u uniformly under the envelope at that x, and keep x only if u also falls under \tilde p.
1. \tilde p(x)=x(1-x) peaks at x=\frac12 with value \frac14. Since \tilde q=1, the smallest c with c\ge x(1-x) for all x is c=\frac14.
2. The acceptance rate is the ratio of areas, \frac{Z_p}{cZ_q}. Here Z_p=\int_0^1x(1-x)\,dx=\frac12-\frac13=\frac16 and Z_q=1, so the rate is \frac{1/6}{1/4}=\frac23.
3. With c=\frac14, u is drawn on [0,\frac14]. For x=0.2, \tilde p(0.2)=0.16\ge0.1: accept. For x=0.9, \tilde p(0.9)=0.09<0.2: reject.
4. Yes. Any c with c\,\tilde q\ge\tilde p gives exact samples; the proof only uses the envelope inequality. A looser envelope wastes proposals: the rate drops to \frac{1/6}{1}=\frac16.
Answer. (1) c=\frac14. (2) \frac23. (3) Accept 0.2, reject 0.9. (4) Still exact, but only \frac16 of proposals are accepted.
Takeaways.

The envelope needs c\,\tilde q\ge\tilde p everywhere, so the smallest valid c is the maximum of \tilde p/\tilde q.
The acceptance rate is the ratio of areas, \frac{Z_p}{cZ_q}.
A looser envelope still gives exact samples. It only wastes more proposals.

title: Midterm practice: Weeks 1–6
text:
Section 5: Conditional independence
Two hidden chains z_1\to z_2\to\cdots\to z_T and w_1\to w_2\to\cdots\to w_T evolve side by side, and each observation x_t has both z_t and w_t as parents.


  
  Two chains feeding each observation
  
    
    
    
    
  
  
    
    
  
  
    
  
  
    z1z2z3
    w1w2w3
    x1x2x3
  
  
    . . .. . .. . .
  


Figure 3. The DAG for Section 5, drawn for t=1,2,3. The pattern continues to T.

Problem 5.1: The factorization
Write the joint distribution p(z_{1:T},w_{1:T},x_{1:T}) implied by the DAG, with brackets to avoid ambiguity.






TipWorked solution





This reteaches Week 2, Directed graphical models: one factor per node, conditioned on exactly its parents.

z_1 and w_1 have no parents: p(z_1), p(w_1).
For t\ge2, z_t has the single parent z_{t-1}, and w_t has w_{t-1}.
Every x_t has the two parents z_t and w_t.

Answer.
p(z_1)\Big[\prod_{t=2}^Tp(z_t\mid z_{t-1})\Big]\;p(w_1)\Big[\prod_{t=2}^Tp(w_t\mid w_{t-1})\Big]\;\Big[\prod_{t=1}^Tp(x_t\mid z_t,w_t)\Big]
Takeaways.

One factor per node, conditioned on exactly its parents. Brackets make the range of each product unambiguous.
A node with two parents (here each x_t) gets a single factor conditioned on both, not two separate factors.






Problem 5.2: Eight independence queries
Answer yes or no, with the path or rule that decides it.

z_1\perp w_1?
z_1\perp w_1\mid x_1?
z_1\perp w_2\mid x_1?
z_1\perp w_2\mid x_1,w_1?
x_1\perp x_2?
x_1\perp x_2\mid z_1,w_1?
z_1\perp z_3\mid z_2?
z_1\perp z_3\mid z_2,x_1,x_3?







TipWorked solution





This reteaches Week 2, The Bayes Ball algorithm. Shade the conditioning set. A path is active only if every node on it lets the ball through: a chain or fork node must be unshaded, and a collider must be shaded or have a shaded descendant. The independence holds when every path is blocked.
The structural fact that decides most queries: the only connections between the z chain and the w chain run through some x_t, and every x_t is a collider (z_t\to x_t\leftarrow w_t) with no descendants.
1. Yes. Every path from z_1 to w_1 passes through some collider x_t. Nothing is shaded, so every collider blocks.
2. No. The path z_1\to x_1\leftarrow w_1 has one node, the collider x_1, and it is shaded, so the path is active. This is explaining away: once we see x_1, learning z_1 changes what we believe about w_1.
3. No. The path z_1\to x_1\leftarrow w_1\to w_2: x_1 is a shaded collider (open), and w_1 is a fork on this path (x_1\leftarrow w_1\to w_2) that is unshaded (open). The path is active.
4. Yes. The same path is now cut at w_1, a shaded fork. Any other route must reach the w chain through an unshaded collider x_t with t\ge2, which blocks. Every path is blocked.
5. No. The path x_1\leftarrow z_1\to z_2\to x_2 goes through a fork z_1 and a chain node z_2, both unshaded. It is active.
6. Yes. x_1 has no children, so every path out of x_1 starts through z_1 or w_1. Neither has a parent, so on any such path each is a fork (x_1\leftarrow z_1\to z_2, or x_1\leftarrow w_1\to w_2), and both are shaded. Every path is blocked at its first step.
7. Yes. The direct path z_1\to z_2\to z_3 is blocked at the shaded chain node z_2. Every other path detours through the w chain and therefore through unshaded colliders x_t, which block. This is the Markov property of a single chain.
8. No. Shading x_1 and x_3 opens a detour around z_2:
z_1\to x_1\leftarrow w_1\to w_2\to w_3\to x_3\leftarrow z_3.
x_1 and x_3 are shaded colliders (open), and w_1, w_2, w_3 are unshaded fork or chain nodes (open). In a single-chain HMM, z_2 would separate z_1 from z_3 whatever we observe; the second chain is what creates a path around it.
Answer. (1) Yes. (2) No. (3) No. (4) Yes. (5) No. (6) Yes. (7) Yes. (8) No.
Takeaways.

Chain and fork nodes block when shaded. A collider blocks unless it or one of its descendants is shaded.
Find the structural fact first (here, the two chains connect only through colliders x_t). Most queries then follow quickly.
Shading colliders can open a long detour around a node that would otherwise separate two variables, as in query 8.

title: Midterm practice: Weeks 1–6
section: Section 6: Markov chains and their stationary distributions
text:
Section 6: Markov chains and their stationary distributions
A two-state chain on \{1,2\} has transition matrix
A=\begin{pmatrix}3/4&1/4\\1/2&1/2\end{pmatrix}, \qquad A_{ij}=p(x_t=j\mid x_{t-1}=i).

Problem 6.1: Stationary distribution and convergence

Solve A^\top\pi=\pi for \pi=(\pi_1,1-\pi_1).
With p_t=P(x_t=1), write p_{t+1} in terms of p_t.
Show |p_t-\pi_1|\to0 as t\to\infty.
Starting from x_0=1, find P(x_2=1).







TipWorked solution





This reteaches Week 5, The stationary distribution and n-step transitions.
1. A^\top\pi=\pi says \pi_j=\sum_i\pi_iA_{ij}: the probability of being in j next step equals the probability of being in j now. Its first row is
\pi_1=\tfrac34\pi_1+\tfrac12\pi_2 \;\Longrightarrow\; \tfrac14\pi_1=\tfrac12\pi_2 \;\Longrightarrow\; \pi_1=2\pi_2.
With \pi_1+\pi_2=1, \pi=(\frac23,\frac13). As a check against the two-state formula with \alpha=A_{12}=\frac14 and \beta=A_{21}=\frac12: \pi_1=\frac{\beta}{\alpha+\beta}=\frac{1/2}{3/4}=\frac23.
2. To be in state 1 at time t+1, either stay in 1 or move from 2 to 1:
p_{t+1}=p_tA_{11}+(1-p_t)A_{21}=\tfrac34p_t+\tfrac12(1-p_t)=\tfrac12+\tfrac14p_t.
3. Subtract \pi_1=\frac23 from both sides:
p_{t+1}-\tfrac23=\tfrac12+\tfrac14p_t-\tfrac23=\tfrac14p_t-\tfrac16=\tfrac14\big(p_t-\tfrac23\big).
So |p_{t+1}-\pi_1|=\frac14|p_t-\pi_1|, and by induction |p_t-\pi_1|=\big(\frac14\big)^t|p_0-\pi_1|, which goes to 0. The factor \frac14 is 1-\alpha-\beta: the closer it is to 0, the faster the chain forgets where it started.
4. Apply the recursion twice from p_0=1: p_1=\frac12+\frac14=\frac34 and p_2=\frac12+\frac3{16}=\frac{11}{16}. Equivalently, (A^2)_{11}=\frac34\cdot\frac34+\frac14\cdot\frac12=\frac{11}{16}.
Answer. (1) \pi=(\frac23,\frac13). (2) p_{t+1}=\frac12+\frac14p_t. (3) The gap shrinks by a factor \frac14 per step. (4) \frac{11}{16}.
Takeaways.

Solve A^\top\pi=\pi together with \sum_i\pi_i=1. For two states, \pi_1=\frac{\beta}{\alpha+\beta} with \alpha=A_{12} and \beta=A_{21}.
For a two-state chain the distance to \pi shrinks by the factor 1-\alpha-\beta each step.
n-step probabilities come from iterating the one-step recursion, or from A^n.






Problem 6.2: Metropolis-Hastings with this chain as proposal
Use A as the proposal, q(x'\mid x)=A_{xx'}, to sample from the target p=(\frac13,\frac23) on \{1,2\}.

Give the acceptance probability for each of the four possible proposals.
Write the transition matrix of the resulting MH chain.
Check detailed balance with respect to p.







TipWorked solution





This reteaches Week 5, The Metropolis-Hastings algorithm and Why Metropolis-Hastings works.
The MH acceptance probability for a move from x to x' is
\alpha(x'\mid x)=\min\Big\{1,\ \frac{p(x')\,q(x\mid x')}{p(x)\,q(x'\mid x)}\Big\}=\min\Big\{1,\ \frac{p(x')\,A_{x'x}}{p(x)\,A_{xx'}}\Big\}.
1.

1\to1 and 2\to2: numerator and denominator are identical, so \alpha=1.
1\to2: \dfrac{p(2)A_{21}}{p(1)A_{12}}=\dfrac{\frac23\cdot\frac12}{\frac13\cdot\frac14}=\dfrac{1/3}{1/12}=4, so \alpha=\min\{1,4\}=1.
2\to1: the reciprocal, \frac14, so \alpha=\frac14.

2. A move actually happens with probability (proposal probability) times (acceptance probability); otherwise the chain stays put.

From 1: move to 2 with probability A_{12}\cdot1=\frac14; stay with \frac34.
From 2: move to 1 with probability A_{21}\cdot\frac14=\frac18; stay with \frac78.

R=\begin{pmatrix}3/4&1/4\\1/8&7/8\end{pmatrix}.
3. Detailed balance asks for equal flow in both directions: p(1)R_{12}=\frac13\cdot\frac14=\frac1{12} and p(2)R_{21}=\frac23\cdot\frac18=\frac1{12}. They match, so p is stationary for R. The two-state formula agrees: \alpha=\frac14, \beta=\frac18 give \pi_1=\frac{1/8}{3/8}=\frac13.
Answer. (1) Stay moves and 1\to2 always accepted; 2\to1 accepted with probability \frac14. (2) R above. (3) Both flows equal \frac1{12}.
Takeaways.

MH accepts with probability \min\Big\{1,\frac{p(x')\,q(x\mid x')}{p(x)\,q(x'\mid x)}\Big\}. Stay proposals always accept, and a move and its reverse have reciprocal ratios.
The chance of actually moving is proposal times acceptance. Rejected probability goes to staying put.
Check the result with detailed balance: equal flow p(i)R_{ij}=p(j)R_{ji}.






Problem 6.3: When the target is the chain’s own stationary distribution
Repeat the acceptance calculation of Problem 6.2 with target p=(\frac23,\frac13). What do you notice, and why?






TipWorked solution





This reteaches Week 5, Detailed balance.
For 1\to2: \dfrac{p(2)A_{21}}{p(1)A_{12}}=\dfrac{\frac13\cdot\frac12}{\frac23\cdot\frac14}=\dfrac{1/6}{1/6}=1. The move 2\to1 is the reciprocal, also 1. Every proposal is accepted, so the MH chain is A itself.
The ratio is exactly \frac{p(x')A_{x'x}}{p(x)A_{xx'}}, which equals 1 precisely when p(x)A_{xx'}=p(x')A_{x'x}: detailed balance. Every two-state chain satisfies detailed balance with respect to its own stationary distribution, so there is nothing for MH to correct.
Answer. All acceptance probabilities are 1, because A already satisfies detailed balance with respect to (\frac23,\frac13).
Takeaways.

The MH ratio is the detailed-balance ratio, so it equals 1 when the proposal already satisfies detailed balance with respect to the target.
MH only corrects a proposal where it is wrong for the target. If nothing is wrong, nothing is rejected.

title: Midterm practice: Weeks 1–6
text:
Section 7: Belief propagation
Binary variables x_i\in\{0,1\} sit on the tree below. Every edge has the potential
\psi_{ij}(x_i,x_j)=\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}
(3 when the two values agree, 1 when they differ). The node potentials, written as (\psi_i(0),\psi_i(1)), are \psi_1=\psi_2=\psi_5=(1,1), \psi_3=(3,1), and \psi_4=(1,3). We observe \bar x_5=1.


  The tree for Section 7
  
    
    
  
  
    
  
  
  
    x1x2x3
    x4x5
  
  observed: x5 = 1


Figure 4. The tree for Section 7. The observed node x_5 is drawn in the data colour.

Problem 7.1: Messages into x_3 and its marginal

Compute m_{5\to3}(x_3).
Compute m_{1\to2}(x_2) and m_{4\to2}(x_2).
Compute m_{2\to3}(x_3).
Compute p(x_3\mid\bar x_5).







TipWorked solution





This reteaches Week 4, Messages and beliefs.
The message from j to i multiplies j’s own potential, the edge potential, and every message j has received from its other neighbours, then sums out x_j:
m_{j\to i}(x_i)=\sum_{x_j}\psi_j(x_j)\,\psi_{ij}(x_i,x_j)\prod_{k\in N(j)\setminus\{i\}}m_{k\to j}(x_j).
We write each message as a vector (m(0),\,m(1)).
1. Observed leaf. Node 5 is observed, so its value is fixed at \bar x_5=1 and there is no sum. It has no other neighbours, so the product is empty:
m_{5\to3}(x_3)=\psi_5(1)\,\psi_{35}(x_3,1)=\big(1\cdot1,\ 1\cdot3\big)=(1,\ 3).
The evidence “x_5=1” pushes x_3 toward 1 by a factor of 3, because the edge rewards agreement.
2. Unobserved leaves. Now we sum over the leaf’s two values.
m_{1\to2}(x_2)=\sum_{x_1}\psi_1(x_1)\psi_{12}(x_1,x_2):\quad x_2=0:\ 1\cdot3+1\cdot1=4,\quad x_2=1:\ 1\cdot1+1\cdot3=4.
So m_{1\to2}=(4,4). A leaf with a flat potential sends a flat message: it carries no preference.
m_{4\to2}(x_2)=\sum_{x_4}\psi_4(x_4)\psi_{24}(x_2,x_4):\quad x_2=0:\ 1\cdot3+3\cdot1=6,\quad x_2=1:\ 1\cdot1+3\cdot3=10.
So m_{4\to2}=(6,10).
3. A node with several neighbours. Node 2 sends to 3 after hearing from 1 and 4, so both incoming messages appear in the product:
m_{2\to3}(x_3)=\sum_{x_2}\psi_2(x_2)\,\psi_{23}(x_2,x_3)\,m_{1\to2}(x_2)\,m_{4\to2}(x_2).

x_3=0: \;1\cdot3\cdot4\cdot6+1\cdot1\cdot4\cdot10=72+40=112.
x_3=1: \;1\cdot1\cdot4\cdot6+1\cdot3\cdot4\cdot10=24+120=144.

Dividing by 16 gives m_{2\to3}\propto(7,\ 9). Rescaling is safe: it multiplies every entry of the final belief by the same constant.
4. Belief. Node 3 has now heard from both neighbours, 2 and 5:
\tilde b(x_3)=\psi_3(x_3)\,m_{2\to3}(x_3)\,m_{5\to3}(x_3)=\big(3\cdot7\cdot1,\ 1\cdot9\cdot3\big)=(21,\ 27).
Normalizing by 21+27=48: p(x_3=0\mid\bar x_5)=\frac{21}{48}=\frac7{16} and p(x_3=1\mid\bar x_5)=\frac{27}{48}=\frac9{16}.
Answer. (1) (1,3). (2) (4,4) and (6,10). (3) (112,144)\propto(7,9). (4) p(x_3\mid\bar x_5)=(\frac7{16},\frac9{16}).
Takeaways.

A message multiplies the sender’s potential, the edge potential, and the sender’s other incoming messages, then sums out the sender.
An observed node has a fixed value: no sum, just the terms at the observed value.
Messages can be rescaled freely. Normalize once, at the belief.






Problem 7.2: The marginal of x_2

Compute m_{3\to2}(x_2).
Compute p(x_2\mid\bar x_5).
Recompute m_{2\to3} with the normalized messages m_{1\to2}=(\frac12,\frac12) and m_{4\to2}=(\frac38,\frac58), and confirm Problem 7.1’s belief is unchanged.
Which messages did p(x_3) need, and which extra ones did p(x_2) need?







TipWorked solution





This reteaches Week 4, Belief propagation on trees.
1. Node 3 sends to 2 after hearing from its other neighbour, node 5:
m_{3\to2}(x_2)=\sum_{x_3}\psi_3(x_3)\,\psi_{23}(x_2,x_3)\,m_{5\to3}(x_3).

x_2=0: \;3\cdot3\cdot1+1\cdot1\cdot3=9+3=12.
x_2=1: \;3\cdot1\cdot1+1\cdot3\cdot3=3+9=12.

The message is flat, (12,12): node 3’s own potential favours 0 by a factor of 3 and the evidence from x_5 favours 1 by a factor of 3, and these cancel.
2. Node 2 has three neighbours, so its belief multiplies three messages:
\tilde b(x_2)=\psi_2(x_2)\,m_{1\to2}(x_2)\,m_{4\to2}(x_2)\,m_{3\to2}(x_2)=\big(4\cdot6\cdot12,\ 4\cdot10\cdot12\big)\propto(6,\ 10).
Normalizing, p(x_2\mid\bar x_5)=(\frac6{16},\frac{10}{16})=(\frac38,\frac58). Only node 4’s preference survives.
3. With the normalized messages:

x_3=0: \;3\cdot\frac12\cdot\frac38+1\cdot\frac12\cdot\frac58=\frac9{16}+\frac5{16}=\frac78.
x_3=1: \;1\cdot\frac12\cdot\frac38+3\cdot\frac12\cdot\frac58=\frac3{16}+\frac{15}{16}=\frac98.

This is (7,9) divided by 8, so the normalized belief (\frac7{16},\frac9{16}) is unchanged.
4. With x_3 as the root, one inward pass suffices: m_{5\to3}, m_{1\to2}, m_{4\to2}, then m_{2\to3}. Node 2 also needs m_{3\to2}, which only exists once node 3 has heard from 5. That is one message of the outward pass.
Answer. (1) (12,12), flat. (2) (\frac38,\frac58). (3) (\frac78,\frac98)\propto(7,9), same belief. (4) Four inward messages for x_3; x_2 additionally needs m_{3\to2}.
Takeaways.

A flat message carries no information. Opposing pulls can cancel, as node 3’s potential and the evidence from x_5 do here.
Normalizing messages changes no belief.
Each new marginal reuses the stored messages and needs only the incoming messages not yet computed.

title: Midterm practice: Weeks 1–6
text:
Section 8: HMMs and variational inference
The practice midterm stops at Week 5, but Week 6 is examinable. These problems use the same short-calculation style. Problems 8.1 and 8.2 share one HMM with two hidden states \{1,2\} and binary observations:
\pi=\begin{pmatrix}1/2\\1/2\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \Psi=\begin{pmatrix}3/4&1/4\\1/4&3/4\end{pmatrix},
\begin{array}{c|cc}&x=0&x=1\\\hline z=1&3/4&1/4\\z=2&1/2&1/2\end{array}

Problem 8.1: Two steps of the forward algorithm
For observations x_{1:2}=(0,1), compute \alpha_1, \alpha_2, and p(x_{1:2}).






TipWorked solution





This reteaches Week 6, The forward algorithm.
The forward vector \alpha_t(j)=p(z_t=j\mid x_{1:t}) alternates two steps: predict by pushing the previous filter through the transition matrix, then update by multiplying in the new emission and normalizing.
\alpha_1\propto\psi_1\odot\pi, \qquad \alpha_t\propto\psi_t\odot\big(\Psi^\top\alpha_{t-1}\big).
Step 1. x_1=0, so the emission vector is the x=0 column, \psi_1=(\frac34,\frac12). Then \psi_1\odot\pi=(\frac38,\frac14), which sums to \frac58. Normalizing, \alpha_1=(\frac35,\frac25). The sum \frac58 is p(x_1=0).
Step 2, predict. (\Psi^\top\alpha_1)(j)=\sum_i\Psi(i,j)\alpha_1(i):
\begin{aligned}
\Psi^\top\alpha_1&=\Big(\tfrac34\cdot\tfrac35+\tfrac14\cdot\tfrac25,\ \ \tfrac14\cdot\tfrac35+\tfrac34\cdot\tfrac25\Big)\\
&=\Big(\tfrac{11}{20},\ \tfrac{9}{20}\Big).
\end{aligned}
Step 2, update. x_2=1, so \psi_2=(\frac14,\frac12). Multiplying entrywise gives (\frac{11}{80},\frac{18}{80}), which sums to \frac{29}{80}=p(x_2=1\mid x_1=0). Normalizing, \alpha_2=(\frac{11}{29},\frac{18}{29}).
Likelihood. Each normalizer is the probability of the new observation given the past, so their product is p(x_{1:2})=\frac58\cdot\frac{29}{80}=\frac{29}{128}.
Answer. \alpha_1=(\frac35,\frac25), \alpha_2=(\frac{11}{29},\frac{18}{29}), p(x_{1:2})=\frac{29}{128}.
Takeaways.

Forward step: predict with \Psi^\top\alpha_{t-1}, multiply in the emission vector entrywise, then normalize.
Each normalizer is p(x_t\mid x_{1:t-1}), and their product is the likelihood p(x_{1:t}).






Problem 8.2: Viterbi over three steps
For x_{1:3}=(0,1,0), run the Viterbi recursion with backpointers and give the most likely hidden path. Which state has the larger \delta_2, and is it on the final path?






TipWorked solution





This reteaches Week 6, The Viterbi algorithm.
\delta_t(j) is the probability of the best path that ends in state j at time t, together with the observations so far. It replaces the forward algorithm’s sum over the previous state with a max, and records which previous state won:
\delta_t(j)=\psi_t(j)\max_i\big[\delta_{t-1}(i)\,\Psi(i,j)\big], \qquad \theta_t(j)=\arg\max_i\big[\delta_{t-1}(i)\,\Psi(i,j)\big].
t=1 (x_1=0): \delta_1=\psi_1\odot\pi=(\frac34\cdot\frac12,\ \frac12\cdot\frac12)=(\frac38,\ \frac14).
t=2 (x_2=1, \psi_2=(\frac14,\frac12)):

j=1: candidates \frac38\cdot\frac34=\frac9{32} (from 1) and \frac14\cdot\frac14=\frac1{16} (from 2). Best is from 1, so \theta_2(1)=1 and \delta_2(1)=\frac14\cdot\frac9{32}=\frac9{128}.
j=2: candidates \frac38\cdot\frac14=\frac3{32} and \frac14\cdot\frac34=\frac3{16}. Best is from 2, so \theta_2(2)=2 and \delta_2(2)=\frac12\cdot\frac3{16}=\frac3{32}.

t=3 (x_3=0, \psi_3=(\frac34,\frac12)):

j=1: candidates \frac9{128}\cdot\frac34=\frac{27}{512} and \frac3{32}\cdot\frac14=\frac{12}{512}. Best from 1: \theta_3(1)=1, \delta_3(1)=\frac34\cdot\frac{27}{512}=\frac{81}{2048}.
j=2: candidates \frac9{128}\cdot\frac14=\frac9{512} and \frac3{32}\cdot\frac34=\frac{36}{512}. Best from 2: \theta_3(2)=2, \delta_3(2)=\frac12\cdot\frac{36}{512}=\frac{72}{2048}.

Backtrack. \delta_3(1)=\frac{81}{2048}>\frac{72}{2048}=\delta_3(2), so \hat z_3=1. Then \hat z_2=\theta_3(1)=1 and \hat z_1=\theta_2(1)=1.
At t=2, state 2 had the larger score (\frac3{32}=\frac{12}{128}>\frac9{128}), yet the best full path passes through state 1. A per-step choice can be overturned by later observations, which is why Viterbi keeps one candidate per state and only decides at the end.
Answer. Path \hat z_{1:3}=(1,1,1) with joint probability \frac{81}{2048}. State 2 has the larger \delta_2 but is not on the final path.
Takeaways.

Viterbi is the forward algorithm with a max in place of the sum, plus backpointers recording which previous state won.
Decide the path only at the end, by backtracking. The best state at an intermediate step need not lie on the best path.






Problem 8.3: KL in both directions
Let p=(\frac12,\frac12) and q=(\frac14,\frac34) on two states.

Compute \mathrm{KL}(q\,\|\,p) and \mathrm{KL}(p\,\|\,q) in terms of \ln2 and \ln3.
Now take q'=(1,0). Compute \mathrm{KL}(q'\,\|\,p) and \mathrm{KL}(p\,\|\,q').
Use part 2 to explain why the I-projection tends to lock onto one mode while the M-projection spreads out.







TipWorked solution





This reteaches Week 6, The KL divergence and Which direction? I-projection and M-projection.
\mathrm{KL}(q\,\|\,p)=\sum_zq(z)\log\frac{q(z)}{p(z)}.
The average is taken under the first argument.
1.
\mathrm{KL}(q\,\|\,p)=\tfrac14\ln\frac{1/4}{1/2}+\tfrac34\ln\frac{3/4}{1/2}=\tfrac14\ln\tfrac12+\tfrac34\ln\tfrac32.
Expanding, -\frac14\ln2+\frac34\ln3-\frac34\ln2=\frac34\ln3-\ln2\approx0.824-0.693=0.131.
\mathrm{KL}(p\,\|\,q)=\tfrac12\ln\frac{1/2}{1/4}+\tfrac12\ln\frac{1/2}{3/4}=\tfrac12\ln2+\tfrac12\ln\tfrac23.
That is \ln2-\frac12\ln3\approx0.693-0.549=0.144. Both are positive, and they differ: KL is not symmetric.
2. Terms with q'(z)=0 contribute 0 to \mathrm{KL}(q'\|p), so only the first state counts: \mathrm{KL}(q'\,\|\,p)=1\cdot\ln\frac{1}{1/2}=\ln2. In the other direction, the second state has p=\frac12 but q'=0, giving the term \frac12\ln\frac{1/2}{0}=+\infty. So \mathrm{KL}(p\,\|\,q')=\infty.
3. In \mathrm{KL}(q\|p), the I-projection’s objective, regions where q is zero cost nothing, so q may ignore part of p (here, a whole state) at finite cost. What it must avoid is putting mass where p is small. In \mathrm{KL}(p\|q), the M-projection’s objective, any region where p has mass and q has none costs infinity, so q is forced to cover all of p. On a two-mode target, the first behaviour gives a q that sits on one mode, and the second gives a broad q covering both.
Answer. (1) \mathrm{KL}(q\|p)=\frac34\ln3-\ln2\approx0.131 and \mathrm{KL}(p\|q)=\ln2-\frac12\ln3\approx0.144. (2) \ln2 and \infty. (3) The reverse KL tolerates missing mass, while the forward KL forbids it.
Takeaways.

KL averages under its first argument and is not symmetric.
\mathrm{KL}(q\|p) (the I-projection) lets q ignore parts of p at finite cost, so it tends to lock onto one mode.
\mathrm{KL}(p\|q) (the M-projection) is infinite if q misses any mass of p, so it spreads to cover everything.






Problem 8.4: Checking the ELBO identity
A latent variable z\in\{0,1\} and an observed x have p(x,z=0)=\frac18 and p(x,z=1)=\frac38.

Find p(x) and the posterior p(z\mid x).
For q=(\frac12,\frac12), compute the ELBO and \mathrm{KL}(q\,\|\,p(z\mid x)), and check that they add to \log p(x).
Which q maximizes the ELBO, and what is its value?







TipWorked solution





This reteaches Week 6, Tutorial: reverse KL and the ELBO.
1. Marginalize: p(x)=\frac18+\frac38=\frac12. By Bayes’ rule, p(z\mid x)=\frac{p(x,z)}{p(x)}=(\frac14,\frac34).
2. The ELBO averages \log p(x,z)-\log q(z) under q:
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{L}&=\tfrac12\Big(\ln\tfrac18-\ln\tfrac12\Big)+\tfrac12\Big(\ln\tfrac38-\ln\tfrac12\Big)\\
&=\tfrac12\ln\tfrac14+\tfrac12\ln\tfrac34=\tfrac12\ln\tfrac{3}{16}.
\end{aligned}
\mathrm{KL}\big(q\,\|\,p(z\mid x)\big)=\tfrac12\ln\frac{1/2}{1/4}+\tfrac12\ln\frac{1/2}{3/4}=\tfrac12\ln2+\tfrac12\ln\tfrac23=\tfrac12\ln\tfrac43.
Adding: \frac12\ln\big(\frac3{16}\cdot\frac43\big)=\frac12\ln\frac14=\ln\frac12=\log p(x). The identity \log p(x)=\mathcal{L}+\mathrm{KL} holds, and since KL \ge0, the ELBO is a lower bound.
3. \log p(x) does not depend on q, so maximizing \mathcal{L} is minimizing the KL, which is zero at q=p(z\mid x)=(\frac14,\frac34). There, \mathcal{L}=\frac14\ln\frac{1/8}{1/4}+\frac34\ln\frac{3/8}{3/4}=\ln\frac12, equal to \log p(x).
Answer. (1) p(x)=\frac12, posterior (\frac14,\frac34). (2) \mathcal{L}=\frac12\ln\frac3{16} and \mathrm{KL}=\frac12\ln\frac43, summing to \ln\frac12. (3) The exact posterior, with \mathcal{L}=\ln\frac12.
Takeaways.

\log p(x)=\mathcal{L}(q)+\mathrm{KL}\big(q\,\|\,p(z\mid x)\big), and \mathrm{KL}\ge0 makes the ELBO a lower bound.
\log p(x) does not depend on q, so maximizing the ELBO minimizes the KL. The bound is tight at the exact posterior.






Problem 8.5: One mean-field sweep
Two binary variables x_1,x_2\in\{0,1\} form an MRF with log-potential \phi_{12}(x_1,x_2)=2\cdot\mathbf{1}[x_1=x_2]. Initialize q_2=(\frac14,\frac34).

Update q_1 with the naive mean-field rule.
Then update q_2.
What is the exact marginal p(x_1=1), and what does this say about the mean-field answer after one sweep?







TipWorked solution





This reteaches Week 6, The coordinate update.
Each update replaces a neighbour by its average effect under its current q:
q_i(x_i)\propto\exp\Big\{\sum_{j\in N(i)}\sum_{x_j}q_j(x_j)\,\phi_{ij}(x_i,x_j)\Big\}.
1. For x_1, the inner sum is \sum_{x_2}q_2(x_2)\cdot2\cdot\mathbf{1}[x_1=x_2]=2\,q_2(x_1), because only the term with x_2=x_1 survives. So
q_1(0)\propto e^{2\cdot\frac14}=e^{1/2}, \qquad q_1(1)\propto e^{2\cdot\frac34}=e^{3/2}.
Normalizing, q_1(1)=\frac{e^{3/2}}{e^{1/2}+e^{3/2}}=\frac{e}{1+e}=\sigma(1)\approx0.731.
2. By the same argument, q_2(x_2)\propto e^{2q_1(x_2)}, so
q_2(1)=\sigma\big(2q_1(1)-2q_1(0)\big)=\sigma(2\cdot0.731-2\cdot0.269)=\sigma(0.924)\approx0.716.
3. The exact MRF gives weight e^2 to (0,0) and (1,1) and weight 1 to the two disagreeing pairs. Swapping 0\leftrightarrow1 leaves it unchanged, so p(x_1=1)=\frac12. After one sweep, mean field reports about 0.73 for x_1: it has inherited the lopsided initialization. Further sweeps drift slowly toward \frac12 here, but in general the coordinate updates converge to a local optimum that depends on where they start.
Answer. (1) q_1(1)=\frac{e}{1+e}\approx0.731. (2) q_2(1)\approx0.716. (3) Exactly \frac12; one sweep of mean field is still far from it because of the initialization.
Takeaways.

A mean-field update replaces each neighbour by its average effect under its current q, then exponentiates and normalizes.
For a binary variable the update is a sigmoid of the difference in expected log-potentials.
Coordinate updates converge to a local optimum that depends on the initialization, and one sweep can sit far from the exact marginal.

title: Midterm practice: Weeks 1–6
text:
Section 9: Miscellaneous

Problem 9.1: Cliques and blankets on a new graph


  The graph for Problem 9.1
  
    
    
    
  
  
    
    
  
  
    123
    456
  


Figure 5. The MRF for Problem 9.1.

List all maximal cliques.
Give the Markov blanket of node 4 and of the set \{2,3\}.
Is X_1\perp X_5\mid X_4? Is X_1\perp X_4\mid X_2?







TipWorked solution





This reteaches Week 3, Worked example: cliques, factorization, and independence.
1. Start from each triangle and try to grow it. \{1,2,3\} is a triangle; adding 4 would need edge 1\text{-}4, which is missing. \{2,3,4\} is a triangle; adding 1 needs 1\text{-}4, adding 5 needs 2\text{-}5. \{4,5,6\} is a triangle, and nothing else touches 5 or 6. Every edge lies inside one of these three, so there are no other maximal cliques.
2. In an MRF the blanket is the set of neighbours. Node 4’s neighbours are 2,3,5,6. For the set \{2,3\}, collect the neighbours of 2 (1,3,4) and of 3 (1,2,4) and remove 2 and 3 themselves: \{1,4\}.
3. Use separation. Every path from 1 to 5 goes 1\to\{2\text{ or }3\}\to4\to\cdots, because 2 and 3 connect only to 1, each other, and 4. Removing 4 cuts them all, so yes, X_1\perp X_5\mid X_4. For the second query, the path 1\text{-}3\text{-}4 avoids node 2, so 2 does not separate 1 from 4: no.
Answer. (1) \{1,2,3\}, \{2,3,4\}, \{4,5,6\}. (2) \{2,3,5,6\} and \{1,4\}. (3) Yes; no.
Takeaways.

Find maximal cliques by growing each triangle until an edge is missing, then check that every edge lies in some listed clique.
The MRF blanket of a set is the union of its members’ neighbours, minus the set itself.
X_A\perp X_B\mid X_S holds when removing S cuts every path from A to B. One path that avoids S is enough to answer no.






Problem 9.2: BP and variable elimination
On a tree, does belief propagation reduce to variable elimination? What does BP add?






TipWorked solution





This reteaches Week 4, Worked example: elimination on a tree becomes message passing.
Yes. Variable elimination on a tree, with the order running from the leaves inward to a root, produces at each step an intermediate factor over a single variable. Those intermediate factors are exactly the messages m_{j\to i}(x_i). One inward pass of BP is therefore one run of variable elimination for the root’s marginal.
What BP adds is reuse. Running variable elimination separately for each of the n nodes would repeat most of the sums. BP keeps every message, and a second, outward pass supplies the few missing ones, so all n marginals cost about twice as much as one.
Answer. Yes; the messages are the intermediate factors of leaf-to-root elimination, and the second pass reuses them to get every marginal at about twice the cost of one.
Takeaways.

On a tree, BP messages are the intermediate factors of leaf-to-root variable elimination.
BP’s gain is reuse: storing the messages gives every marginal for about twice the cost of one.






Problem 9.3: Three ways to use a proposal
Compare importance sampling, rejection sampling, and Metropolis-Hastings on: (i) what they produce, (ii) what they require of the proposal, and (iii) whether their outputs are independent.






TipWorked solution





This reteaches Week 4, Importance sampling, Rejection sampling, and Week 5, Why MCMC.










Importance sampling
Rejection sampling
Metropolis-Hastings




Produces
weighted estimates of \mathbb{E}_p[\phi], not samples from p
exact samples from p
a chain whose samples are approximately from p after burn-in


Proposal needs
a fixed q we can sample and evaluate; works best when q resembles p
a fixed q and a known c with c\,\tilde q\ge\tilde p everywhere
a conditional q(x'\mid x) that may depend on the current state; no envelope


Independence
the draws from q are independent
accepted samples are independent
consecutive samples are correlated


Weak point
weights vary wildly when q is far from p
acceptance rate Z_p/(cZ_q) collapses in high dimensions
slow mixing; must diagnose convergence



All three only need \tilde p, never Z_p.
Answer. Rejection sampling buys independent, exact samples at the price of a global envelope that is hard to find in high dimensions. MH needs no envelope, because its proposal can move locally, but its samples are dependent.
Takeaways.

All three need only \tilde p, never Z_p.
Importance sampling gives weighted estimates; rejection sampling gives exact, independent samples but needs an envelope; MH needs no envelope but gives correlated samples.
Each fails in its own way: wildly varying weights, an acceptance rate that collapses in high dimensions, or slow mixing.






Problem 9.4: Why Gibbs never rejects
Show that a Gibbs update of x_1 in a two-variable distribution p(x_1,x_2), viewed as an MH proposal, has acceptance probability 1.






TipWorked solution





This reteaches Week 5, Gibbs sampling.
The Gibbs move from (x_1,x_2) to (x_1',x_2) uses the proposal q(x_1'\mid x_1,x_2)=p(x_1'\mid x_2), and the reverse move uses p(x_1\mid x_2). The MH ratio is
\frac{p(x_1',x_2)\,p(x_1\mid x_2)}{p(x_1,x_2)\,p(x_1'\mid x_2)}=\frac{p(x_1'\mid x_2)p(x_2)\,p(x_1\mid x_2)}{p(x_1\mid x_2)p(x_2)\,p(x_1'\mid x_2)}=1.
We factored each joint as p(x_1\mid x_2)\,p(x_2), and every term cancels.
Answer. The ratio is exactly 1, so \min\{1,1\}=1 and every Gibbs draw is accepted.
Takeaways.

A Gibbs update is an MH proposal drawn from the exact conditional. Writing each joint as conditional times marginal makes the ratio cancel to 1.
This is why Gibbs sampling has no accept/reject step.






Problem 9.5: True or false on loopy BP

On a graph with cycles, loopy BP returns the exact marginals once it converges.
Loopy BP beliefs tend to be more confident than the true marginals.
Normalizing messages between iterations changes the fixed point.







TipWorked solution





This reteaches Week 4, Loopy belief propagation.

False. On a cycle, a node’s evidence travels around the loop and returns, so it is counted more than once. The beliefs are approximations, and the iteration may not converge at all.
True. That double counting is the over-confidence the lecture compares to hearing your own rumour back from someone else.
False. Scaling a message multiplies every entry of a belief by the same constant, which normalization removes. Normalizing only keeps the numbers from overflowing or underflowing.

Answer. False, true, false.
Takeaways.

Loopy BP counts evidence more than once around a cycle, so its beliefs are approximate and overconfident, and it may not converge.
Normalizing messages is only for numerical stability. It changes neither the beliefs nor the fixed points.






Problem 9.6: What each graph type cannot say
Give one independence pattern that a DAG can express and no MRF can, and one that an MRF can express and no DAG can.






TipWorked solution





This reteaches Week 3, What MRFs can express that DAGs cannot, and vice versa.
DAG only: the collider X\to Z\leftarrow Y, with X\perp Y but X\not\perp Y\mid Z. An MRF would need edges X\text{-}Z and Z\text{-}Y. With no X\text{-}Y edge, separation would give X\perp Y\mid Z, the wrong statement; adding the edge loses X\perp Y. In an MRF, conditioning never creates a dependence.
MRF only: the 4-cycle A\text{-}B\text{-}C\text{-}D\text{-}A, with A\perp C\mid\{B,D\} and B\perp D\mid\{A,C\}. Any orientation of the four edges without a directed cycle creates at least one collider, and conditioning on that collider makes its two parents dependent, breaking one of the two statements.
Answer. The collider (marginal independence that conditioning destroys) for DAGs; the 4-cycle’s pair of statements for MRFs.
Takeaways.

DAGs can express the collider pattern (independent until we condition on a common child). MRFs cannot, because conditioning in an MRF never creates a dependence.
MRFs can express the 4-cycle’s pair of statements. Every acyclic orientation of the cycle adds a collider that breaks one of them.






Problem 9.7: What detailed balance does and does not give
True or false:

If a chain satisfies detailed balance with respect to \pi, then \pi is stationary.
Every stationary distribution satisfies detailed balance.
Detailed balance guarantees the chain converges to \pi from any start.







TipWorked solution





This reteaches Week 5, Detailed balance and When is the stationary distribution unique?.

True. Sum \pi_iA_{ij}=\pi_jA_{ji} over i: the right side becomes \pi_j\sum_iA_{ji}=\pi_j, which is A^\top\pi=\pi.
False. Detailed balance is sufficient, not necessary. A chain that cycles 1\to2\to3\to1 with probability 1 has the uniform distribution as its stationary distribution, but \pi_1A_{12}=\frac13\ne0=\pi_2A_{21}.
False. The deterministic swap chain (A_{12}=A_{21}=1) satisfies detailed balance with (\frac12,\frac12), yet started in state 1 it alternates forever and never converges. Convergence needs extra conditions, such as regularity.

Answer. True, false, false.
Takeaways.

Detailed balance implies stationarity, but not the other way around.
Stationarity does not imply convergence from any start. That needs extra conditions, such as regularity.
